proposals.title: Lake Barebone
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: 3.8 mi. W of Agricola, 5.3 mi. SW of Dadeville
proposals.name_history: The name refers to the quantity of legal-sized fish in the lake
proposals.other_names: • Published names: o Oakwood Lake: StillWaters Residential Association (landowner) • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Lake Barebone is proposed for an unnamed 4.8-acre reservoir in Tallapoosa County. The reservoir lies along an unnamed tributary of an unnamed stream that flows into Martin Lake, 5.3 miles southwest of Dadeville. The proponent, a resident of Sterrett, states "I believe this feature deserves a name because the lack of a name can lead to confusion about the local lakes. Name origin/significance is due to the low numbers of legal-sized fish, despite the abundant quantity of juvenile fish." When asked to elaborate, he added "There are many minnows which are visible from the shoreline, but from many accounts, no success in catching [them]. Barebone is slang, but it just means not many fish, similar to barren. Less fish than there should be for a pond that size." The reservoir is owned by StillWaters Residential Association which labels it on a map as "Oakwood Lake." The proponent will attempt to get support from StillWaters Residential Association and wishes to pursue the proposal because they fish at the lake a few times a month and would like the reservoir "to have a unique name." The proponent owns property within the StillWaters Residential Association community. GNIS lists one other stream in Alabama named "Barebone": Barebone Creek (BGN 1937) is located in Sumter County, 145 miles west of the stream in question. ALASKA

proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Located E of Horseshoe Lake, W of Orchid Lake
proposals.name_history: The name is descriptive of the shape of the lake
proposals.other_names: • Published names: None found • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Feather Lake is proposed for a 45-acre lake in Matanuska-Susitna Borough. The proponent, who recently purchased land at the south end of the lake, reports that the name is descriptive of the shape of the lake and is also "a tribute to the local avian population that have called this area home for thousands of years." She notes also that "this lake is one of the only ones in the area that has remained unnamed, due to the fact that it is unsettled."

proposals.title: High School Peak
proposals.proposal_type: new associative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: On a hill within the City of Valdez, E of Mineral Creek
proposals.name_history: Named after a locally used name for a lookout and ridge SW of the peak that overlooks Valdez High School
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name High School Peak is proposed for a 4,210-foot summit in the City of Valdez and within the Chugach Census Area. The proponent stated: There is a minor lookout on the southwest ridge leading up to the proposed 'High School Peak' that is locally called 'High School Hill.' [The ridge begins at Valdez High School.] However, there is no local name for the larger peak that is very visible from the town. This peak is a popular destination for hikers, and it would be useful to have a standard name to refer to it by. It seems prudent to elevate the local name for the lookout to a more official level. When asked about his interest in naming the summit, the proponent responded that names "allow for easy communication between hikers about their experiences." He added: By proposing a name for this peak I simply hope to inspire more qualified people to continue naming land formations in the area, improving communication, increasing information, and fostering a stronger hiking community, thereby allowing more people to experience the beauty of the Alaskan landscape. This would also bring more tourism to the town, benefitting the local economy. Although the peak is not the highest on the ridge, he noted "It is also the easiest peak to access from the main town area and therefore is likely summitted the most." CalTopo labels the summit "Peak 3724." Local sources refer to the ridge below the summit as "Town Mountain" and some note that it is also known as "High School Hill." The Valdez Avalanche Center labels the summit in question "High School Hill," while the Alaska Avalanche Information Center refers to it as "Peak 3724/ Highschool Hill."

proposals.title: Change Lion Head to Natsede'aayi
proposals.proposal_type: change name to restore native name
proposals.feature_description: at the confluence of Caribou Creek with the Matanuska River

proposals.other_names: • Published names: o Glacier Point: USGS 1951, 1962; Shem Pete's Alaska: The Territory of the Upper Cook Inlet Dena'ina, 2016 o Lion Head: USGS 1948, 1952, 1962, 1976, 1979, 1993 o Lions Head: Shem Pete's Alaska: The Territory of the Upper Cook Inlet Dena'ina, 2016; Mat-Su Trails & Parks Foundation website, 2018 o Lion's Head: National Weather Service Advanced Hydrologic Prediction Service, 2022; Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway website, 2011; Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway Final Plan, undated; alaska.org website, 2022 o Lion's Head Mountain: Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway website, 2011; Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway Final Plan, undated o Natsede'aayi: Shem Pete's Alaska: The Territory of the Upper Cook Inlet Dena'ina, 2016; Ahtna, Incorporated website, 2021 o Nutsada'iy: Shem Pete's Alaska: The Territory of the Upper Cook Inlet Dena'ina, 2016 o Stone Woman: Mat-Su Trails & Parks Foundation website, 2018 o Tssisyu Ts'akae: Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway website, 2011; Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway Final Plan, undated • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Lion Head, a 3,150-foot summit, located on State lands in Matanuska-Susitna Borough at the confluence of Caribou Creek with the Matanuska River, to Natsede'aayi. The name, which is the Ahtna name for the summit meaning "rock that is standing," was proposed by the Tribal Administrator of the Native Village of Tazlina. The summit is a prominent feature along the Glenn Highway. The proponent states that the summit "is culturally significant to the Tazlina people as well as other tribal community members in the Copper River Valley." The Native Village of Tazlina is located about 75 miles to the east-northeast. The Tribal Administrator provided a statement from the President of the Native Village: I think Lion's Head should be changed back to the Ahtna name. My understanding about this mountain/rock is that Ahtna People used to and some probably still do pray before leaving our lands. The Ahtna name is Natsede'aayi [meaning] Rock that is protruding [or] Rock that stands. We believe that Natsede'aayi should be restored to the traditional name. USGS maps have shown the name Lion Head since 1948. Some smaller-scale USGS maps appeared to label the summit as Glacier Point; however, Glacier Point is shown on the edge of Lion Head on larger-scale maps and is recorded in GNIS as a cape. A Dictionary of Alaska Place Names (Orth, 1971) reported that Lion Head was "a local name reported in 1952 by USGS." Some sources have used variants of the official name, including Lions Head, Lion's Head, and Lion's Head Mountain. The latter two are used in Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway documents. The Ahtna name Natsede'aayi is reported in Dr. James Kari's 2016 Shem Pete's Alaska: The Territory of the Upper Cook Inlet Dena'ina where the translation is given as "Rock that is Standing" and notes that the name refers to "Lion Head, formerly called Glacier Point." The same source reports the Dena'ina name for the summit as Nutsada'iy, and that name is listed first. Dr. Kari provided the following notes from various authorities about the feature (bolding in original): • "Glacier Point at the end of Matanuska Glacier represents a Tcisyu [Tsisyu] and her baby who were coming from Chitina and turned to stone." • "Tsisyu ts'akaey [paint can women], three sisters started walking. One sister was packing a baby. They sat down and took a rest. They had left their country and I guess the lord has led them to an unknown country. So they sat down. All of a sudden they turned into big rocks, the sisters. Natsede'aayi, what they call it. . . ." • "One Ahtna informant cited the location of Natsede'aayi, which is a humped mountain called Glacier Point between the Glenn Highway and the Matanuska River near Sheep Mountain, where the present-day Indians believe that a Tsisyu woman and her baby were turned to stone. . . ." Natsede'aayi is also reported in a list of Ahtna Place Names in the 2014 Susitna-Watana Hydroelectric Project report with a translation of "rock that stands out." A 2010 paper by Dr. Kari, "The Concept of Geolinguistic Conservatism in Na-Dene Prehistory," reported the translation of Natsede'aayi as "rock that extends across." Glenn Highway National Scenic Byway documents reported that the summit has the Athabascan name Tssisyu Ts'akae, a variation of a term in Dr. Kari's Shem Pete's Alaska, but this text does not seem to indicate that "Tsisyu ts'akaey" is a name for the summit. The proponent noted that "[t]he Native Village of Tazlina agrees with Dr. Kari's position in the original name."

proposals.title: Northernmost Glacier
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: in the eastern part of the Shublik Mountains
proposals.name_history: the northernmost glacier known in continental North America
proposals.land_ownership: Arctic National Wildlife Refuge / Mollie Beattie Wilderness
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Northernmost Glacier is proposed for an approximately 55-acre glacier in the Shublik Mountains in North Slope Borough. The glacier is located within the Mollie Beattie Wilderness in Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The proponent notes that the glacier is "unique as the northernmost glacier of continental North American and proves prior USGS documentation wrong as existing 10 miles further north than they are said to exist." The proponent, who runs the Alaska Guide Co. based in Valdez, reported that he discovered the glacier in November 2022 by looking at satellite images to trace glacier outlines for his website's map of Alaska place names. A December 27, 2022 Anchorage Daily News (ADN) article about the glacier reported that when the proponent "moved to Alaska 15 years ago, he came across the Dictionary of Alaska Place Names (Orth, 1967). About 13 years ago, [he] started putting all locations from the book into a digital database to catalog the geography of Alaska. Today, [he] is still working on the same database." The database includes names not in GNIS, differences in official names, and already includes an entry for Northernmost Glacier. It notes that the glacier is "the northernmost above ground glacier in the United States. Named by [the proponent], 2022. A subterranean glacier was found next to Kaktovik [a community on the north coast of Alaska] in August 2008." The same ADN article quoted U.S. Geological Survey glaciologist Louis Sass as saying "It is the northernmost glacier in the U.S. It isn't registered or recorded." According to the article, Sass reported that glaciers from the Shublik Mountains were added to the Randolph Glacier Inventory in the 2000s but that "[w]e don't have the ability to manually verify that the inventory is correct or complete. This means that the existing inventory is likely missing hundreds or even thousands of glaciers." Sass also noted that although the glaciers in the Brooks Range don't get much precipitation in the winter, summers can be wet and the Sadlerochit Mountains and the Shublik Mountains extend further north and get more precipitation. The article referred to USGS Professional Paper 1386, "Satellite image atlas of glaciers of the world" (1988), which stated in Chapter K "Glaciers of North America - Glaciers of Alaska" that "Alaska's glaciers extend . . . as far north as lat 69°20'N., long 143°45'W., in the Brooks Range." The Shublik Mountains is often considered to be a part of the eastern Brooks Range. When asked to address the Wilderness Area Geographic Names Policy, which states that "The BGN will not approve proposed names for unnamed features within wilderness areas . . . unless an overriding need can be demonstrated by the proponent," the proponent replied that the name is needed because the glacier: • "is located in an area that has been labeled too arid in modern history for the formation of glaciers" • "is the northernmost glacier on the continent" • "has been overlooked and defies modern scientific opinion" • it "defy[s] existence especially in this era of global warming and the extinction of glaciers" ARKANSAS *** Note: the following proposal has been withdrawn; see Wahzhazhe Summit (Review List 451)

proposals.title: Buffalo Lookout
proposals.proposal_type: make official a name in local use
proposals.proponent: Dr. Richard Lanman; Los Altos, CA
proposals.feature_description: Highest point in the Ozark Plateau, in the Boston Mountains, in Ozark National Forest, 13.4 mi. E of Pettigrew
proposals.name_history: Named in association with other "Buffalo" features in the area
proposals.other_names: • Published names: Buffalo Lookout (peakbagger.com; listsofjohn.com; Wikipedia) • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Buffalo Lookout for a 2,561-foot summit in Newton County, 20 miles southwest of Jasper, within the Boston Mountains and Ozark National Forest. The proponent reports that the summit is the highest point on the Ozark Plateau and that the Buffalo Lookout Tower (fire tower) was once located at its peak. Although the proponent did not provide details on the history of the name, the Buffalo River and several of its named tributaries are located nearby. A stream named Main Prong Big Buffalo Creek flows within a mile of the summit. The name Buffalo Lookout is mentioned at the hiking websites peakbagger.com and listsofjohn.com, and at the Wikipedia entry for the Ozarks. The generic term "Lookout" is used for 23 summits throughout the U.S.; none are in Arkansas. CALIFORNIA

proposals.proposal_type: make official a name in local use
proposals.feature_description: In Klamath National Forest, N of the Klamath River, 22 mi. WNW of Yreka
proposals.name_history: The name refers to "the local 'legend' of the blue colored bears sighted in the area"
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Blue Bear Mountain for a 3,851-foot summit in Klamath National Forest and Siskiyou County, north of the Klamath River and 22 miles west- northwest of the community of Yreka. The proponent reports that the name is used locally and "there is a running story of the 'Great California Blue Bear' being sighted in the areas around Hamburg." He also referred to "the local 'legend' of the blue colored bears that the locals jokingly maintain live on that mountain." According to GNIS, there are 52 features in Siskiyou County with "Bear" in their names, including nine summits and three ridges. An additional 15 features, including three summits, are named "Blue," including Blue Mountain, 7 miles to the west of the summit in question. None of the features are named "Blue Bear," nor are there any elsewhere in California.

proposals.proposal_type: new descriptive name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: In San Bernardino National Forest, along Indian Creek 3 mi. W of Indian Mountain, 1.6 mi. SE of Angelus Hill
proposals.name_history: named for a heart-shaped pile of rocks at the top of the falls
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Hidden Heart Falls is proposed for an unnamed 33-foot-high falls in Riverside County. The falls are along Indian Creek in San Bernardino National Forest and 0.1 miles east of the boundary of the Soboba Indian Reservation. The proponent states "This waterfall is tucked away deep in the mountain range around a bend, making it very difficult to see by air, impossible to drive or ride to, and a challenging hike through a rocky riverbed to get to. The word heart derives from a pile of rocks forming a heart at the top." The proponent included a picture of the falls with the heart-shaped rock indicated. Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X

proposals.stakeholders: Local government Riverside County State Names Authority California Federal Agency U.S. Forest Service Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X The proponent owns property through which the stream flows, and states that he wishes to "pay homage to the Pacific Coastal Giant Salamander . . . [which are] native to the region [and] are often found in the cool clear waters of the creek." In researching the proposal, it was discovered that in the fall of 2022, California Water Boards sent the proponent two Notices of Violation for "recent tree and stump clearing and grading, without permits, and in a manner that threatens water quality," including deterioration of amphibian habitat along the stream. The first notice noted that a large mound on the property "was recently constructed reportedly to build a largescale mound feature in the shape of a salamander." When asked to address the issue, the proponent clarified that he assumed he was in compliance with the State's new (effective January 1, 2023) fire suppression regulations, which require that superfluous flammable material and debris be removed from around homes. He believed that clearing the property would be an appropriate way to address that need. With regard to the use of the disposed material, he referred to: The individual spiritual significance of the Salamander effigy mound and other land art features at Salamander Ranch. [We are] descendants of people indigenous to North America, [whose] culture has emphasized harmony with nature, endurance of suffering, respect, and non- interference toward others. During the Summer of 2022, [we] experienced a spiritual moment during deep meditative prayer at the site of the Salamander effigy mound. During this religious experience, a Salamander Spirit Guide came to [the proponent] and presented a vision of a mound rising from the Earth in the shape of a Salamander, emerging from the creek. The Salamander is a native species to the parcel. The Spirit Guide presented a vision that this [mound] would one day be a place where spiritual rituals such as prayer circles, rites of passage such as celebrations of birth, funeral ceremonies, celebrations of harvest and unions of holy matrimony and other spiritual ceremonies would take place there. The proponent proceeded to create the effigy mound, adding: On several occurrences during site visits, investigators from county, state, and federal agencies have openly verbally mocked, belittled, and openly disregarded any religious and spiritual significance when explaining to investigators the creation of the Salamander effigy mound. The First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States outlines clear protections to freedom of religion. We hold a deep reverence for this land and have to this date complied with full transparency and communication all deadlines for the development, implementation, and completion of all plans related to the stabilization and remediation of the land. He indicated he is hoping to develop the site into a park, with a sculpture garden and walking paths. He stated that there was no commercial enterprise related to "Salamander Ranch." The Klamath River Advocate with the Environmental Protection Information Center (EPIC), which "works to protect and restore ancient forests, watersheds, coastal estuaries, and native species in Northern California," submitted a letter of support, "provided that any tribes with ancestral ties to the land are consulted and are not in opposition." COLORADO

proposals.name_history: Named for Col. John Hughes (1922-2002), one of the most decorated veterans of the U.S. military, and a local community leader at Red Feather Lakes Village
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Mount Hughes is proposed for an unnamed 10,884-ft. summit in Larimer County and Roosevelt National Forest, approximately 35 miles west-northwest of Fort Collins. The proposal was submitted by a representative of the Red Feather Historical Society. The name would honor Colonel John C. Hughes (1922-2002), who is described by the proponent as "a longtime and illustrious resident of Red Feather Lakes Village. Col. Hughes is recognized as one of the fifty most-decorated veterans in American military history. Hughes fought in three wars -- WWII, Korea and Vietnam. He received 79 medals and citations, including two Distinguished Service Medals, five Purple Hearts, the Silver Star, the Bronze Star, and the Medal of Saint Maurice, the patron saint of infantry (his was medal #9. Bob Dole and Colin Powell received #7 and #8 respectively). He was also nominated for the Congressional Medal of Honor, but reportedly turned it down." Hughes was the most decorated serviceman in the 100-year history of the 29th Infantry Regiment, which in 2000 made Hughes an honorary "colonel commander for life." In 1954, Hughes bought a vacation cabin in Red Feather Lakes Village, "in the shadows of the summits," to which he moved upon retirement after 33 years of military service. "He quickly became a volunteer community leader, serving on the board of nearly every community organization. This included terms as President and Vice President of the Mountain Lion's Club, the Red Feather Property Owners Association, and the Red Feather Historical Society. He loved taking his sons hiking and fishing in the vicinity of the summit which we propose be named in his honor." The proponent notes that three of the four summits that comprise "the Baldies" (North Bald Mountain, Middle Bald Mountain, and South Bald Mountain) are named, but this summit is not and so the community believes it should be named. Col. Hughes' family still lives in Red Feather Lakes Village, which is also the location of Colonel Hughes Veterans Park. CONNECTICUT

proposals.submitter: Roger Barlow; Silver Spring, MD Date submitted same
proposals.proposal_type: change name and location to recognize local and historic use
proposals.feature_description: Between Lake Naraneka and Fox Hill Lake, SE of Seth Low Mountain
proposals.name_history: Named for John Barlow (1744-?), a blacksmith who had a forge on the north side of the mountain
proposals.land_ownership: Seth Low Pierrepont State Park Reserve / Town land / private
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Barrow Mountain in the Town of Ridgefield in the Western Connecticut Planning Region to Barlow Mountain and to correct its location to recognize local and historic use. USGS maps have labeled a ridge south of the Seth Low Pierrepont State Park Reserve as Barrow Mountain since 1951. However, the proponent, a resident of Ridgefield, reports that the name should be Barlow Mountain and that it applies instead to a 970-foot summit within the reserve and 0.75 miles north-northeast of its current position. Research shows that the name commemorates John Barlow (1744-?), a blacksmith who resided in the town from 1769 to 1802 and who operated a forge on the north side of the mountain and. He was known for shoeing horses along an early stagecoach road and for producing andirons. This information has been confirmed by an employee of the USGS National Geospatial Program whose surname is Barlow. A plaque on the summit cites the history of John Barlow and his smithy shop, and foundations of the old Barlow farm still exist in the woods within the State Park. Park trail maps refer to the summit in question as Barlow Mountain. Barlow Mountain Road, Old Barlow Mountain Road, and Barlow Mountain Elementary School are in the vicinity. A map published in 1935 on the occasion of the Connecticut Tercentenary shows the name Barlow Mountain. The existing GNIS entry for Barrow Mountain was obtained from the volume Connecticut Place Names (Hughes, 1976); this source also states "the name could be Barlow Mountain." Another volume, Ridgefield in Review (Bedini, 1958), refers to "Asproom Mountain (now Barlow Mountain)" and includes a short biography of John Barlow. The summit in question has been known by many names, most of which have been cataloged by a local historian. These include Aspetuck Mountain, Asproom Loaf, Loaf Mountain, and Sugar Loaf Mountain. The historian added, "there was never any place in Ridgefield called 'Barrow' anything. It was clearly some sloppy cartographer's error." If this proposal is approved, the ridge currently labeled as Barrow Mountain will be unnamed. The name in local use appears to be Stonecrest Mountain or Copps Mountain, but the proponent of the change to Barlow Mountain has declined to initiate a proposal for either of those names at this time. IDAHO

proposals.title: Candice Creek
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Heads in Boise NF, flows into small pond just W of Johnson Creek
proposals.name_history: The name means pure and shining
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None
proposals.case_summary: The new name Candice Creek is proposed for an unnamed 1.38-mile-long stream in Valley County; the majority of the stream flows through the Boise National Forest, with a small section at the mouth flowing into a small pond on the proponent's private property. The proponents state "[It is] a name that means pure and shining. A treat like candy for the wildlife that uses it year round. The aquifer queen of this side of the mountain feeding a pond with pure, shiny and sparkling water for a wildlife bath tub. #1 source of antimony in the U.S." When asked to elaborate, they added, "Antimony minerals have been part of the history in this area for 150 years. Credited for saving millions of lives during a forieng [sic] war in this country. The connection is antimony in the stream that feeds the pond on our property plus being a mineral that is needed for our future lowering the carbon footprint. Birth of the stream & pond most likely have been since 332BC here as long. It coincides with the name Candice and time of her realm of Queen, also Greek word meaning 'glowing.'" Antimony is a chemical element, i.e., a lustrous gray metalloid From online sources, "During World War II, antimony was key to U.S. production of tungsten steel and the hardening of lead bullets used in combat; at the time up to 90 percent of antimony demand was fulfilled through domestic production" and "Antimony is considered to be a 'strategic metal' and wartime applications include antimony oxide used as a flame retardant in plastics and textiles for vehicles and aircraft, antimony metal used in storage batteries and in ordnance to harden lead, and antimony tri-sulfide for primers in ordnance and rockets." Further research shows that "Candice" is an alternate spelling of Candace from the Bible and derived from Meroitic (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Candace). The reference to "332BC" appears to be to the era of the Ethiopian monarch Nikawla Kandake II (ruled 342-332 BCE).

proposals.title: Change Minneha Creek to Minnehaha Creek and South Fork Minneha Creek to South Fork Minnehaha Creek
proposals.proposal_type: change names to reflect correct history
proposals.feature_description: In Boise National Forest, flows into Mores Creek, 8.5 miles SW of Idaho City
proposals.name_history: A Siouan word meaning 'waterfall'
proposals.topo_map: Dunnigan Creek 1:24,000 State Idaho County Boise
proposals.land_ownership: USFS BGN decisions: None • Published names*: Minneha Creek (USGS 1969; USFS 1956, 1966; Boise County highway map, 2018; Idaho Place Names: A Geographical Dictionary, 1987), Minnehaha Creek (USGS 1894-1962) • Published names**: Fork Minneha Creek (Boise County highway map, 2018), South Fork Minneha Creek (USGS 1969; USFS 1956, 1966); Minnehaha Creek (USGS 1894- 1962) • Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Minneha Creek, a 5.45-mile-long tributary of Mores Creek in Boise County and Boise National Forest, to Minnehaha Creek. The proponent, a resident of Meridian, believes the name should be corrected because "historically the name was Minnehaha, the word Minnehaha has meaning (Laughing Waters or Laughing Falls), cultural significance (Native American name), and literary significance (popularized by Song of Hiawatha), [and] there is no meaning to the word Minneha --- it is but a meaningless truncation of the original name." The proponent did not mention South Fork Minneha Creek, but the staff is presuming the change applies to that name also. The primary stream was named Minnehaha Creek on USGS topographic maps from 1894 to 1962; however, on the 1955 edition of the 1:250,000-scale map and all editions of the 1:24,000-scale map since 1969, it has been labeled as Minneha Creek. It is not clear why the change occurred, and the BGN was not involved. U.S. Forest Service maps published in 1956 and 1966 also labeled the stream Minneha Creek, as did the 2018 Boise County highway map. Minneha Creek Road is in the vicinity of the stream. Lalia Boone, in her 1987 volume Idaho Place Names: A Geographical Dictionary, reported "Name was once Minnehaha, but somehow the final syllable was dropped. The gulch [sic] was the site of the Minnehaha way station, operated by F. Cooper in 1863. Minnehaha is Siouan, 'waterfall'". An Idaho State Historical Society account of the Boise - Idaho City Toll Road (1977) included references to "the bubbling, rippling waters of the Minnehaha," "Minnehaha" station, and "Cooper's Minnehaha Ranch." There is also a stream named Minnehaha Creek in Camas County. In Kansas, there is a community of Minneha and Township of Minneha. Kansas Place- Names, by John Rydjord (1972) noted "A community on the border of Sedgwick County was known as Minneha before its name changed to Midland, back to Minneha, then to Cloud or Cloud City, and finally to Andover [note: Andover is actually a different community a few miles to the east]. Minneha looks like Minnehaha and it evidently has the same Siouan meaning. The name in Kansas may well have come from Minnehaha in Minnesota." Minnesota contains a Minnehaha Creek and Minnehaha Falls.

proposals.name_history: Named for Woodrow Weeber (1912-2011), Glen Yoder (1916-1990), and Glenn Miller (1916-1996), all members of the 3rd generation of a family that has farmed the land since 1867
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None
proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Woodglenn Creek is proposed for an unnamed 5.48-mile- long tributary of Old Mans Creek in Liberty Township and Sharon Township in Johnson County. The proponent, a resident of Rock Island, is proposing the name in memory of three individuals who were all members of the third generation of their families to live and farm along the stream. The name is a combination of the names of Woodrow Weeber (1912-2011), Glen Yoder (1916-1990), and Glenn Miller (1916-1996). Mr. Yoder was a manager at the Sharon Telephone Company for 35 years and a member of a number of civic organizations in the area. Mr. Miller operated coin laundries and was a local businessman; his family's home, built in 1867, is still standing. The three men are all buried in Sharon Center Cemetery, close to the source of the stream. The name was originally proposed as Glenwood Creek, but a BGN member expressed concerns that the name "Glenwood" applies to a prehistoric culture that lived in western Iowa along the Missouri River; the present-day Pawnee and Arikara are descended from these people. She consulted with the Iowa Office of the State Archaeologist, who agreed that applying the name Glenwood Creek to a feature in eastern Iowa might cause confusion. The proponent agreed to amend her proposal to Woodglenn Creek.

proposals.case_summary: These proposals are to change the names of Free Negro Point (BGN 1980) and Free Negro Point Crevasse (a feature formed by a 1949 levee breach) in West Baton Rouge Parish to Wilkinson Point and Wilkinson Point Crevasse, respectively. The first proposal would recognize a local name used on some Mississippi River navigation charts. The cape is located on the west bank of the Mississippi River a few miles north of Baton Rouge. The bend in the Mississippi River adjacent to the cape is named Mulatto Bend, and Mulatto Bend Landing is listed as a populated place, as are many other landings along the river. This proposal does not address the "mulatto" features. Prior to 1963, the cape was labeled as Free N_ Point but was changed to Free Negro Point following the Department of the Interior directive to remove the derogatory word from Federal maps. In 1980, the BGN was asked by NOAA to address a discrepancy between USGS maps, which showed Free Negro Point, and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) maps and local navigation charts, which showed Wilkinson Point. The 1980 proposal noted that "Wilkerson [sic]" might have been a landowner on the point: "[t]here was a General James Wilkinson in late 1700s & early 1800s who participated in the transfer of Louisiana Territory in 1798." The current proposal was submitted by NOAA to recognize local use of Wilkinson Point, which has been shown as a variant on NOAA charts since 1999. The name likely refers to "Horace (born Horatio) Wilkinson [1817-1902] . . . a son of Joseph Biddle Wilkinson, who in turn descended from Gen. James Wilkinson, mentioned in the 1980 decision." His 1902 obituary in the New Orleans Times-Picayune (reprinted at the Find a Grave website page) reported that he was a country doctor, a sugar planter, and a member of the Louisiana secession convention. The current NOAA proposal also notes that he "may not have owned enslaved persons, and more research would be needed. No slaves are listed with his family in the 1850 or 1860 Censuses." The Interstate 10 bridge over the Mississippi River south of Free Negro Point was officially named the "Horace Wilkinson Bridge" in 1968 by the Louisiana Legislature to honor "three generations of the family [that] have served in the Legislature of Louisiana, including Horace Wilkinson, Sr., who was a member for twenty-six years; Horace Wilkinson, Jr., who was a member for sixteen years; and Horace Wilkinson III, who was a member for ten years." Most people call the bridge the "New Bridge" and there have been many attempts since 1968 to rename it. The names Free Negro Point and Mulatto Bend both derive from a community that was reportedly founded in the late 1700s by free or freed descendants of French and enslaved people of African descent. Another reported origin of the name Free Negro Point is that enslaved persons on the east bank of the Mississippi River, on the plantation that would later become the site of Southern University and A&M College, could escape to freedom if they swam across the river to land that was not part of the Louisiana Purchase. Various sources spell the name as Wilkinson Point or Wilkerson Point. A 2015 USACE chart shows both Wilkinson Point and "Wilkerson Point Boat Ramp." Mapcarta webpages for the features show the name "Free Harmony Point" and "Free Harmony Point Crevasse"; the origin of these names is unknown and they seem to have no local use. Blues musician Slim Harpo was born in the Mulatto Bend community and is buried at the cemetery there, still called Mulatto Bend Cemetery (sometimes called the Benevolent Society Cemetery), located at the south end of Mulatto Bend Road. Most of the community along the riverbank has reportedly been washed away. The populated place recorded in GNIS as Mulatto Bend Landing is located at the north end of Mulatto Bend Road. The landings along the Mississippi River should be reclassified as crossings in GNIS ("A place at which a river or stream may be crossed (landing, ferry, ford)." These landings appear to be places for barges and other boats to dock or anchor. MAINE

proposals.title: Change Negro Islands to Meguntic Islands
proposals.submitter: Shawn Blodgett; Castine, ME Date submitted same
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered derogatory
proposals.proponent: Town of Castine Selectboard; Castine, ME
proposals.feature_description: A pair of islands in the Bagaduce River northwest of Lords Cove
proposals.name_history: Named for the Penobscot word meaning "smooth area in choppy waters"
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Nego Island (The Dictionary of Maine Place-Names, 1970) o Negro Island (OCS 2000-2016; Blue Hill Heritage Trust, 2018) o Negro Islands (USGS 1902, 1904, 1905, 1941, 1943; OCS 1881-1993; Atlas of Hancock County, Maine, 1881) o N_____ Islands (History of Castine, Penobscot, and Brooksville, Maine, 1875)
proposals.case_summary: The Town of Castine Selectboard submitted this proposal to rename Lower Negro Island and Upper Negro Island, as well as the collective name Negro Islands, all located in the Town of Castine in Hancock County. The islands are located in the Bagaduce River. Lower Negro Island is a public preserve owned by Maine Coast Heritage Trust and is listed on the Maine Island Trail. Upper Negro Island is privately owned. USGS maps applied the name Negro Islands between 1902 and 1943; the islands were labeled individually beginning in 1973. The collective name first appeared on Office of Coast Survey (OCS) charts in 1881. It was incorrectly entered into GNIS as Negro Island; this name appeared on OCS charts after 2000 and on USGS maps after 2011. The Maine Coastal Island Registry lists both islands. The volume History of Castine, Penobscot, and Brooksville, Maine (Wheeler, 1875) used the more pejorative form of the name without applying names to the individual islands. The author wrote in a footnote: "Is it not possible that the name of these islands is derived from the 'Negew,' over which Edward Naylor had command, in 1662? There is no satisfactory tradition to account for the name of these islands." In 1970, Phillip Rutherford repeated this supposition as fact in The Dictionary of Maine Place-Names by reporting the name as Nego Island, explaining "For the 'Negew,' ship commanded by Edward Naylor, 1662." No connection could be found between the islands and the ship, which operated primarily in the nearby Penobscot River. The individual island names are proposed to be changed to Emanuel Island and Esther Island, respectively, and the name Meguntic Islands is proposed as the collective name. They resulted from a binding survey issued to voters in November 2022; the Town had engaged in a lengthy process to determine if the existing names should be changed, and then what the replacements should be. Emanuel and Esther are the names of two of the earliest known individuals of African descent recorded in Castine. They were likely enslaved. Their names were recorded in an account book kept by Colonel Gabriel Johonnot from 1785 to 1790, "showing names, occupations, and places of residence of those with whom he had business" (printed in The Bangor [Maine] Historical Magazine, Volume I, No. IV, October 1885 as "Castine and Penobscot Names, Etc."): • "Matthias Rich, merchant, wife and 'girl Esther.'" • "Richard Hunnewell, trader, and negro man Emanuel." Meguntic is an Abenaki word that reportedly means a smooth area of water within rougher water, or a "smooth area in choppy waters" and reflects the river at this location and the Native history of the area. When asked to comment on the original proposal, which was to replace the word "Negro" with "Bagaduce," in reference to the river where the islands are located, the Town decided to add the question to the May 2021 Town Warrant. By a vote of 44 to 33, the matter of changing the existing names was approved. The Town then established an Island Name Change Committee (INCC) "to conduct exhaustive research and community outreach." The INCC's voting members included a representative of the Maine Coast Heritage Trust, which owns Lower Negro Island, and the owner of Upper Negro Island. The Director of the Castine Historical Society served as the historical advisor. The committee was charged with the task of generating new suggested names to be considered by the Selectboard and, pending their approval, placed on the Town ballot at the November 2021 election. A request by a town resident to delay the decision resulted in a deferral until August 2022. The community was asked to vote on the matter in November 2022, with one of the options being "none of the above," which if selected by a majority of voters, would mean that the Town would officially take no opinion. The Town Manager commented that the INCC "met for over 15 months, held over 30 public mtgs, etc. which were open to the public for anyone to participate, give input and present additional options." In proposing the names Emanuel Island and Esther Island, the INCC noted "Historians have found no conclusive origin for the name. But [we] didn't want to erase the islands' connection with African Americans, no matter how hazy the association." The local historian confirmed that "the local lore that it was part of the Underground Railroad is a myth. The name predated and had no connection to the network of secret routes and safe havens used to get enslaved African-Americans to free states and Canada. Castine also wasn't a hotbed for abolition and the town had ties with the Southern slave economy and cotton trade - something that was typical of many Maine coastal towns with industries on the ocean." One local resident, who represents a group called Castine Friends, has expressed concerns regarding the Town's actions. He noted the low turnout, primarily because the vote was conducted when most property owners were away. He believes the change would "hide local history," adding "There is historical reference to the island being used by British Loyalists to shelter Negro Loyalists during the winter of 1783-84 when they were bound from New York City to Nova Scotia. They were on one of the last vessels to evacuate British forces and civilian Loyalists from NYC in November 1783. They were either British Army civilian workers or members of the British military unit called the Black Pioneers." His own survey showed that "most Castine residents do not want to change the name." He also cited recorded deeds with the name Negro Island dating back to 1785 and suggests a change would lead to confusion. An individual who owned Lower Negro Island for 50 years reports that he was always told "the island was a dropoff point for escaped Negro slaves, who would be hidden in the cellar of the house and by stealth picked up and transported to Canada. If nothing else, long periods of customary use should be sufficient to preserve the name." Lower Negro Island was donated to the Maine Coast Heritage Trust in 2014, and according to its land steward, "conversations about the name started pretty much right out of the gate . . . throughout this whole process, we've been actively listening and seeking feedback." Another local resident noted that the BGN had changed all occurrences of the N___ word to "Negro" in 1967 [sic] and therefore "there is nothing wrong with it." The vice chair of the INCC reported that he had spoken with a Maine Penobscot Nation elder who commended Castine for going through the process of making the change, but they "did not want to be involved or have the task of putting suggestions for changes onto them." MICHIGAN

proposals.title: Change Mino-kwe jiigibiik to Burns Landing Beach
proposals.submitter: Cait Sternberg, Big Bay, MI Date submitted same
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize local use and preference
proposals.feature_description: In Powell Township, along the S shore of Big Bay, E of Burns Landing Historical Park, 23 mi. NW of the City of Marquette.
proposals.name_history: Named in association with nearby Burns Landing
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Mino-kwe jiigibiik: USGS National Map; NOAA ENC catalog o Sq___ Beach: USGS 1954, 1985, 2011, 2019
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Mino-kwe jiigibiik, a 1.8-mile-long beach in Powell Township in Marquette County, to Burns Landing Beach. It was submitted by the Powell Township Board. Prior to September 8, 2022, the beach was named Sq___ Beach. On that date, the BGN renamed it to Mino-kwe jiigibiik, in response to a proposal from the Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force, which in turn had received the name from the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians. The Tribe reports that it means "good woman beach," adding "[The] Sault Tribe Repatriation & Historic Preservation Specialist met with staff members and Elders who speak the language on replacement names in the Anishinaabe language (Anishinaabemowin). The recommendation from community members and the Elders was to replace sq* with a culturally appropriate expression of womanhood. It is believed these places were name for association with Anishinaabe women and/or women's activities and we have replaced that term with respective words for women in various stages of life. Non- Native American alternatives further remove Anishinaabe from our landscape. The purpose of this renaming should be replacement with cultural place names rather than omission of Native Americans. Working with the language team we identified mino-kwe (good woman) . . . ." The Powell Township Board, in proposing a change to Burns Landing Beach, reports that it is the name already used locally and that it is associated with Burns Landing Historical Park, located at the west end of the beach. A small unincorporated community named Burns Landing is also located in the area. The name commemorates Charles Burns (1853-1932), who arrived in Big Bay in the 1880s and worked in the lumber industry, and as a fisherman and highway commissioner. Burns was married to a native woman named Margaret LeClaire, whose father Maurice (Morris) LeClaire (b. 1839) is believed to be the first person to have lived at Big Bay, having built a log cabin "a short jaunt away from Lake Superior" in 1860. Burns, along with his father-in-law, wife, and children are listed in the 1910 Federal Census as living in the Big Bay Boarding House. Although the origin of the name Sq___ Beach has not been determined, it has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1954. Following the September 2022 approval of the change to Mino-kwe jiigibiik, the latter name appears in the geographic names layer of the USGS National Map and in NOAA's electronic nautical chart catalog. MINNESOTA

proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Black Brook: An Atlas of the State of New York, 1840 o Negro Brook: USGS 1955, 1978, 1985, 1999 o N_____ Brook: USGS 1902, 1904; AMS 1948, 1951, 1953, 1961; Map of the New York Wilderness and the Adirondacks, 1879, 1890
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Negro Brook, a 15.3-mile-long tributary of Twobridge Brook in the Town of Franklin in Franklin County, to John Thomas Brook. The stream flows through property owned by Paul Smith's College. The proponent, a Paul Smith's College professor, states "the name is still considered by residents of the area to be derogatory and is frequently described as such . . . . This offensive name has also been a chronic source of inconvenience and embarrassment to Paul Smith's College, which owns headwaters of the brook in Onchiota and whose faculty have often expressed discomfort in having to explain the label to students and visitors." The proposed name would honor John Thomas (1810-1894), one of the first African Americans to settle in the area around the stream. He was born enslaved in Maryland and escaped to New York in 1840. He accepted a plot of land from abolitionist and philanthropist Gerrit Smith who gave 120,000 acres of his land in the Adirondacks to Black pioneers in the area. Mr. Thomas later purchased a farm near the mouth of the stream, where he and his wife Mary raised two daughters. He died there and is buried in a local cemetery. An obituary at the time stated that "Mr. Thomas was an honest, upright and fair dealing man, a good citizen and much respected in the community where he lived so long." The proponent also reported the following: In 1872, Mr. Thomas sent a letter to Gerrit Smith . . . . "I have breasted the storm of prejudice and opposition," he wrote, "until I begin to be regarded as an American citizen." In the diary of Rainbow Lake hotelier James Wardner . . . the writer told pathetically racist anecdotes about a "Negro Thomas" who lived nearby. In contrast, local lore has it that when Mr. Thomas' former enslaver Ezekiel Merrick sent bounty- hunters to recapture him Adirondack residents helped drive the intruders away. James Wardner's diary also described the community of Black farmers in Vermontville, some of whom tended onion gardens beside a stream that thereby became known as "N_____ Brook." USGS first labeled the stream as N_____ Brook in 1902 and began showing the name Negro Brook in 1955. An 1840 Franklin County map used the name Black Brook. Commercial maps from the Late 1800s used the name N_____ Brook. An 1876 Franklin County atlas does not label the stream but shows the residence of "J. Thomas" nearby. A summit named Negro Mountain is located near the mouth of the stream; the proponent is working with the local groups to develop a proposal to change its name. NORTH CAROLINA

proposals.proposal_type: to make official a name in local use
proposals.proponent: Boyce Allen Hudson II; Holly Springs, NC
proposals.feature_description: located along the north shore of the Pamlico River just E of Mare Point
proposals.name_history: Named for the "bluebill," the duck hunters' term for the Greater Scaup/Lesser Scaup, which is common in the winter along coastal rivers and sounds
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: Bluebill Hill (proponent)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Bluebill Hill for a bluff located along the north shore of the Pamlico River, just east of Mare Point, in Beaufort County. The bluff is approximately 0.3 miles long with an elevation of 17 feet. The proponent, who owns one of several properties on the bluff, reports that the name has been used locally since the 1980s and that "the bluebill is a species of waterfowl known to frequent the beaches, surrounding area, and [the] hill itself. [The name has] represented the town and the population of Waterfowlers and hunters that have resided on the hill for generations." Research shows that "bluebill" is a term used by duck hunters for the Greater Scaup/Lesser Scaup, which is very common in the winter along coastal rivers and sounds. An online search shows that a sign at the property reads "Bluebill Hill." There are no other features in North Carolina named "Bluebill."

proposals.name_history: Named for the Skinner family, who are among the oldest and most prominent ranching families in the region, specifically, Silas Skinner (d. 1886) who in 1866 built a 70- mile-long toll road from Silver City, ID to the Owyhee River
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None
proposals.case_summary: This proposal, forwarded by the Oregon Geographic Names Board, is to make official the name Skinner Hill for a 4,528-foot basalt butte in the Jordan Valley in Malheur County and on land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The name is intended to commemorate the Skinner family, who according to the proponent are among the oldest and most prominent ranching families in the region, specifically, Silas Skinner (d. 1886) who in 1866 built a 70-mile-long toll road from Silver City, Idaho through the Jordan Valley to the Owyhee River. An extensive account of the toll road is available at http://skinnerfamilynw.org/history/Skinner%20Toll%20Road.htm. The proponent reports that between 1978 and 1983, he studied the stratigraphy of the Jordan Valley, where he camped at the Skinner Ranch and "developed a lasting friendship with the Skinner family, and [from them] gained invaluable insights on the southeast Oregon geography, roads, and people." In the February 1983 edition of Oregon Geology newsletter, he referred to the feature and described a volcanic flow as being "east of Rocky Butte (Skinner Hill)." There is no listing in GNIS for Rocky Butte at this location, although another summit named Rocky Butte is located 20 miles to the north and also in Malheur County. Skinner Ranch and Skinner Road are located a few miles to the south of the summit in question, while the 1969 USGS topographic map of the area also depicted Skinner Ranch Airport and Skinner Dam.

proposals.title: Mushpekat Run
proposals.proposal_type: make official a name in recent local use
proposals.feature_description: heads near the northeast end of the North Valley Hills, flows generally northeast into Pickering Creek
proposals.name_history: In local use since 2014; "mushpekat" is Lenape for "clear water"
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: o Mushpekat Run (Charlestown Township, since 2014) • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Mushpekat Run is proposed for an unnamed 2.4-mile-long tributary of Pickering Creek in Charlestown Township in Chester County. According to the county's records, the current owner of the property is the Great Valley Nature Center. In 2014, a local middle school student service group, the Kids Leadership Academy, asked the Charlestown Township Board of Supervisors for permission to name the stream. According to the April 7, 2014 Charlestown Township Board of Supervisors Business Meeting Minutes, the Supervisors encouraged the students to choose a name. "Mushpekat was chosen because the Lenape name translates to Clear Water Run." A member of the Charlestown Township Environmental Advisory Committee submitted this proposal to the BGN, noting: Since becoming aware of the proposed naming of the stream [in 2014] I wondered if the process for officially naming the stream had ever been undertaken. I contacted the original adult leader of the Kids Leadership Academy to inquire what the status of the naming was and was informed that she had looked at the process and it seemed daunting and never followed up with requesting the formal naming. . . . The proponent adds: We believe that all streams should be named because without a name they are not recognized, they are overlooked. Many are not mapped. How can we protect something that doesn't appear on a map or have a name? Head water streams such as this one are extremely important. They are the very sources of clean cold water. This stream is a wild trout nursery and a source for drinking water. If it is not named how can it be regulated and protected. People must know of its existence and its special attributes. SOUTH CAROLINA

proposals.title: Change Lake Pelham to Lake Culpeper
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive
proposals.feature_description: SW of the Town of Culpeper, N of U.S. Hwy 29
proposals.name_history: Named for the nearby community of Culpeper
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Lake Pelham: USGS 1979, 1986, 1997 o Pelham Lake: USGS National Water Information System, 2022 o Pelham Reservoir: Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources, 2022
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Lake Pelham, an approximately 250-acre reservoir in Culpeper County and just outside the corporate boundary of the Town of Culpeper, to Lake Culpeper. The reservoir was constructed in 1972 and is owned by the Town of Culpeper and used as its water source. The proposal was submitted by the Town of Culpeper Department of Community Development. The change was approved by the Town Council on October 11, 2022 by a vote of 5-4. The proposal states that "The existing name of Lake Pelham stems from an Alabama-native Confederate soldier, Major John Pelham. The Town would prefer that the name of the reservoir not stem from a divisive individual. The name 'Lake Culpeper' is felt to be more representative of the entire community." According to the October 11, 2022 Town Council minutes: • on February 9, 2021, the Council approved a motion to rename the reservoir and referred the item to the Light & Power and Environmental Services Committee to initiate the process for a name change. • on May 11, 2021, the Council did not approve a motion to change the name to Lake Culpeper, a name recommended by the Light & Power and Environmental Services Committee • on September 27, 2022, the Public Safety, Public Works, Planning & Community Development Committee passed a motion to recommend the name change to the Town Council Many local news articles cited comments from council members and the public, both for and against the change. They also referenced a 1975 Culpeper Star-Exponent article which stated that the name Lake Pelham had been selected through a contest sponsored by the Town and the Culpeper Soil and Water Conservation Service. John Pelham (1838-1863) was an artillery officer under J.E.B. Stuart who was mortally injured in the 1863 Battle of Kelly's Ford and died from his injuries at the Culpeper courthouse. Culpeper and the surrounding area have several historic markers noting Pelham's life and participation in nearby battles. Culpeper County was chartered in 1749 and was named for Lord Thomas Colepeper (often spelled as Culpeper) (1635-1689), the Colonial Governor of Virginia from 1677 to 1683. The Town of Culpeper was originally chartered as the Town of Fairfax in 1759 and renamed by the Virginia General Assembly in 1869. The USACE National Inventory of Dams lists the reservoir's dam name as "Mountain Run Dam #50" with an alternate name of Lake Pelham. The Town of Culpeper owns and operates a boat rental business near the dam, which will have new signs in the 2023 season showing the name "Lake Culpeper Adventures" in place of the existing "Lake Pelham Adventures." The Town plans to spend $9,000 to change reservoir signs. The Town has no plans to rename or remove any other reference to Major Pelham. A neighborhood north of Culpeper is named Pelham Manor and is recorded in GNIS as a populated place. The streets of the neighborhood are named after Confederate generals. The Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources uses the name Pelham Reservoir. The USGS National Water Information System refers to a water monitoring station at the reservoir as Pelham Lake.

proposals.title: Change Pine Mountain to Piney Mountain
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize local and historic use
proposals.feature_description: Located partly within Shenandoah National Park, between Pass Run and North Fork Dry Run on the W side of the Blue Ridge E of Luray
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: o Piney Mountain: historical and local use, reported by proponent • Published names: o Pine Mountain: USGS 1933, 1965, 1986, 1994
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Pine Mountain (BGN 1933), located between Luray and Thornton Gap in Page County, to Piney Mountain. The summit is partly in Shenandoah National Park. The proponent, who lives on the southwestern edge of the summit, is proposing that the BGN "restore the correct historical legal name to this geological feature." He states that Piney Mountain is shown in historical records and in his property's land deeds from 1886 and 1890 and that "[r]esidents even today call the mountain 'Piney Mountain' and not 'Pine Mountain' (a name locals consider wrong)." He also states, "It seems likely the current name is a typographical error when the USGS database was first created (typist failed to type the 'y' at the end of the name)." Piney Mountain Road is located on the western side of the mountain. Pine Mountain (FID 1472363) (BGN 1933) and Piney Mountain (FID 1472410) (BGN 1933) The name Pine Mountain was a 1933 BGN decision for the summit in question. The decision card notes that Pine Mountain was shown on "U.S. Geol. Survey map of 'Proposed Shenandoah National Park' sheet 4, 1927-1929" and that the locally used name based on a "field c[hec]k" was Pine Mountain. At the same 1933 meeting, the BGN also approved the names Pine Mountain for a 2,100-foot summit in southern Page County and Piney Mountain for a 2,076-foot summit in adjacent Rockingham County. Both of these names were also shown on the "Proposed Shenandoah National Park" maps and are about 18 miles southwest of the summit in question. The name Pine Mountain for the summit in question was first shown on the 1929 advance sheet copy of the USGS 1:48,000-scale Stone Man quadrangle. The name Piney Hill was shown for a summit 1.8 miles to the southwest but was not a BGN decision. These names have been consistently shown on large-scale USGS maps beginning in 1933. Pine Mountain (FID 1496198) (BGN 1933) and Piney Hill (FID 1486249) A ridge named Piney Mountain in Page County was first shown on a 1967 1:24,000-scale USGS map and is located 12 miles southwest of the summit in question. Public Law 86-775, passed in 1960, used the name Piney Mountain for the summit in reference to a Shenandoah National Park property exchange. The Park's headquarters is located on a parcel of Park land on the northeastern slope of the mountain. Henry Gannett's 1904 The Gazetteer of Virginia reported a Piney Mountain in Page County with an elevation of 1,500 feet. None of the summits in Page County with "Pine" or "Piney" in their names have a similar elevation, so it is unclear which summit this refers to. WASHINGTON

proposals.proposal_type: amend the application to reflect local use
proposals.feature_description: heads at the end of Hopkins Ditch (q.v.), 2.5 miles WNW of South Union
proposals.name_history: local name of unknown origin, presumably for salmon in stream
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Salmon Creek (USGS 1916, 1944, 1949, 1959, 1980, 1990; AMS 1958, 1962, 1964; Metsker's Thurston County Map, 1946, 1970; Metsker's Thurston County Atlas, 1962, 1973, 1977, 1985)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to rename and reclassify a portion of a stream that is currently named Salmon Creek. The stream is a tributary of the Black River in Thurston County. USGS maps have consistently labeled its entire 11.5-mile-long length as Salmon Creek, a name that was also used on Metsker maps from 1942 until the 1980s. However, if approved, the proposal would result in a new entry in GNIS for Hopkins Ditch (7.3 miles long and classified in GNIS as canal) and limit the name Salmon Creek to the 3.8- mile-long stream below Jones Road. According to the proponent, who is one of the commissioners of the Hopkins Drainage Ditch District #2, this would recognize the names in local use since 1878. The drainage district has operated the ditch as Hopkins Ditch since 1904. The origin of the name has not been determined, although an online search shows that there were individuals named Hopkins in Thurston County as early as the 1870s, including in the area of Littlerock, two miles south of the mouth of the stream. In 1892, Frank and Josiah Hopkins acquired property a few miles to the south of the area in question. The name Hopkins Ditch appears in many sources, including a listing of emergency projects funded by the Washington Department of Ecology; a 2008 Salmon Recovery Portal published by the Washington State Recreation and Conservation Office (referencing "a barrier culvert on a tributary to Hopkins AKA Salmon Creek"); a 2021 City of Tumwater and Thurston County Joint Plan draft update; a 2009 Thurston County proposed land use plan and rezoning amendment; and a 2004 business report that stated "Hopkins Ditch runs through the south end of the property." The name also appears in a number of news articles.

proposals.submitter: Washington Committee on Geographic Names

proposals.feature_description: In Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, on Twin Sisters Mountain, 9.8 miles SW of the peak of Mount Baker

proposals.other_names: • Harvey Peak (Cascade Alpine Guide, Beckey, 2008; listsofjohn.com)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new commemorative name Kloke Peak to a 6,506-foot peak on Twin Sisters Mountain in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Whatcom County, 9.8 miles southwest of the peak of Mount Baker. The proposal was submitted by the Washington Committee on Geographic Names on behalf of the President of the Skagit Mountain Rescue Unit. The name would commemorate Dallas Kloke (1939-2010), who was active in the climbing community and who put up twelve new routes from the 1960s to the 1980s in the Twin Sisters Mountains; he first summited the peak in question in September 1972. According to the proposal, "Dallas was active in developing hundreds of sport climbs at Mount Erie and other crags, was the mastermind behind dozens of first ascents in the Cascades, devoted countless hours to coaching high school track, organized running races in and around Fidalgo Island, and was a case worker for the Society of St. Vincent de Paul. proposals.title: Change Gathering Creek to Noskeliikuu
proposals.submitter: Washington Committee on Geographic Names Date submitted 1/26/23
proposals.proposal_type: change a name to reflect Tribal name
proposals.feature_description: In Olympic National Park / Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, flows into the North Fork Quinault River between Elip Creek and Wild Rose Creek
proposals.name_history: Quinault name for the feature which means "the place where the whale dropped," referencing an event witnessed there
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Gathering Creek: Secretary's Order 3404 Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force name changes announcement and media coverage, 2022 o Sq___ Creek: USGS 1947, 1950, 1988, 1990
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Gathering Creek, a 0.75-mile-long tributary of the North Fork Quinault River in Jefferson County, to Noskeliikuu. The stream is located in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness in Olympic National Park. In April 2022, in response to Secretary's Order 3404, the Washington Committee on Geographic Names (WCGN) solicited input from Tribes and other interested parties. In June 2022, the Quinault Indian Nation submitted the name Noskeliikuu to the WCGN and it was approved by the Washington Board of Natural Resources in January 2023. The Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force received the name Gathering Creek through public comment, and it was approved by the BGN in September 2022. (The Task Force also recommended that another "sq___" feature, in Oregon, be changed to Gathering Creek; this name was recommended by the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon.) The name Noskeliikuu was proposed by the Quinault Indian Nation's Historic Preservation Technician, who reported: • This area is known to have been used by the Native Americans of the area for their seasonal rounds. Many important high elevation medicinal plants might be found at this elevation and only collected during the summer months. It is possible that the [Seattle Washington Press Expedition in 1889-1890] or other historic colonial-settler may have seen a Native American gathering. The Olympic National Park historian . . . researched the origin of the name but we have not heard back. The name has been used in oral histories for at least four generations by Quinault Tribal members. • The current name is based in racism towards the People of the area and we are replacing this derogatory name with an event place name from the language of the People. • "This proposed name change has been vetted through the Quinault Cultural Advisory Committee, the Natural Resources and Community Development subcommittee, [and] advised by appropriate cultural leaders. • Noskeliikuu basically means 'the place where the whale dropped' . . . an event witnessed by Quinault ancestors in the area and was named for the actual event. 'nos' roughly translates to 'place' in Quinault so that signifies that were talking about a place.

proposals.title: Change Reads Bay to Reeds Bay
proposals.submitter: Washington State Geographic Names Committee Date submitted 1/26/23
proposals.proposal_type: correct spelling to reflect honoree's name
proposals.feature_description: on the SW side of Decatur Island
proposals.name_history: named for the Reed family who settled and lived on the bay, specifically Mary Tacee (1846-1918) and John P. Reed (1831-1895), who moved there in 1867
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Reads Bay: USGS 1943, 1957, 1973, 1975, 1998; OCS 1979-present; Metsker's Map/Atlas of San Juan County, 1933, 1949, 1961, 1970, 1994 o Reed Bay: Journal of Northwest Anthropology Vol 48 No 1; local real estate listings o Reeds Bay: local real estate listings
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the spelling of Reads Bay, located on the southwestern side of Decatur Island in San Juan County, to Reeds Bay. According to the proponent, a local resident, the latter spelling is in local use and refers to the Reed family that has lived along the bay since the 1860s. Mary Tacee (1846-1918) and John P. Reed (1831-1895) moved to Decatur Island and built a cabin there. They were reportedly the first settlers on the island. (Their daughter Mary married Henry Cayou, for whom Cayou Channel (BGN 2022) is named.) Online sources list Mrs. Reed as Mary Tacee "Little Bird" Weldon Gustoff Reed and report that • Tacee means 'Little Bird.' • Mary was the niece of Chief Shaksh 'Chief Seattle' of the Wrangell, Alaska Tlingit tribe, and a slave of the Tlingits [who] escaped to Victoria. • Tlingit Indians attempted to take Mrs. Reed back but her husband holed up in the cabin [where they lived] and scared them off with his rifle. The cabin is now Decatur Island Community Centre, restored in 1970. • On Decatur, no one spoke of Mrs. John P. Reed or Mary Reed or Tacee Reed, but of 'Grandmother Reed.' By this, she was always lovingly referred to by all of the island residents. Much of this information came from Native American Wives of San Juan Settlers, written by a relative of the proponent. USGS maps have labeled the bay as Reads Bay since 1943. Office of Coast Survey charts first labeled the bay in 1979 and also used the name Reads Bay. Two roads near the bay are named Reeds Bay Road and Reeds Shipyard Road.

proposals.title: Rizeor Lake
proposals.submitter: Washington Committee on Geographic Names Date submitted 10/28/2022
proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: In Methow Wildlife Area/Rendezvous Wildlife Area Unit, 2.7 mi. NW of Winthrop
proposals.name_history: Named for Henry Jackson Rizeor (1849-?), who in 1898 homesteaded a quarter section of land surrounding the lake
proposals.other_names: • Riser Lake (Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife; Methow Trails)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal was submitted by the Washington Committee on Geographic Names (WCGN) on behalf of a resident of Twisp to apply the commemorative names Rizeor Lake to an
proposals.stakeholders: Local government San Juan County State Names Authority Washington Support Federal Agency NOAA Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other Author, Maritime Place Names Inland Washington Waters Support officially unnamed 7.1-acre lake in Okanogan County. The lake lies within the Rendezvous Wildlife Area Unit, part of the Methow Wildlife Area, 2.7 miles northwest of the community of Winthrop. The proposal was originally submitted to the WCGN to correct the spelling from Riser Lake to Rizeor Lake, noting that the former name was listed in Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife records; however, the lake is not listed in GNIS, so the BGN is being asked to consider Rizeor Lake as a new name for an unnamed feature. If approved, Riser Lake will be added to GNIS as a variant name. The lake would be named for Henry Jackson Rizeor (1849-?), described as "a ne'er do well, who in 1898 homesteaded a quarter section of land surrounding the lake." General Land Office records confirm Rizeor's land patent in 1898, and he was listed as a farmer in the 1900 Federal Census of Okanogan County. By 1910, he had relocated to Douglas County, Oregon, where his occupation was recorded as "odd jobs." A 1904 volume entitled History of North Washington included a reference to Mr. Rizeor: [Born in Illinois] the family crossed the plains in 1853 with ox teams and located in Benton county, Oregon, where our subject grew to manhood. He was there educated in the public schools and continued assisting his father on the farm . . . . After his majority, Mr. Rizeor went from Oregon to Idaho, and settled near Eagle Rock, where two years were spent in prospecting and trapping. From that place, Mr. Rizeor went to Juneau, Alaska, and there prospected for one year. Later he went to Ashcroft, British Columbia, where he prospected and did trapping until 1889, when he came to Okanogan county. He located a squatter's right on the land he now owns and afterward took it as a homestead. He does general farming and raises good fruit and melons, having a lake from which he irrigates a portion of his land. Mr. Rizeor is also greatly interested in mining. He owns stock in various gold mines in eastern Oregon and also has properties in different localities. He owns a portion of the Ninety-nine on Slate creek and other properties in this county. Mr. Rizeor has given names to several creeks in this county, among which is Cub creek, which flows into the north branch of the Methow river. The incident that named the creek was the slaying of two cubs by Mr. Rizeor when out hunting. The renaming effort was covered in an April 2022 article in the Methow Valley News: https://methowvalleynews.com/2022/04/06/riser-lake-or-is-it-rizeor-may-get-a-rename/. The Executive Director of the Methow Field Institute suggested to the proponent that perhaps the lake could be given a native name instead but did not submit one.
