proposals.title: Mary-Pamela Falls
proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: located along an unnamed tributary of the Sultan River, 0.95 mi. S of Echo Lake
proposals.name_history: Named for Mary Pamela Awad (1945-1993), who visited the location in the late 1980s
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Mary-Pamela Falls is proposed for a 85-foot tall waterfall located along an unnamed tributary of the Sultan River on land managed by the Washington Department of Natural Resources, in Snohomish County. The surrounding land is managed by the U.S. Forest Service (Snoqualmie National Forest) and the Washington State Forest Board. The name would commemorate the proponent's late mother Mary-Pamela Awad (1945- 1993), who according to the proponent: . . . [W]as an early discoverer of the falls located in a very remote and isolated part of the Cascade foothills. We believe the currently nameless waterfall is worthy of a name and feel our family is amongst the very few, if not only people to visit the area in the past thirty plus years. As a child our mother . . . instilled a passion and reverence for the beauty of the outdoors and the Pacific Northwest. Being an avid hiker, mountaineer and skier, our family outings were filled with adventures in the Cascade Mountains. These trips were filled with lessons on safety, nature and being good stewards to the land. In the late 80's while on a short hike with our Boy Scout troop to Explorer Falls our mother spoke with an elder local who told her of an unknown and magnificent waterfall further east through the forest. The proponent continued that after further research and exploration, they located the falls. Decades after his mother's death, he and his brother attempted to revisit the "mystery falls." With "the convenience of the internet and online mapping," they were to find it, but learned that their previous route was no longer accessible due to the City of Everett now owning the surrounding watershed. In December 2021, they managed to visit the location and "The falls were just as beautiful as I remembered them." He adds: Surveying the surrounding area, we guessed that very few, if any humans have set sight on these falls since we were previously there. The Northwest Waterfall Survey lists the falls but labels them as 'Unnamed'. We feel that the most befitting name these unnamed falls could have would be one that paid tribute to our mother. Please consider the name Mary-Pamela Falls as we feel it would honor her legacy of adventure and exploration in the Pacific Northwest. Change Grass Lake to Nathaniel Sargent Lake, and new name Rodney White Slough These proposals relate to a pair of waterbodies near Tahuya in Mason County: a lake with the current official name Grass Lake and a swamp with no official name. Federal maps labeled the swamp as N____r Slough as early as 1943; however, on a 1952 map the name was transferred to the lake and the swamp was unnamed. In 1970, the name became Negro Slough, a result of the 1963 Secretary of the Interior directive to replace "n____r" with "negro" when maps were reprinted. A 1985 USGS map labeled the lake as Grass Lake, presumably based on local use recorded during field work; the name was added to GNIS in 1992 citing this 1985 map. None of these names have been the subject of BGN review or a BGN decision. State sources and commercial maps have variously labeled each waterbody with the names Grass Lake, N____r Slough, and Negro Slough, resulting in much confusion. The new proposals for Nathaniel Sargent Lake and Rodney White Slough were submitted to the Washington Committee on Geographic Names (WCGN) by the Living Arts Cultural Heritage Project, in an effort to reflect the Black history of the local community and of the larger Great Peninsula region (locally called Kitsap Peninsula), as well as to address the former official and unofficial names of these features.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Grass Lake, near Tahuya in Mason County, to Nathaniel Sargent Lake. The change would commemorate Nathaniel Sargent (1863-1954) who was a well-known and well-liked Black homesteader, writer, artist, and justice of the peace in the Seabeck-Crosby area, about 15 miles north-northeast of Grass Lake. The proponents do not object to the existing name but wish to recognize the regional Black community because the lake had formerly been called Negro Slough and N____r Slough. They also reported that the change would be "corrective/restorative history to honor a black pioneer who didn't receive the recognition he deserved during his lifetime." According to a digital exhibit from the Kitsap History Museum on Black Trailblazers of Kitsap County: Nathaniel J. Sargent was known as "Nat" to his friends. He was born into slavery and after emancipation was adopted by a white family in the north. They sent him to the University of Illinois where he graduated, then came west with his family to Oregon. Because Oregon laws forbad Negroes, he came to Kitsap County where he earned a living working in the woods as a logger. He homesteaded in Crosby [~15 miles north- northeast of Grass Lake] after his arrival in 1882, and as settlers started arriving, he worked as a handyman alongside the homesteaders, building their homes, starting their orchards, butchering, harvesting. He was their friend although he never "imposed" and was often an invited guest. . . . He returned to his home in the East one year to seek a bride, but returned home empty- handed. He filled his lonely hours by writing poetry (which was published) and oil painting. Until four years before his death, he would walk over the hills to Bremerton [~22 miles northeast of Grass Lake] and back again in one day. In 1894, he was elected Justice of the Peace at Seabeck. He also donated land for a school in the Seabeck- Crosby area. Nathaniel Sargent died in 1954. Everyone from Crosby showed up for his funeral. . . . The former names of the lake (potentially a misapplication of the "slough" names) may have been a reference to Rodney White (q.v.), a Black man who homesteaded the land around the lake and the adjacent swamp.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Rodney White Slough to an unnamed swamp in Mason County near Tahuya. The name would commemorate Rodney White (1861-1913), a Black farmer, rancher, and road builder whose homestead included the swamp. The proponents report that the name is proposed for "corrective history: reconciliation and healing of oppressive and harmful history that African Americans endured during that period [Rodney White's lifetime]." The proposal included an August 4, 2022 Kitsap Sun article which reported: Born into slavery in Missouri, White went on to develop his own ranch and farm in Mason County while cutting roads through the peninsula that remain in use today. . . . White arrived in the area in 1890 on the steamer Delta and survived a capsizing skiff that ferried six Black men to the shore where they hoped to homestead. Two men died and White appears to be the only survivor that remained in the area. Atop a high-wheeled wagon, White plowed and rode the hinterlands of the Tahuya River Valley, pushing a team of oxen to build the road to Dewatto [3.5 miles northwest of the swamp] and create a ranch and homestead out of the untamed wilderness from the time after the boat accident to his death in 1913. With "a voice like a foghorn," he'd command his livestock, especially his two leading donkeys. . . . After White's death, the animals were transported to the Woodland Park Zoo in Seattle to live out their days. . . . White came to Tahuya seeking acreage under the federal Homestead Act, passed during the Civil War with the aim of distributing western lands. His "four forties," the nickname for the total of 160 acres, were divided between the area west of Maggie Lake and the Tahuya River valley. . . . White built a barn, cabin, root cellar and chicken coop out of logs and farmed an orchard of fruits that included apples, prunes, pears and peaches. . . . There were great challenges to farming in the 19th and early 20th centuries on the timber-covered Tahuya River valley. Logged or not, the stumps made it next to impossible to plant fields. So sometimes farmers, like White, would empty ponds and small lakes with the aim of farming their basins. [It is] believed that was how White shaped the land in the area that became known as the slur-named slough."

proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: Swastika Lake: USGS 1961, 1992, 2012, 2021; Publications in Science: Botany, 1922; Ecological Monographs, Blake 1945 State Names Authority Washington Support Federal Agency n/a Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other U.S. Representative Derek Kilmer Support One individual Support
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Swastika Lake to Fortune Lake. The 12-acre lake is located in the Snowy Mountain Range, 33 miles west of Laramie in Albany County, and within the Medicine Bow-Routt National Forests. The proponent believes the name should be changed due to its present-day negative connotation. She notes: The swastika emerged as an ancient symbol used by cultures to connotate well-being and fortune. Since its adoption as the symbol for the Nazi Party beginning in 1920, the swastika has become indelibly linked with the atrocities of the Nazi regime and is forever a symbol of hate, anti-Semitism and infamy in Western cultures. Today, antisemitic incidents throughout the United States are at the highest levels ever recorded. The swastika symbol is often present in these incidents as it is the most effective way to communicate hatred of Jews. The proponent further reports that the local Forest Service office was unable to find any information regarding the origins of the current name, adding "While it could be argued that Swastika Lake was named before the Nazis came to power, this name must now be changed. This proposal is [to change the name] to Fortune Lake as a nod to the origins of the swastika as a symbol of fortune but without the undeniable hatred that this symbol represents today." Swastika Lake has been labeled on USGS maps since 1961. The earliest known reference to the name is the 1922 volume Publications in Science: Botany, Volume 1, "Algae of the Medicine Bow Mountains, Wyoming, in the vicinity of the University of Wyoming Summer Camp," published by the University of Wyoming. The lake is adjacent to the camp, which was reportedly built in the 1920s. The name also appeared in a subsequent university publication in 1935 and in An Ecological Reconnoissance in the Medicine Bow Mountains (Ecological Monographs, Blake 1945). In 2011, the camp property was purchased by The WEST Institute, a Christian-based organization that operates out of Laramie Valley Chapel. At its April 2023 meeting, the DNC approved a proposal to rename Swastika Mountain in Lane County, Oregon to Mount Halo. The new name honors Chief Halito (d.1892), leader of the Yoncalla Kalapuya native group. During the State and Federal review of the proposal, the Hindu American Foundation (HAF) expressed concerns that the change was presented as necessary "because the symbol is offensive." They wished to emphasize that it has been a sacred symbol for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Zoroastrians for 4,000+ years and is also significant in many Native American cultures. They did not object to efforts to commemorate a native leader but noted that "renaming [the mountain] because of ignorance about a sacred symbol for more than a billion people in the world is not something we can support." A small community in Clinton County, New York is named Swastika and a post office of the same name operated there from 1913 until 1958. In September 2020, the town voted to retain its name.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Golden Goose Wash is proposed for an unnamed 0.8-mile-long arroyo on Bureau of Land Management land in Maricopa County. The proponent reports that they hold a mining claim, Golden Goose 30, at the head of the arroyo. They report: The Golden Goose line of mining claims in this area is vast. Over 50 claims (1000 acres approx). The arroyo/intermittent stream starts on Golden Goose 30 Mine and meanders through many other "Goose" claims to meet with Vulture Wash south west down slope. It is 2.5 miles north east of Vulture Mine. The name Golden Goose for a mining claim will be entrenched in this area of Maricopa County for a very long time. In the spirit of the desert area, its rich mining heritage and the typical naming of a feature by "first in" prospectors, I would submit this name for your discussion and I believe future approval. The proponent owns White Widow Mining Company, located in Florida. According to its LinkedIn page, the company "buys, sells, and actively mines lode and placer claims nationally. Each claim is researched and documented with the appropriate state and federal agencies. We conduct precious metal and targeted mineral assays." There are no other features in Arizona named "Golden Goose"; there are five with "Goose" in their names, just one of which, Goose Lake, is in Maricopa County, 20 miles from the arroyo in question.

proposals.title: Halfmoon Crater
proposals.proposal_type: make official name in local use
proposals.feature_description: 1.6 mi. NE of Black Bottom Crater, 4.6 mi. NNE of Moon Crater
proposals.name_history: Named for the shape of the crater when viewed from one side and in association with Moon Crater
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: o Halfmoon Crater (locals, 30 years, according to proponent) • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Halfmoon Crater is proposed for a crater on Arizona State Trust land in Coconino County. The crater has an elevation of 6,111 feet and is about 0.5 miles in diameter. The proponent, who lives in the area, states that the crater "looks like a halfmoon from one side." He reports that the name has been used in the area for 30 years and that it also references Moon Crater, located 4.6 miles away. Further, "I believe this crater should be named because it is a very prominent unnamed geologic feature on the drive between Sunset Crater National Monument and Wupatki National Monument." The proponent provided support from the Grand Canyon Postmaster who wrote: My family and I have lived at the bottom of this crater for twenty-four years. We whole heartedly agree with this request and hope that BGN will agree to the naming. Half Moon Crater fills the view from our front porch and has been the backdrop for three generations of family pictures. It represents peace, home, and family for us, and I believe also for our neighbors and friends.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the local name Boomer Creek for a 2.3-mile-long tributary of an unnamed tributary of Branciforte Creek in Santa Cruz County. Until recently, the stream was labeled as Redwood Creek in Santa Cruz County GIS data; however, after receiving a request from the proponent, the county GIS staff amended it to Boomer Creek. The road that runs along the stream is Redwood Drive. The proponent stated that long-time residents of Redwood Drive know the stream as Boomer Creek, adding, "Since the name Boomer Creek goes back at least 50 years or 60 years at least, we would like that name to be official." She noted that the 1986 Santa Cruz Place Names, A Geographical Dictionary by University of California, Santa Cruz librarian Donald Thomas Clark reported the name as Boomer Creek and that it commemorates George Boomer (1844-?) and Harvey John Boomer (1847-1915), who moved from Nova Scotia to Santa Cruz around 1868. They started a sawmill along the stream sometime prior to 1875. Clark erroneously reported that USGS maps labeled the stream as Blackburn Gulch, which is instead three miles to the northeast at the head of Branciforte Creek. (Clark also reported the name of the stream, or the valley that contains the stream, as Boomer Gulch.) Santa Cruz County GIS data and FEMA maps label the stream into which the proposed Boomer Creek flows as "Glen Canyon"; the road along this stream is Glen Canyon Road. Clark reported the name of this stream as "West Branch Branciforte Creek." USGS maps have never labeled either stream.

proposals.proposal_type: change name to commemorate local family
proposals.proponent: Mark Kilkenny & Anne Kilkenny; Shaker Heights, OH
proposals.feature_description: Located along Habematolel Creek 2 mi. E of Gravelly Valley, 1 mi. SW of Cabbage Patch
proposals.name_history: Named for the Kilkenny family, who have owned property in the area since 1907, specifically, Catherine Lydon Kilkenny (1845-1921)
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: o Kilkenny Valley (landowners) • Published names: o Habematolel Valley: The National Map Viewer; Secretary's Order 3404 Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force name changes announcement and media coverage, 2022 o Big Sq___ Valley: USGS 1951, 1967; USGS/USFS 1996; many other sources
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Habematolel Valley, a flat in Lake County, to Kilkenny Valley. The feature is located on both private lands and within Mendocino National Forest. In April 2022, in response to Secretary's Order 3404, the California Natural Resources Agency, on behalf of the Habematolel Pomo of Upper Lake, California, submitted the name Habematolel Creek as a replacement for nearby Sq___ Valley Creek. The stream flows through the northern end of what is now called Habematolel Valley. The Task Force selected Habematolel Creek for the stream, and Habematolel Valley for the related flat (the latter feature was not included in the CNRA submission). Also during the S.O. 3404 process, the Kilkenny family submitted to the Task Force the names Kilkenny Valley and Catherine's Creek. The Task Force recommended Habematolel Creek and Habematolel Valley and those were approved by the BGN on September 8, 2022. The name Kilkenny Valley has been proposed directly to the BGN by the Kilkenny family. Kilkenny Ranch is a private inholding in Mendocino National Forest that occupies the southern three-quarters of the flat. The family has used the name Kilkenny Valley since 2022 and states that it is "wholly owned by the Kilkenny Family." However, there appears to be disagreement about the extent of the flat. A 1908 property description provided by the family recorded the following: The S. E. 1/4 of S. E. 1/4, W. 1/2 of S. E. 1/4 and the S. E. 1/4 of the S.W. 1/4 of Sec. 4; W. 1/2 of W. 1/2 and Lots 2 and 3 of Sec. 5; E. 1/2 of E. 1/2 of Section 6; N. 1/2 of N. 1/2 of Sec. 8; All in Township Eighteen (18) N., Range Nine (9) West, M. D. M. [Mount Diablo Meridian]; and Lots 3 and 4 of Sec 32 in Township 19 N., Range 9 West, M. D. M. containing 800 acres. This corresponds to the private inholding shown on the USGS Lake Pillsbury topographic map. Habematolel Valley does fall within Kilkenny Ranch lands in Section 5, T18N, R9W, but it also extends into U.S. Forest Service lands in Section 36, T19N, R10W. The feature was originally classified in GNIS as a valley with two coordinates, but the characteristics do not correspond to GNIS convention and so it was reclassified as a flat, with a single coordinate at the center. The Kilkenny family has owned Kilkenny Ranch since 1907 when Catherine Lydon Kilkenny (1845-1921) purchased the land. Catherine and her husband Anthony (1843-1886) emigrated from Ireland to the United States during the Irish Potato Famine and settled near Dixon. Catherine purchased the land that became the ranch for one of her sons to recuperate from tuberculosis. In 1949, her heirs formed the non-profit Kilkenny Family Incorporated, the by-laws of which state "The purpose of the corporation is to enhance and preserve for current and future generations the property known as 'Big [Sq___] Valley' and the other tangible and intangible assets of the extended family of the descendants of Anthony & Catherine Lydon Kilkenny. . . ." They add, "During the 20th Century, the Valley was a popular destination for Catherine's surviving sons for recreation and vacations, in constant use during the summers. Family members have created a Memorial Garden in a corner of the valley where there is a lovely view. At the center of the garden is a monument with a Memorial Plaque to Catherine and her 9 sons and a bench for quiet contemplation. Uncounted family members have had their ashes strewn in or near the Memorial Garden, and a couple dozen families have erected memorial plaques for their antecedents." Regarding the choice of Habematolel Valley, the Kilkenny family states the following: The word 'Habematolel' is a Pomo word which means 'the people of rock village.' There are no major rock formations in the Valley [sic], so that name does not have any geologic connection to it. For more than 150 years, the area encompassing the Valley has consistently been determined to be within Yuki and not Pomo territory. . . . Consequently, the name 'Habematolel' also has no historic, geographic or ethnologic relationship to the Valley. . . . As the Valley was never Pomo land, the imposition of a Pomo name on a place that has been used by the Kilkenny family for more than seven generations for over a century, as well as the Yuki people who used it before the Kilkenny family, is at best inappropriate and at worst an affront. Three Native American (presumably Yuki) sites were actually in the Valley, and one was a seasonal encampment. No villages or graves were found. The nearest known Yuki settlement was located three miles southwest in Gravelly Valley, now submerged by Lake Pillsbury. . . . If the proposed name "Kilkenny Valley" is accepted, the persons making this request will endeavor to find and propose a suitable Yuki name for the creek that runs through it [this is presumably the unnamed stream flowing north through the ranch into Habematolel Creek]. This may be difficult because the Yuki tribe no longer exists and there are no living native Yuki speakers. They cite "Barrett's Map of the Territory of the Pomo Linguistic Stock" from The Ethno- geography of the Pomo and Neighboring Indians to show that the flat is located in what was Yuki lands, and add: The Kilkenny Family's state-approved Timber Management Plan recognizes the significance of the two known Yuki sites within the Valley and has thus specified that no timber removal or other physical disturbances will be allowed within 25 feet of those sites. If additional Native American sites in the Valley are identified, they will be similarly protected. In a family-wide poll taken in 2022 by Kilkenny Family Inc., the name 'Kilkenny Valley' was selected to be the new official name proposed for it. It is therefore extremely unlikely that the members of the Kilkenny family or any visitors to the Valley will call it anything other than 'Kilkenny Valley'- regardless who imposes another name for it. [The family has installed a sign showing "Kilkenny Valley.] One of the proponents describes calling the nearest commercial establishment, Soda Creek General Store, as well as an employee of the Upper Lake Ranger Station to ask if they knew the location of "Habematolel Valley." Both individuals could describe how to get to "Kilkenny Valley" but were unfamiliar with the name "Habematolel Valley." (Note that the name Habematolel Valley has only been official since September 2022.) The name Log Valley was approved by the BGN as a replacement for Little Sq___ Valley, located five miles away on the other side of Lake Pillsbury. The Task force presumably derived that name from Log Ridge, the closest geographic feature listed in the Task Force's candidate list.

proposals.title: Change Klamath Strait (BGN 1945) and Klamath Strait Drain Outlet to Klamath Straits Drain
proposals.proposal_type: name and application changes to recognize present-day local use
proposals.feature_description: connects the Klamath River and Lower Klamath Lake
proposals.name_history: The name refers to the canal draining Lower Klamath Lake to the Klamath River
proposals.land_ownership: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation / Lower Klamath National Wildlife Refuge / Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife lands / private
proposals.current_name: Klamath Straits / Klamath Strait Drain Outlet
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Klamath Strait: USBR [as United States Reclamation Service] map, 1906; USBR report, 2005; Metsker map, 1916 o Klamath Strait - in part: USGS 1957, 1986, 1991; Oregon Water Resources Department map, 1971 o Klamath Strait Drain - in part: Oregon Water Resources Department map, 1971 o Klamath Strait Drain Outlet - in part: USGS 1957, 1986; Metsker map, 1961 o Klamath Straits - in part: many USBR sources; some USGS sources o Klamath Straits Drain: USBR map, 2004 o Klamath Straits Drain - in part: many USBR sources; some USGS sources o Klamath Straits Drain Outlet: USBR schematic, 1949; Klamath Drainage District map, 2007 o Link River - in part: USGS 1921
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Klamath Straits Drain for the 10-mile-long waterway that connects the Klamath River and Lower Klamath Lake. The feature currently has two official and separate names, Klamath Strait (a six-mile-long stream) and Klamath Strait Drain Outlet (a four-mile-long canal). The name Klamath Strait was made official by the BGN in 1945. The proponent, a U.S. Geological Survey hydrologist, states that the entire 10-mile-long feature is now a "drainage canal" that was: Originally a short natural connection between Lower Klamath Lake and the Klamath River. After Lower Klamath Lake was drained by U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) in the early 1900s, Klamath Straits Drain was extended down to just over the OR/CA border in 1945. The capacity of the Drain was increased from 300 to 600 cubic feet per second in 1981 by USBR. Water is pumped uphill in Klamath Straits Drain from south to north and northwest by pumps located at two pump stations along its length. USGS maps printed in the late 1800s show that water flowed from the Klamath River into Lower Klamath Lake (labeled as Little Klamath Lake on some maps). According to USGS Scientific Investigations Report 2007-5050, "Ground-Water Hydrology of the Upper Klamath Basin, Oregon and California": Lower Klamath Lake was connected to the Klamath River through a channel known as the Klamath Strait, and probably through the expansive wetland that separated the lake from the river elsewhere. In the early 1900s, a railroad dike was constructed across the northwestern margin of the Lower Klamath Lake subbasin, cutting off flow between the lake and river except at the Klamath Strait. In 1917, the control structure at the Klamath Strait was closed, cutting off flow to the lake. As a result, Lower Klamath Lake is now largely drained, with much of the former lake bed and fringe wetlands under cultivation. The 1921 edition of the USGS 1894 Klamath 1:250,000 topographic map mislabeled the waterway as part of the Link River, although the latter name applies to a different section between Upper Klamath Lake and Lake Ewauna. In 1945, the BGN was asked to determine if the stream's name should be Klamath Strait or Klamath Straits. Most sources used the name Klamath Strait, including USGS maps, the first and second editions of Lewis McArthur's Oregon Geographic Names, State highway maps, and a U.S. Forest Service map. However, USBR used the name Klamath Straits. Despite the 1945 decision, the USBR continued to use the name Klamath Straits and it continues to be used locally. Also in 1945, the USBR began a project to construct a drain outlet that would allow water to be pumped uphill from Lower Klamath Lake to the Klamath River. By this time, water was being pumped from nearby Tule Lake. The area was being converted to agriculture and the drain outlet would help control water levels. USGS did not publish a map of the area again until 1957, when an area of natural-looking flow was labeled as Klamath Strait, and the canal connecting Klamath Strait to Lower Klamath Lake was labeled as Klamath Strait Drain Outlet. The proponent reports that: Over time, Klamath Straits Drain has become the dominant usage, both in Federal and other documents and also locally. Having the BGN name as Klamath Strait Drain is difficult. For instance, for us at USGS, our gages and water quality monitors include "Klamath Straits Drain" in the name. Many USGS reports have been written that include "Klamath Straits Drain." USBR is a major cooperator and Department of Interior partner in the Klamath Basin and they use "Klamath Straits Drain." It is not only the Federal agencies who use this name, however. Over time, the usage of Klamath Straits Drain has taken over, so that currently irrigators, locals, State agencies, consultants, and others also use "Klamath Straits Drain." If the proposal is approved, the GNIS entry for Klamath Strait (the stream) would be marked historical.

The 1921 edition of the USGS 1894 Klamath 1:250,000 topographic map mislabeled the waterway as part of the Link River, although the latter name applies to a different section between Upper Klamath Lake and Lake Ewauna. In 1945, the BGN was asked to determine if the stream's name should be Klamath Strait or Klamath Straits. Most sources used the name Klamath Strait, including USGS maps, the first and second editions of Lewis McArthur's Oregon Geographic Names, State highway maps, and a U.S. Forest Service map. However, USBR used the name Klamath Straits. Despite the 1945 decision, the USBR continued to use the name Klamath Straits and it continues to be used locally. Also in 1945, the USBR began a project to construct a drain outlet that would allow water to be pumped uphill from Lower Klamath Lake to the Klamath River. By this time, water was being pumped from nearby Tule Lake. The area was being converted to agriculture and the drain outlet would help control water levels. USGS did not publish a map of the area again until 1957, when an area of natural-looking flow was labeled as Klamath Strait, and the canal connecting Klamath Strait to Lower Klamath Lake was labeled as Klamath Strait Drain Outlet. The proponent reports that: Over time, Klamath Straits Drain has become the dominant usage, both in Federal and other documents and also locally. Having the BGN name as Klamath Strait Drain is difficult. For instance, for us at USGS, our gages and water quality monitors include "Klamath Straits Drain" in the name. Many USGS reports have been written that include "Klamath Straits Drain." USBR is a major cooperator and Department of Interior partner in the Klamath Basin and they use "Klamath Straits Drain." It is not only the Federal agencies who use this name, however. Over time, the usage of Klamath Straits Drain has taken over, so that currently irrigators, locals, State agencies, consultants, and others also use "Klamath Straits Drain." If the proposal is approved, the GNIS entry for Klamath Strait (the stream) would be marked historical. Stakeholder Input Local government Klamath County Siskiyou County

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Sacramento Mountain, a 3,354-foot summit in Shasta County, to Yohala-mi. The summit is on private land within the proclaimed boundary of the Shasta National Forest, east of Shasta Lake, a reservoir on the Sacramento River. The proponent owns most of the summit in their property named "Lightning Canyon Ranch" and wishes to make official the Wintu name for the summit, Yohala-mi. He references the name in The Wintun Indians of California and their Neighbors by Peter M. Knudtson. The name Yohala-mi translates to "Frog Mountain," and the proponent speculates that the name refers to the many springs and streams on the mountain. He further states that the summit and the surrounding land is the ancestral home to the Winnemem Wintu peoples. He provided a letter of support from the Wintu Tribe of Northern California, a non-federally recognized group; the group wrote that Yohala-mi means "frog" in the Wintu (Penutian) Language . . . ., adding, "You are most welcome to use 'Yohala-mi' (Frog) or 'Yohala-mi Puyuk' (Frog Mountain). Either name honors the Wintu People and we appreciate you coming to us." The proponent also provided a letter of support from an individual who stated "my grandmother published a book containing a collection of Wintu legends and religious stories. She called the book "A Bag of Bones". The title . . . is a translation of the name given by the Wintus to a striking rock formation located on the southern slopes of Sacramento Mountain. [It] would be highly appropriate that such an important landmark for the Wintu tribe bear the name given to it by the Wintu, "Yohala-mi". For the mountain to bear this ancient name would be a powerful reminder that the lands to the south of this mountain boundary zone were once the home of the Wintu, and would be a warm gesture of healing of past wounds."

proposals.title: Wunnee-Neetunah Cave
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.name_history: named for the Podunk woman Wunnee-Neetunah, who according to legend lived in the cave with her Dutch husband Peter Hagar in the 1600s
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Sq___ Cave: many published and online sources o Sq___'s Hole: A New England Pattern: The History of Manchester, Connecticut, 1973
proposals.case_summary: The new name Wunnee-Neetunah Cave is proposed for an unnamed cave in the Town of Bolton in the Capitol Planning Region. The cave is not recorded in GNIS and has never been shown or labeled on USGS maps. The name Sq___ Cave has been in long-term use. The cave's name appears to originate in the 1934 The Story of Wunnee-Neetunah, or The Life of an Indian Princess of Connecticut by Mathia Spiess; the work is subtitled "A Tale of Truth." The Manchester Historical Society "presents the book . . . as a work of fiction, acknowledging the inclusion of the facts available at the time, as well as mention of 'Sq___ Cave' on the 'new highway' in Bolton, that is, Route 44, near Bolton Notch." In this legend, Wunnee-neetunah (also called Wunnee), was the daughter of a Podunk chief named Tantonimoh. Her family adopted Peter Hagar, the cabin boy of a Dutch trader named Captain May, after Peter fell in love with Wunnee and the Captain encouraged him to live among the Podunks to learn their language and customs. After a few years, Peter and Wunnee traveled to Boston with Wunnee's mother to get married but learned that there was a law against intermarriage. While they stayed outside the city, Peter was seen gathering wood on the Sabbath and was arrested and whipped. Before he was imprisoned, Wunnee and her mother rescued Peter and they fled back to Connecticut. Along the way, they were attacked, presumably by Massachusetts colonists, and one died in the fight. Peter was accused of killing the man. Peter and Wunnee did not return to Wunnee's home but were married in another Podunk community in Connecticut. Bailiffs from Boston were sent to capture or kill Peter, but the Podunks warned Peter and Wunnee. As they sought safety from the bailiffs and from other native groups attacking the Podunks, Peter and Wunnee "removed their belongings farther east to a cave on the south side of a rocky mountain known as Wiashqua-ompsk-ut [Wiashguagwumsuck]." After about 30 years, Peter and Wunnee planned to move north to a Podunk settlement in an area without European colonists or hostile native groups. However, a group of Mohegan men "found Peter, the outlaw, living with his Indian wife in the cave 'where the main trail goes through the Notch in the mountain, on the east side of the Connecticut River.'" The Mohegans reported them to local bailiffs who shot Peter. He reached the cave, and Wunnee was sent in after him. They remined in the cave for several days and when the bailiffs went into the cave, the found it empty. Wunnee had either snuck out the cave entrance with Peter's body or found a deeper passage in the cave through the mountain. Peter was reportedly buried in "the royal burying ground. . . of the Podunk Tribe" and Wunnee was reportedly taken in by a Windsor couple and was reportedly buried in Windsor. Spiess wrote: The cavern home of Peter and Wunnee-neetunah now faces a newly constructed highway at Bolton Notch and is still known as the sq___ cave. The name as it came down to us seems to substantiate the belief that few white folks, if any, ever knew that Peter lived there, for he was ever on the alert. His Indian wife was known by many of the white squatters who had settled in the vicinity on land, without any title and against the will of the original proprietors of Hartford. The land on which the cave is located has been purchased by the State of Connecticut and is now classed among the state parks. The interior of the cave leads into a narrow neck which is now impassable. Tradition has it that this narrow channel once led into a large chamber from which a passage extended to an opening on the other side of the mountain, as we have already seen. . . . The cave is visited by thousands of people annually. It is unknown how much of the legend is truth or fiction. Other sources spell Wunnee- neetunah's name as Wunneeneetmah, including the 1938 Federal Writer's Project Connecticut volume. The cave seems to also have been called Sq___'s Hole, cited in the 1973 A New England Pattern: The History of Manchester, Connecticut and on an undated postcard that appears to be from the early 1900s. The proponent has been advised that if the name is approved, it would not be retrievable via the GNIS public query. According to the GNIS FAQ Why are there no entries for caves in the GNIS?: GNIS does include caves, but the entries are not publicly available. In response to the 1988 National Cave Management Resources Act, Department of the Interior Regulation 43 (CFR Subtitle A, Part 37) forbids the release of information regarding the location of all caves on Federal lands. Currently, GNIS does not distinguish between features on Federal versus non-Federal lands, so all features classified as "cave" are blocked from public access.  FLORIDA

proposals.submitter: same Date submitted same

proposals.feature_description: flows E through Matthews Lake to enter Dick Creek
proposals.name_history: the name refers to "the abundance of magnificent pine trees surrounding the creek"
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Pine Creek to a 0.95-mile-long tributary of Dick Creek in Forsyth County. The proponent, a local resident, states "As I explored the area, I couldn't help but notice the abundance of magnificent pine trees surrounding the creek, creating a picturesque setting. The soft sound of the water flowing gently through the rocks combined with the subtle scent of pine needles in the air made it an enchanting spot. Hence, I decided to pay homage to the dominant natural feature of the area by naming it 'Pine Creek.' This name serves as a reminder of the creek's tranquil beauty and its connection to the magnificent pine forests that grace the Georgia landscape." GNIS lists 131 geographic features in Georgia with "Pine" in their names; of these, 15 are streams. Four are named Pine Creek, but none of these are in Forsyth County. The closest is 53 miles from the stream in question. There are two bodies of water in Forsyth County named Pine Lake. IDAHO

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Iona Butte for "a summit of a broadly sloped early Pleistocene shield volcano." The summit is located 2.5 miles northeast of Iona in Bonneville County, and its western slope is within land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The proponent reports that the summit is "a prominent feature in the local area and can be seen from many nearby population centers including Idaho Falls, Rigby, Ririe, and Shelley." He notes also that the Idaho Geological Survey, a Department of Energy telecommunications project, and an FCC license all refer to the feature as "Iona Butte", while news articles from 2018 mentioned "the Iona Hill." In April 2023, the City of Iona referred to plans for "the Iona Bike Path up on Iona hill."

proposals.title: Change Jessie-Ca Lake to Hidden Valley Lake
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize local preference
proposals.feature_description: 0.4 mi. S of Sand Lake
proposals.name_history: Descriptive name
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Jessie-Ca Lake: USGS 1965, 2010, 2022
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Jessie-Ca Lake, a 3.5-acre reservoir in Green Township in Noble County, to Hidden Valley Lake. The reservoir was first labeled on USGS topographic maps in 1965. The proponents, who own the entire reservoir, report that they purchased the land 27 years ago and that the name Jessie-Ca Lake refers to the former owner. The Noble County parcel report records that the proponents purchased the land from Jessie A. Clouse (1913-2012). County atlases from 1874 to 1933 show that members of the Clouse family owned many properties in the area. The proponents report that they have called the reservoir Hidden Valley Lake since they purchased the land and that they cleaned up the "poorly maintained [lake that was]. . . completely covered with algae and cattails," developing it into "a beautiful location for fishing and relaxing." They also note that two years ago they "completely remodeled a cottage on the property with the intention of renting it out to folks as a peaceful vacation getaway, and named it Hidden Valley Lake Cottage." They add that "Updating the lake's name would help vacationers find its location on the internet, as well as maintain the aesthetic of the property." GNIS does not list any nearby features with similar names. There are two other reservoirs in Indiana named Hidden Valley Lake, both over 100 miles away. MASSACHUSETTS

proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Long Pond: USGS 1888, 1893, 1942, 1950, 1961, 1974; Barnstable, Dukes and Nantucket Counties map, 1858; Atlas of Massachusetts, 1891
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Long Pond, a 7-acre lake in the Town of Yarmouth in Barnstable County, to Caboose Pond. The proponent notes that many features in the Cape Cod area are named Long Pond and believes this one should be renamed "to represent the historical train presence that is characteristic of this area of Yarmouth." He references the former Yarmouth Station, a name preserved in that of an unincorporated place near the lake. He also states that trains are heard passing the area and that "This new name references a part of a train to represent this railroaded past, rather than just calling the pond long." USGS maps have labeled the lake as Long Pond since 1888. Online references to Long Pond in Yarmouth overwhelmingly refer to the larger pond 3.5 miles to the southeast. GNIS includes records for eight features named Long Pond on Cape Cod in Barnstable County; two are in the Town of Yarmouth.

proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: Lake Carlson (proponent's family) • Published names: Cordes Lake (USGS 1972, 1985, 2011, 2023), Lake Carlson (Kent County highway map 1974, 1984, 1996, 2000, 2001, 2008)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Cordes Lake, a 3.3-acre lake in Courtland Township in Kent County, to Lake Carlson. The lake is located on the proponent's property. The name Cordes Lake has appeared on USGS topographic maps since 1972, when the area was first mapped at a scale of 1:24,000. However, the proponent reports that in 1973 the township supervisors and the Board of County Road Commissioners voted to change the name to Lake Carlson and that name appeared on local maps from 1974 to 2008. The change was never forwarded to the BGN, so Cordes Lake remained on Federal maps. The origin of "Cordes" has not been determined, although online records show that individuals with that name were granted property in the area as far back as 1848 and the family name appears in the Federal Census throughout the first half of the 20th century. In the mid-2000s, Kent County, in populating its new GIS dataset, extracted names from GNIS and the name reverted to Cordes Lake. The proponent is requesting that it be changed to recognize the name approved locally in 1973. He states that it commemorates Josef Carlson (1896-1938), an immigrant from Sweden, who joined the U.S. military and served during World War I. He went on to become the Heavyweight Military Champion and the top Golden Gloves heavyweight amateur fighter. After leaving the military, Josef was a member of the East Grand Rapids Fire Department and eventually became its chief. Josef died as a result of smoke inhalation encountered on the job. The proponent provided copies of the 1973 local approval and maps from 1974 to 2008 showing Lake Carlson. He also submitted newspaper clippings that demonstrated Josef's accomplishments, both as a boxing champion and as a firefighter; in the latter, these included "numerous times running into fires to save trapped people and livestock." He adds, "It simply seems logical that the same name be applied to a specific place or item on all maps of an area regardless of the issuing body. Along with this, local boards and individuals are definitely closer to the people asking and more cognizant of the reasons presented for a specific name, thus making them the reasonable deciding governmental body." The proponent confirmed that Josef Carlson did not have a direct association with the lake but "he was a local hero/celebrity . . . and we believe this fits the 'significant contributions to the community' criterion."

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Wolf Pond, an approximately 2,000-acre lake in the Town of Tupper Lake in Franklin County, to Big Wolf Lake. The lake is owned by the Big Wolf Lake Association, which was founded in the 1940 and which preserves about 4,000 acres of the surrounding land that is not otherwise privately owned. The lake is north of Little Wolf Pond, an approximately 150-acre lake. The proponent is the most recent past president of the association. In 1916, a local lumber company owner named Ferris Meigs purchased the "Big Wolf Tract" to preserve as a game refuge. Meigs was co-owner of the Dodge, Meigs & Company, until 1898, the Santa Clara Lumber Company until 1927, and the Big Wolf Corporation after that. The proponent states that since the purchase of the tract "and very likely before, the lake has been called Big Wolf Lake by the residents who own property along the lake shore as well as by the local community of Tupper Lake." Although USGS maps have labeled the pair of lakes as Wolf Pond and Little Wolf Pond since 1905, earlier publications labeled them as Big Wolf Pond and Little Wolf Pond. The 1934 A Biological Survey of the Raquette Watershed by the State of New York Conservation Department variously used the names Wolf Pond, Big Wolf Pond, and Big Wolf Lake. The section dedicated to the lakes lists it as "Wolf Pond (Big Wolf Lake)" which "is a privately owned lake with fishing rights controlled by the Big Wolf Club." The proponent noted that other features named Wolf Lake are in the Adirondacks, which causes confusion. GNIS lists 54 features in New York with "Wolf" in their names, including three lakes named Wolf Lake and 15 named Wolf Pond. The proponent commented that "While there is apparently no universal definition of a lake, it is also quite clear from research that Big Wolf does not meet the accepted scientific parameters of a pond."

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Negro Marsh, an approximately 200-acre marsh in the Town of Putnam in Washington County. The proponent, who owns property along the marsh states "Our purpose is to remove an offensive name that pops up on our property in Google and Alltrails, for example. We thought the Algonquin name for marsh would be a good fit. We would be happy to just have the name removed from all maps." "Poquoson" is one spelling of a word that is reportedly of Algonquian origin meaning "great marsh," "swamp-on-a-hill," or another sense of a wetland feature. It is sometimes attributed to Powhatan groups. In ecology and geography, the term (generally spelled as pocosin) refers to a palustrine wetland with acidic and nutrient-deficient sandy peat soils. Pocosins are generally found from Virginia to South Carolina. GNIS includes records with many spellings of the word Pocosin or Poquosin as generics; most of these are in North Carolina. The term is sometimes used as a specific in the name, such as in Poquoson River, Pocosin Pond, and Pocoson Swamp. Spellings of the word in GNIS include Pocosin, Pocoson, Poquoson, and P-kaw-shun (the latter for a stream in Louisiana); variant names also contain the additional spellings Pocosan and Poquosin. An incorporated city in Virginia is name Poquoson. This spelling is overwhelmingly associated with features in the city. The proponent was asked if they wished to add another word to the name besides "Poquoson," either as a specific or generic term, but did not respond. The 1887 History of Putnam by Thomas W. McArthur (republished in 1901) used the name Negro Marsh for the feature and also reported that nearby Sixmile Point (named Six Miles Point in the text) was also known locally as Negro Point "from the fact that years ago a negro employed on one of the lake craft was taken with small pox and put off there where he died." This is also reported in the 1878 History of Washington County, New York. The first use of the name for the marsh is unknown, but an 1884 New York State Supreme Court case report referred to N____r Marsh. This name also appeared on USGS maps between 1927 and 1950; no new large-scale maps of the area were published after 1950. Some sources report other origins of the name. A 2000 Adirondack Life article reported "Sir Philip Skene, the local land baron, staunch Tory and the biggest slave owner in the region, freed a few of his oldest slaves and let them settle in a cabin on a marshy point along Lake Champlain. Hence the long-lived nickname of that remote site: N- Swamp." The 2017 volume Blacks in the Adirondacks: A History reports "Philip Skene sent slaves to extract ore . . . . [They] transported the ore up Lake Champlain to Skenesborough, stopping overnight when necessary at shelters built for the purpose on a point of land six miles south of Ticonderoga that became known as [N____r's] Marsh [sic]." The name of the marsh was the subject of some news reports and a 1988 Executive Order by then-Governor Mario Cuomo. After the name "N____r Marsh" was found on New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) maps, Executive Order 113 directed: • "No map prepared by or for any division of the Executive Department or any other department of the State shall contain any derogatory racial, ethnic or religious name or other epithet" • "Each division within the Executive Department and all other departments of the State which become aware of any derogatory place name to immediately refer such information to the State Committee on Geographic Names and to cease using such derogatory name pending the adoption of a replacement name" • "Each division within the Executive Department and all other departments of the State which have mapping responsibilities to meet promptly with the State Committee on Geographic Names to establish a procedure to identify and eliminate problem names from all State maps. As part of such procedure, each department or division shall, in any revision or review of existing maps and the development of new maps, identify any derogatory placenames on maps prepared by or for such division or department; immediately refer any derogatory name to the State Committee on Geographic Names; and remove any derogatory name prepared by or for such division or department prior to the map being issued, or reissued" • "Each division within the Executive Department and all other departments of the State to assist the State Committee on Geographic Names in its function to insure the prompt adoption of replacement names in consultation with the interested local community" No records were found to indicate that this Executive Order resulted in any proposals submitted to the BGN. The order expired at the start of the next Governor's term. Dr. Mark Monmonier describes the situation in his 1995 book Drawing the Line: Tales of Maps and Cartocontroversy. A New York Post reporter asked NYSDEC about a report on releasing pheasants in "N____r Marsh." The DEC noted that the name still appeared on USGS maps. Although the name had been changed in 1963 at the direction of the Secretary of the Interior, along with all other names that contained "n____r," the most recent large- scale map (1950) still showed the old name. Dr. Monmonier reports that he spoke with a State Museum official and learned: The historian originally in charge of the effort had died suddenly in 1990, the Education Department had eliminated a number of positions in the State Museum, the remaining staff were overworked, and funding for research and travel had not been approved. Another historian had only recently been assigned to work on geographic names. Although several offensive names had been found, no recommendations for their deletion had yet been sent to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. . . . By November 1989, the State Committee on Geographic Names had devised a policy for accepting or rejecting questionable geographic names based upon a distinction between intent and impact. For example, although a place named Coon Hill to commemorate either an abundance of raccoons or a nearby settler named John Coon might reflect an acceptable intent, the perceived derogatory impact was clearly unacceptable. In the committee's eyes, "clear impact" was more important than intent-a name perceived as derogatory had to be changed even if the intent of the original namer was unknown or benign. Of course, an investigation of intent might conveniently suggest a straightforward nonderogatory alternative, such as Raccoon Hill or John Coon Hill.

proposals.title: Change Negro Point to Tenkenas Point
proposals.submitter: Daniel Davis; New York, NY Date submitted same
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered derogatory
proposals.feature_description: On the S end of Wards Island, extends into Hell Gate in the East River
proposals.name_history: Named for the recorded Lenape name for Wards Island
proposals.land_ownership: Wards Island Park [New York City Department of Parks & Recreation]
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Negro Point: OCS 1875-present; area maps since at least 1867; Federal document since at least 1896 o Scylla Point: New York City Department of Parks & Recreation since 2011
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Negro Point in the Borough of Manhattan in New York City to Tenkenas Point. The point is within Wards Island Park on the southern end of Wards Island and extends slightly into the Hell Gate of the East River. (Negro Point is sometimes said to be at the southern end of Randalls Island; Wards Island and Randalls Island were formerly separated but are now one island.) The name Negro Point was a 1982 BGN decision. It appeared as early as 1851 on Office of Coast Survey charts and since 1867 on commercial maps of the area. The name was never shown on USGS topographic maps. The 1982 decision resulted from a request from the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration to establish the name in local use. The proposed name Tenkenas Point references the reported Lenape name for Wards Island. The origin of the name Negro Point has not been determined. In 2001, the City of New York Parks and Recreation Department Commissioner submitted a proposal to the BGN to change the name to Scylla Point. This name referred to Scylla and Charybdis, two monsters from Greek mythology said to have been located at the Strait of Messina between Sicily and the Italian mainland. Negro Point lies along a stretch of the East River known as Hell Gate. In 2001, the New York Parks and Recreation Department had already renamed a playground in Astoria, Queens opposite Negro Point as Charybdis Playground. In 2011, the BGN voted not to approve the change, citing "a reluctance to change a name in longstanding use and in the belief that changing it would create a navigation hazard. The committee also cited a lack of evidence that the name is offensive." The decision was made based on the following stakeholder recommendations: Local government Mayor of New York Support Manhattan Borough Council No response State Names Authority New York No objection Federal agencies National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Oppose U.S. Coast Guard Oppose Other New York Parks and Recreation Department [proponent] Support Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Support Sandy Hook Pilots Association Oppose Manhattan Psychiatric Center No opinion The recommendation from NOAA cited input from a spokesperson for the Sandy Hook Pilots Association who stated that "[i]f the name is changed, mariners familiar with the area will still continue to use the present name when giving security calls thus confusing transient vessel operators." The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) supported NOAA's recommendation: "DHS [Department of Homeland Security] [specifically USCG] as a customer of NOAA charts will defer to NOAA. . . . the USCG would have no objection to a name change." The 1851 Office of Coast Survey (OCS) chart "Hell Gate and its Approaches" showed the name Negro Point, along with "Negro Point Bluff" 0.2 miles upstream and two rocks labeled as "Negro Head" and "Little Negro Head" 0.7 miles downstream. These rocks were removed from Hell Gate by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in the late 1800s during efforts to improve navigation in Hell Gate; they are not shown on the 1892 chart. Neither the rocks nor the bluff are recorded in GNIS. OCS charts stopped labeling "Negro Point Bluff" after 1916. On July 21, 2019, the Netflix show Patriot Act with Hasan Minhaj posted a video on YouTube titled "What's With The Racist Names Of So Many American Places?" In the video, Mr. Minhaj described the BGN and pointed out official place names that contain words that are considered offensive. He stated: In New York City, there's a place called "Negro Point." It's actually on Randalls Island [sic] [it is the southern end of Wards Island; the passage between Randalls Islands and Wards Island has been filled in]. . . . It's no longer Negro Point on Google Maps, but it's still Negro Point on Federal maps. Here's the thing: it doesn't have to be this way. The names of these places can actually be changed. . . . The name changing process is handled by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. Now I had a lot of questions, so I gave them a call. In 2011 there was a hearing to rename Negro Point, but there were several groups opposed to it, including the Sandy Hook Pilots Association, NOAA, and the Coast Guard. These groups claimed that changing the maps would potentially confuse tugboat captains. This is crazy to me. I live by Negro Point. I've been there. You guys, it's beautiful. It doesn't deserve this disgusting name. So I went to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names' website and submitted a form to rename Negro Point once and for all. The video showed a typed BGN proposal form with the "Recommended Name" field "Tenkanas Point - based on the Native American name for the island." The BGN never received this form. Mr. Minhaj went on to encourage viewers to submit proposals to the BGN to change any names that included words considered offensive or racist. The BGN received a few proposals in the following week, but dozens of proposals were submitted during the following two weeks once the Greatest Internet Scavenger Hunt included an item on that year's list for teams to earn points for submitting proposals to the BGN after watching Mr. Minhaj's video. Approximately three dozen proposals were received and determined to be eligible for consideration; many were not processed because they did not satisfy the BGN's criteria. Eight of the original proposals have since been approved, while an additional 14 names were changed to something other than what was originally submitted. Three were not approved, thus retaining the existing name, and three are still pending. Some features had several changes proposed by different teams or individuals. During a May 2023 office move, BGN staff found an unopened letter from Daniel Davis, the then-producer of Patriot Act with Hasan Minhaj. The proposal was handwritten but was for Tenkenas Point, i.e., the same name as in the typed version shown on the video. The Tenkenas Point proposal states that "Wards Island was known as Tenkenas Island at the time of its appropriation from its native inhabitants to the Dutch in 1637. 'Tenkenas' is Native American [sic] for 'Wild Lands' (NYC Gov Parks website) [this site is presumably the one for Wards Island Park]." A 2010 article by Ives Goddard in New York History titled "The Origin and Meaning of the Name 'Manhattan'" includes the following in a footnote: A Dutch deed of 1637 refers to "the two islands, situate in the Hellegadt, of which the larger is called Tenkenas [Wards Island] and the smaller Minnahanonck [Roosevelt Island, formerly Blackwells Island], lying to the west of the larger"; The identification of these islands follows J.H. French, Gazetteer of the State of New York [1860]. . . . Roosevelt Island (called Blackwell's Island until 1973) was about six-tenths the size of Ward's Island and lies southwest of it. Grumet [in Native American Place Names in New York City, 1981] identifies Minnahanonck as Randall's Island, but this was directly north of Ward's Island, to which it is now joined by landfill. NORTH CAROLINA

proposals.title: Change application of Indian Gap
proposals.proposal_type: application change to recognize present-day and historic use
proposals.feature_description: 1.2 mi. WSW of Newfound Gap
proposals.name_history: named for an Indian trail that crossed the mountains here
proposals.land_ownership: Great Smoky Mountains National Park / Appalachian National Scenic Trail
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the application of the name Indian Gap, located between Swain County, North Carolina and Sevier County, Tennessee. The gap is in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (GRSM) along the Appalachian National Scenic Trail. The gap's current location, north of Luftee Gap and 0.7 miles west of Newfound Gap, has been labeled on USGS maps since 1966; earlier maps placed the name at the proposed location, south of Mingus Lead and 1.2 miles west-southwest of Newfound Gap. The name was the subject of a 1932 BGN decision, which reported that "[a] prehistoric Indian trail crossed the mountains through this gap. The gap has been variously called Grassy, Lufty [sic], Road, and Wares." The GRSM website, as well as NPS sources from the 1930s and 1940s, support a change to the proposed location. An NPS sign at the proposed location reads: Traffic of all sorts once passed through here-Indians, explorers, Confederate soldiers, farmers with livestock herds, merchants, and families traveling for varied reasons. This is Indian Gap. The road trace that descends the hill in front of you is a remnant of the Indian Gap Road, at one time the major north-south route through the Great Smoky Mountains. For centuries this had been an Indian trail, but in the 1830s it was widened as a toll road, with charges for pedestrians, riders, vehicles, and livestock. The new road was steep, rocky, rutted, and only about five feet wide. Ice and fallen trees often obstructed the way. But until the Newfound Gap Road opened in the 1930s, travelers had no better way to cross the mountains. To avoid the arduous crossing, many opted for lengthy routes around. The GRSM website states: The old road over the Smoky Mountains crossed at Indian Gap, located about 1.5 miles west of [Newfound Gap] . . . . [In 1872, Arnold Henry Guyot's] work revealed Newfound Gap as the lowest pass through the mountains, displacing nearby Indian Gap. When the lower, easier crossing was discovered, it became known as the "newfound" gap. A new road followed, and it became the forerunner of Newfound Gap Road. Some older sources, including the 1882 Map of North Carolina by North Carolina State Geologist W. C. Kerr, labeled the gap as Road Gap and show the name Indian Gap on a gap further to the north.

The GRSM website states: The old road over the Smoky Mountains crossed at Indian Gap, located about 1.5 miles west of [Newfound Gap] . . . . [In 1872, Arnold Henry Guyot's] work revealed Newfound Gap as the lowest pass through the mountains, displacing nearby Indian Gap. When the lower, easier crossing was discovered, it became known as the "newfound" gap. A new road followed, and it became the forerunner of Newfound Gap Road. Some older sources, including the 1882 Map of North Carolina by North Carolina State Geologist W. C. Kerr, labeled the gap as Road Gap and show the name Indian Gap on a gap further to the north.

proposals.proposal_type: new name for an unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: flows NE into Beaver Creek NE of Statesville
proposals.name_history: The name references the River Tay in Scotland, due to the large numbers of Scottish and Scotch-Irish settlers in the area in the 18th century
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name River Tay is proposed for an unnamed two-mile-long tributary of Beaver Creek in Iredell County. A short section of the stream flows through the City of Statesville. The proponent, who owns property along 0.2 miles of the stream near its mouth, wishes to name the stream after the River Tay in Scotland, due to the large numbers of Scottish and Scotch-Irish settlers in the area in the 18th century. He states that many of the local place names reference "the Scottish Highlands and also Biblical names from their deep presbyterian faith." Further, Scotland's River Tay "passes through the ancestral home of several of the families that settled and still reside in this area. This name would both honor those who farmed the area but also their home in Scotland to remind future generations of the rich history of this area of North Carolina." Names of rivers in Great Britain commonly have the generic "River" as the first word. GNIS lists only a few streams with "River" as the first word. Six are named River Styx (in addition to three named Styx River); one is River Lethe, another name from Greek mythology; others include French names found in areas of French settlement and exploration. Scotland's River Tay is about 120 miles long and is the longest river in Scotland. A 60-mile- long Canadian river named Tay River is reportedly named after the River Tay and also derives from Scottish settlement in the area. OREGON

proposals.case_summary: The new name Blue Heron Creek is proposed for an unnamed, approximately 0.2-mile long, tributary of Bear Creek in the City of Phoenix in Jackson County. The name is proposed by members of a group called Save the Phoenix Wetlands and refers to both Blue Heron Park, a city park through which the stream flows, and the great blue herons (Ardea herodias) that nest there. The stream, which is fed by three springs, is not recorded in NHD nor shown on printed USGS quadrangle maps. The proponents state that the stream: [I]s part of a unique system of several small, unnamed creeks emanating from a complex of nearby springs and seeps that provide cold clean water to Bear Creek in an area where summer water temperatures are high. This influx of cold water provides critical baseflow for Coho and other salmon during the hot summer months. They contacted local landowners for support, including Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT), the Phoenix Urban Renewal Agency, and a private landowner. The private landowner and ODOT's regional manager support the proposal. The City of Phoenix Planning Manager responded on behalf of the renewal agency and the city, stating: Neither the Phoenix Urban Renewal Agency [PHURA] or the City has the authority to classify a drainage as a stream or creek nor can PHURA or the City assign an official name. The Oregon Department of Forestry (ODF) is responsible for identification and classification of waterways and has a very prescribed process outlined in OAR Chapter 629. . . . Considering neither PHURA or the City have authority to make the requested change [sic] and. . . [s]ince this is not a local decision, I would recommend contacting the Oregon Department of Forestry for guidance on their administrative processes relating to classification and naming.

proposals.title: Smokejumper Falls
proposals.submitter: Oregon Geographic Names Board Date submitted 4/28/2023
proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: along Negro Creek (proposed Freedom Creek or Triple Nickles Creek)
proposals.name_history: Named for the all-Black 555th Infantry Battalion (the Triple Nickles), which served on firefighting missions in the area
proposals.other_names: Katalyst, Inc. former President and Principal Hydrogeologist Support Circle Culture Support Western Fishes Support Indigo Creek Outfitters Support Travel Phoenix Support • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Negro Creek Falls: Northwest Waterfall Survey website, 2023
proposals.case_summary: The new name Smokejumper Falls is proposed for an waterfall along Negro Creek in Douglas County and on the Umpqua National Forest. The BGN has received two proposals to change the name of Negro Creek, to Freedom Creek (Review List 437) or Triple Nickles Creek (Review List 448). The Oregon Geographic Names Board (OGNB) supports changing the name but does not recommend approval of Freedom Creek and deferred a vote on Triple Nickles Creek pending landowner input. The name Smokejumper Falls would commemorate the 555th Parachute Infantry Battalion, nicknamed the "Triple Nickles" (using the English spelling of 'nickel'), a World War II African American unit of the U.S. Army that was stationed in Pendleton in 1945. According to a U.S. Forest Service (USFS) account: The 555th Parachute Infantry Battalion was a pioneering paratrooper unit of the United States Army. Instated in 1943 during World War II, the unit was given the unprecedented and undeniably dangerous job of jumping into forests that were set on fire by the nation's enemy at war. The unit was nicknamed the Triple Nickles because of its numerical designation and because 17 of the original 20-member "colored test platoon" came from the 92nd Infantry Division, or Buffalo Division. Hence, the nickname Buffalo Nickles, symbolized by three buffalo nickels joined in a triangle. The unit's 75-year legacy intersects with USDA Forest Service history in a very special way. Further details are available in an Oregon Historical Society article about the Triple Nickles -- 555th Parachute Infantry Battalion (oregonencyclopedia.org). PFC Malvin L. Brown (1920- 1945), an African American medic and a member of the Division, was the first casualty in the USFS Smokejumper Program in Oregon. In January 2023, the BGN approved a proposal to change the name of the adjacent Negro Ridge to Malvin Brown Ridge. The waterfall was reportedly recorded as "Negro Creek Falls" in the World Waterfall Database, but both it and the Northwest Waterfall Survey list is as "Unnamed Waterfall."

proposals.name_history: Named for local settlers from the Douglass family, specifically, George Douglass, Sr. (1726-1799), District Magistrate, iron trader, and store owner, and his son George Douglass, Sr. (1767-1833), founding shareholder in a local covered bridge company.
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Douglass Island to a 1.7-acre island in the Schuylkill River in Amity Township, west of Douglassville, in Berks County. The proponent reports that he has owned the property for seven years and that the name refers to "local settlers from the Douglass family, which is how we ended up with [nearby] Douglass (Berks), Douglass (Montgomery), and Douglassville." According to the Historic Preservation Trust of Berks County, which endorses the name: George Douglass, Sr. [1726-1799] was a prosperous and patriotic resident living and prospering on his property, which encompassed several hundred acres just down-river from the subject island. [He] built a 'manor house' on the site; served as District Magistrate for the region; founded and operated the 'Amity Store,' the first 'general store' in the region; served as captain in a Pennsylvania Flying Camp division in the Revolutionary War; traded in iron with local furnaces, forges, foundries, and blacksmiths; and built the 1765 White Horse Tavern, a stone's throw from his house. Both these stone-masonry structures are still standing and being restored and preserved by this Trust. Further, "Douglass, Sr.'s son and namesake, George Douglass, Jr. [1767-1833] was a founding shareholder in the covered bridge company which constructed the 1832 bridge which carried the road . . . across the river." The 1790 Federal Census of Amity Township lists George Douglass and his family and one enslaved person. Father and son are buried in Saint Gabriel's Episcopal Church Cemetery, a short distance to the east of the island in question. SOUTH CAROLINA

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Cherokee Creek to an unnamed 0.7-mile-long tributary of the Tugaloo River in Oconee County. The stream heads just inside the boundary of the Francis Marion and Sumter National Forests, and its mouth enters the Hartwell Recreation Area, managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The proposed name is associated with the Cherokee Creek Boys School, which is located along the stream. The proponents serve as the school's executive director and its science teacher. The school was established in 2003, and according to its website, is "a therapeutic boarding school for boys that offers the benefits of small enrollment, hands-on academics, therapy, counseling, recreation, athletics and a talented staff dedicated to helping middle school-aged boys." GNIS lists 24 geographic features in South Carolina with "Cherokee" in their names; of these, three are streams named Cherokee Creek. Lake Cherokee, a reservoir, and Cherokee Gardens, an unincorporated community, are in Oconee County, 21 miles and 23 miles, respectively, from the stream in question.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Munson Creek, an 11-mile-long stream in Marshall County and Roberts County, to Monson Creek. Portions of the stream flow through the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation. Although the existing name has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1964, the proponent, a resident of Claire City and a member of the Monson family, states that the stream was named for his grandfather Orville James Monson (ca.1883-1963), whose parents "came to this area . . . from Norway; they homesteaded in South Dakota and Minnesota. People started calling the stream in question Monson Creek because Orville was frequently seen watering his oxen in the stream." General Land Office records show that Orville Monson acquired 200 acres along the stream in Marshall County in 1914 and 1918. Monson is also listed in the Federal and State censuses for Marshall County and in draft registration records, and his gravestone, in Sisseton Cemetery, names him Orville Monson. A number of other individuals named Monson, including siblings of Orville, settled in neighboring Roberts County. Other records spell the family name Munson or Monsen. A relative of the proponent stated "It's been the Monson homestead for a long time (it was a centennial homestead or something like that) so would mean a lot to the family to be spelled correctly."
