proposals.title: Change Nazi Creek to Kaxchim Chiĝanaa
proposals.proposal_type: change a name considered offensive
proposals.feature_description: On Little Kiska Island, flows generally E and SE into Beaver Inlet
proposals.name_history: Unangax̂ name meaning "creek or river of Kangchix̂" referring to the Unangax̂ name for Kiska Island
proposals.land_ownership: Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge / Aleutian Islands Wilderness
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Nazi Creek: U.S. Army, ca. 1943; Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, 1967
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Nazi Creek, an approximately one-mile-long stream that flows into Beaver Inlet on the southern coast of Little Kiska Island, to Kaxchim Chiĝanaa. The stream is within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge's Aleutian Islands Wilderness and in the Aleutians West Census Area. (The name was originally proposed as Kangchix̂ Chiĝanaa, but later amended after the proponent consulted with an Unangam Tunuu expert.) Although the stream has never been labeled on USGS topographic names and it is not known whether the name is used today, research shows that it was applied during World War II as part of the U.S. Army's letter grid system. Names were added to military maps ahead of Operation Cottage, which took place in August 1943 in an effort to retake Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island from Japanese forces. The name was added to GNIS citing Donald Orth's 1967 Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, USGS Professional Paper 567, the introduction of which states: This work is an alphabetical list of the geographic names that are now applied and have been applied to places and features of the Alaska landscape. Principal names, compiled from modern maps and charts and printed in boldface type, generally reflect present- day local usage. The entry for Nazi Creek is in normal, not boldface, type and reads: Stream, flowing SE 0.7 mi. to Pacific Ocean, Little Kiska I., Aleutian Is.; 51°56'52"N, 177°40'20"E; (map 14). An arbitrary name beginning with 'N' to correspond to 'N' grid used by the U.S. Army for tactical purposes during World War II; published on a 1953 Army Map Service map. Orth lists over 250 names applied to features on Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island as a result of the Army's project. It also lists approximately 60 "arbitrary names applied to features on Kiska I. by USAAF [U.S. Army Air Force] for tactical purposes during World War II." These names do not follow any pattern, but there are groups of plant, animal, and bird names. The Dictionary does not list the datum or projection used to record the coordinates, but they were presumably in the North American Datum 1927. Many of the GNIS entries on Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island no longer plot correctly due to datum shift. As such, it is difficult to determine the exact location of Nazi Creek. The entry for Beaver Inlet ("one of the animal names arbitrarily applied to features in this area") reports that it was located "at the mouth of Nazi Creek." In GNIS, Beaver Inlet plots 0.1 miles inland. The stream is not recorded in the National Hydrography Dataset, while third-party maps such as OpenStreetMap apply the name Nazi Creek to a stream elsewhere on the island. Although it is unknown why specific names were chosen by the U.S. Army, the letter grid naming system itself is well documented and there appears to be no intentional motive by the U.S. Army in 1943 to "honor" the Nazi regime or Adolf Hitler by applying the name Nazi Creek. The proponent of the change to Kangchim Chiĝanaa is a member of the Qagan Tayagungin Tribe of Sand Point; he states: Nazi Creek is not an appropriate name for anywhere in the United States. Millions of people were murdered by Nazis in the 1930s and 1940s. Retaining the name Nazi Creek honors murderers. Nazis and their Allies seriously disrupted lives in the United States and Europe with the murder of over six million Jewish people, with the bombing of Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941 and the bombing of Unalaska (also known as Dutch Harbor) on June 3, 1942. The Japanese Imperial Military invaded and occupied Kiska and Attu Village, taking 42 Unangax̂ Attuans prisoner of war to Japan where 24 innocent Americans died, mostly from starvation. The United States military forcibly relocated 881 Unangax̂ people from the Aleutian Islands and the Pribilof Islands to southeast Alaska, dumping them in abandoned mines and canneries where there were high rates of wrongful deaths. U.S. Army Private George Fox, born in Unga Village off the coast of Alaska and raised in Unalaska Village in the Aleutian Islands, was killed in action in Italy north of Anzio Beach fighting Nazis and trying to take Rome back from the Nazis. To retain the name Nazi Creek is a dishonor to Private George Fox, a dishonor to the Unangax̂ people who died in World War II [and] a dishonor to the millions of Jewish people and service members who died protecting the world from Adolf Hitler and the Nazis. The proponent originally submitted the name Kangchix̂ Creek; in the Unangax̂ language, "Kangchix̂" is the locally used name for Little Kiska Island and means "gizzard" (Aleut Dictionary; Knut Bergsland at the Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks, 1994). In a letter to the Alaska Historical Commission (AHC), which serves as the Alaska Geographic Names Board, the proponent stated, "Some sources indicate the naming of the creek was arbitrary; I find this challenging to believe." He referred to a 2021 Daily Beast article titled "The Secret History of Nazi Creek, Alaska," stating: In his article, [author Andrew] Kirell implies that the naming of Nazi Creek may not have been arbitrary since nearby geographical place names (apparently named around the same time as Nazi Creek) include Rookie Lake, Sargeant [sic] Cove, and Moron Lake. Kirell added: And though the names [on Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island] are ostensibly arbitrary . . . other place names give some insight into what might have been on the naming personnel's mind at the same time he thought up Nazi Creek. Just 8 miles northwest, across the harbor and up a few ridges on Kiska, there exists another "arbitrarily" named body of water. It's called Moron Lake. The proponent also stated that "The Unangax̂ People" have called this stream Kangchix̂ Creek [sic] for "hundreds or thousands of years." However, this seems to be a reference to the island, not this specific stream. After consulting an Aleut language expert, the proponent modified the proposal to Kangchim Chiĝanaa, meaning "creek or river belonging to Kangchix̂ [gizzard island]." (And then later to Kaxchim Chiĝanaa.) He provided support from the Aleut Corporation, The Eyak Corporation, and the Executive Director of the Museum of the Aleutians. The proponent shared the revised name with these groups; to date, the museum director has replied with support for Kaxchim Chiĝanaa. He adds that he has also obtained support from Unangax̂ leaders and citizens. The AHC has informed the proponent that before they will consider the proposal, he should confirm that there is no pre-existing Unangax̂ name for this stream (or that Kaxchim Chiĝanaa is or was in local use), and to show that all Native groups in the area concur with the change to Kaxchim Chiĝanaa. The proponent reported that the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge Manager has no objection to changing the name, adding that he was unaware of the existing name "but another USFW [sic] employee was." The other "N" names recorded in The Dictionary of Alaska Place Names and added to GNIS are Natural Hill, Neck Creek, New Lakes, Newlin Ridge, Nip Hill, Nude Hill, and Nugget Hill. Nip Hill is on the Advisory Committee on Reconciliation in Place Names list of potentially derogatory geographic feature names submitted to the Secretary of the Interior for consideration under Secretary's Order 3405. CALIFORNIA

proposals.submitter: Jonathan Katayanagi; Lafayette, CA Date submitted 3/6/2024
proposals.proposal_type: make official a commemorative name in local use
proposals.proponent: City of Lafayette Parks, Trails & Recreation
proposals.feature_description: In the City of Lafayette, 1.9. mi. E of Lafayette Reservoir
proposals.name_history: The name honors Mark Mitchell (1957-2018), City of Lafayette Council Member, Mayor, and member and Chair of the Planning Commission
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: Mitchell Ridge (Lafayette City Council Resolution 2019; Lafayette Chamber of Commerce 2019; Lamorinda Weekly 2019; City plaque)
proposals.case_summary: The name Mitchell Ridge is proposed to be made official for a 0.9-mile-long, 663-foot ridge located within the City of Lafayette in Contra Costa County. The name would commemorate Mark Mitchell (1957-2018), who according to the proposal, was "a lifelong Lafayette resident who dedicated his political philosophy to bettering his community of Lafayette." The proposal, submitted by the Director of the City of Lafayette Parks, Trails & Recreation, states that Mitchell "served his community with honor, dignity, and humility" as an elected City Council Member (2012-2018), Mayor (2015-2016), Planning Commissioner (2001-2012), and chair of the Planning Commission in 2008. Furthermore: Mark Mitchell joined Lafayette's Planning Commission to preserve the City's hillsides [and] ridgelines and remained a staunch advocate for open space preservation throughout his time as a volunteer public servant and elected official. Mark Mitchell formulated policies that set the framework for development in Lafayette. Always displaying great deference to the General Plan, some of his work included updating the General Plan and its housing element, helping to guide the Downtown Specific Plan, revising the Hillside Ordinance and the rezoning hillsides to low-density residential, creating more realistic guidelines for senior housing, and supporting the creation of the Lafayette Library & Learning Center. [He] was the first Council member born in Lafayette and [he] raised his family in our community while being active in many endeavors. On February 11, 2019, Lafayette City Council passed resolution 2019-6 believing that Mark Mitchell's accomplishments and dedication to the community fit the commemorative naming criteria set forth by the United States Board on Geographic Names and locally named the ridge located at geographic coordinates 37° 52' 39" North and 122° 06' 27" West as Mitchell Ridge. There is a commemorative plaque on the corner of Sweet Drive and Carlyle Terrace marking the ridge as Mitchell Ridge. GNIS includes entries for Mitchell Canyon and Mitchell Rock (a summit) in Contra Costa County. The canyon was named for a Captain Mitchell who "located a claim in the canyon in 1853" (Durham's Place Names of the San Francisco Bay Area, 2000); given the proximity of Mitchell Rock to the canyon it is possible that it too was named for Captain Mitchell.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Sutter Buttes (BGN 1949) to Sacred Buttes to remove a name considered offensive and to acknowledge the sacred history of the buttes to various Tribes. The buttes comprise a cluster of volcanic hills approximately 10 miles in diameter, northwest of the community of Sutter. The highest point, South Butte, has an elevation of 2,110 feet and the buttes also include North Butte and West Butte. The northern slope is within in Sutter Buttes State Park. The feature was named Marysville Buttes on USGS topographic maps from 1888 until 1912 (with reprints until 1943); however, in 1949 it was renamed by the BGN to Sutter Buttes to recognize its location within Sutter County. A previous request to change the name from Marysville Buttes to Sutter Buttes was denied by the BGN in 1924. The 1949 decision stated: . . . evidence indicates that these hills are, or have been known by at least fifteen different names, of which 'Marysville Buttes' and 'Sutter Buttes' appear to have had most usage. After the naming of Marysville in 1850, they were commonly called 'Marysville Buttes' but a boundary change in 1854 threw them into Sutter County . . . . Since then, local usage has changed to 'Sutter Buttes' . . . therefore, on the basis of history, location, and present local usage, we recommend 'Sutter Buttes' for decision. Variant names recorded in GNIS include Bute Mountain, Bute Mountains, Buttes, Buttes Mountains, Los Picos De Sutter, Los Tres Picos, Marysville Buttes, Picachos, Prairie Buttes, Spirit Mountain, Sutter County Buttes, Sutter's Buttes, Sutters Buttes, The Buttes, The Buttes of Sacramento, The Mountain of the Breathing Spirit, The Three Buttes, and Three Buttes. The proponent of the change to Sacred Buttes writes: The Sutter Buttes are named for John Sutter, a European immigrant known for enslaving, whipping, starving, executing, and stealing the babies of Native Americans. Wikipedia's article on John Sutter currently has five quotations from Sutter's contemporaries reporting on his extraordinarily cruel and inhumane treatment on Native Americans. . . It feels especially harmful for a landmass that is sacred to multiple Native American tribes to retain the name of someone who is infamous for his horrific treatment of Native Americans." The Sutter Buttes are so sacred to Native Americans that they historically were not held in any one tribe's territory, but were territorially shared by the surrounding tribes. The Buttes are known as 'Estom Yanim in Nisenan, Histum Yani or Esto Yamani in Maidu, and Olonai-To in Wintun. Because the Buttes are spiritually significant to multiple tribes, it does not seem appropriate to name them in the language of one tribe. Because the Buttes have always been considered a sacred space, I proposed renaming the range to the Sacred Buttes. This name acknowledges the indigenous history of the area. John Sutter and Captain Edward M. Kern led a series of massacres in March 1846, killing twenty California Indians. To establish his fort and the ranching network, he kidnapped, starved, enslaved Indians under the threat of violence, with one claim by James Clyman stating he "keeps 600-800 Indians in a complete state of Slavery." The massacres had no repercussions for the men involved and preceded the legalization of forced servitude of Indians by White settlers, "Act for the Government and Protection of Indians" (Wikipedia: Kern and Sutter Massacres). Despite the devastation and displacement of Native Americans, Sutter Buttes remained a significant part of Native American mythology. Sacramento Valley natives performed sacred dances, some based on visions of animals and spirits. In the 1870s, the California Ghost Dance and Wintun's Hesi ceremonies combined to create the Big Head dance, still performed today as a dance of renewal (Sacred Land Film Project). GNIS lists 21 features in California named Sutter, including the City of Sutter Creek and the unincorporated communities of Sutter and Sutter Hill, as well as a number of census divisions. Geographic features include South Branch Sutter Creek, South Sutter Ditch, Sutter Basin, Sutter Butte Canal, Sutter By-Pass (lake), Sutter City Lateral (canal), Sutter County Extension Canal, Sutter Creek, Sutter Island, Sutter Slough (gut), and Sutter Slough (stream). There are no features listed in GNIS within California with "Sacred" in the name.

proposals.stakeholders: Local government Sutter County Board of Supervisors State Names Authority California Advisory Committee on Geographic Names Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other California Department of Parks and Recreation The proponent writes, "The notable features of this island include a pool of stagnant, fetid water at the island's center, a few wooden pylons near the pool of water, and a small sand- spit at the northeast end of the island . . . California sea lions can often be spotted resting upon the shores of this island." He adds, "Most residents of Humboldt County that I have spoken to about this island have either been oblivious to its existence . . . I believe it requires a name because it is a relatively untainted area of wilderness on the Humboldt Bay . . . Having a name would give people a little bit more of a reason to remember it, and to consider its existence. I propose the name 'Skate Island' after the skates that reside in Humboldt Bay surrounding the island and are also frequently overlooked or disregarded. . ." According to Wikipedia, skates belong to the ancient lineage of cartilaginous fishes and have a flat body shape with flat pectoral fins that extend the length of their body. GNIS lists no features in California named "Skate." COLORADO

proposals.title: Change Kit Carson Mountain to Mount Crestone
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive
proposals.feature_description: In Rio Grande National Forest, in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, 5 mi. E of the community of Crestone
proposals.name_history: Named in association with the Town of Crestone
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Kit Carson Mountain (USGS 1967, 2001, 2022)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal, to change the name of Kit Carson Mountain to Mount Crestone, was submitted as a counterproposal to two previous proposals to change the name to Frustum Peak (Review List 442) or Tabeguache Ute Peak (Review List 454). An additional proposal, to change the name to Lawrence Peak, was subsequently withdrawn. The approximately 1.8-mile-long ridge is located in Saguache County, on the Rio Grande National Forest, within the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, and five miles east of the Town of Crestone. The proposal for Mount Crestone was submitted by the Mayor and Town of Crestone Trustees, who claim the feature has been known locally for many years as Crestone Peak. However, because the latter name, along with Crestone Needle and the collective name Crestone Peaks, are already applied to summits located a short distance to the southeast, and because the Town does not wish to change any of those, they suggest Mount Crestone would be an appropriate alternative and would better distinguish the features. ("The name Mount Crestone is closer to the regionally used historic name of Crestone Peak. Historically, the whole mountain that now encompasses Columbia, Challenger, and Kit Carson [sic] was called Crestone Peak.") In addition to the town and the three named summits, Saguache County also includes three canals, two lakes, and five streams with "Crestone" in their names. As with the previous proposals, a petition provided by the Town states, "The name 'Kit Carson' is offensive to many Americans as Carson was known for his brutality toward Native Americans. This region of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains is still a place of pilgrimage of many tribes. We believe the time has come for a name change of the beautiful iconic mountain that rises above Crestone, Colorado." The petition included 85 signatures in support of the change to Mount Crestone. In a statement to the Valley Courier newspaper, Saguache County Commissioners also supported the name change without suggesting a replacement: "Kit Carson was noted for his bravery in settling the West, however, he was involved in the massacres of indigenous peoples and suppression of the Apache and Diné among others. This genocide should not be celebrated. I would be in favor of a rename of the highest peak, while consulting the community of Crestone and the Ute and Diné people, said Commissioner Liza Marron." The Town also provided two letters of support from descendants of families whose history goes back to the early mining days. The Director of the RedSun Indigenous Institute expressed support for a change but did not specify a replacement name. One individual noted: I have never met a peak-bagger who was confused about those two [the existing "Crestone" features]. They have two different names. Mount Crestone is a different name. No need for confusion. Furthermore, neither the Peak or the Needle have a shape resembling a cock's comb, the crest of a helmet, or the upper part of a seam of rocks. They were obviously named after the original name of their more prominent neighbor, Mount Crestone. As no doubt was the town of Crestone. It is time restore the original name of the mountain. The Town's proposal packet includes three historic postcards and stationery depicting "Crestone Peak" overlooking the community. The proposal form adds, "Had been called Crestone Peak for 140 years. Name was changed in the 1950s to Kit Carson. A nearby peak was then wrongly given the name Crestone Peak." The name Crestone Peak was made official by the BGN in 1969; the decision distinguished the individual peak from Crestone Peaks. The name Kit Carson Peak was made official by the BGN in 1906, and then in 1970 it was changed to Kit Carson Mountain. In 2008, the BGN was asked to change the name of Kit Carson Mountain to Mount Crestone; although the town and county governments endorsed the change, the BGN rejected it, citing input from the Colorado Board on Geographic Names and the U.S. Forest Service, both of which stated "a reluctance to change a name in longstanding published use, and a concern that changing the name and adding an additional Crestone name to the area would lead to further confusion." The proponent at the time disputed the claims of confusion "since there has been confusion for 100+ years." Also in 2011, the BGN considered two proposals to name the highest (unnamed) point on Kit Carson Mountain either Kit Carson Peak or Tranquility Peak (the latter being to continue the "theme" of Challenger Point (BGN 1987) and Columbia Point (BGN 2003)). Both proposals were rejected, and the highest point has remained unnamed. There continues to be confusion as to the application of the various names in the area. FLORIDA

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of one of two lakes in Osceola County that are both named Buck Lake to West Buck Lake. The lake in question is located at Four Corners in the western part of the county; the other one is located 29 miles to the east-southeast. Both lakes have been named on USGS topographic maps since 1953. The proposal was submitted by the Osceala County Office of Community Development on behalf of the County Board Commissioners; it states: "A Base Flood Elevation is being established for Buck Lake [GNIS FID 279574], and this is causing a duplication of names within [our] Flood Insurance Study. To alleviate this confusion, we would like to rename Buck Lake [FID 279575] to West Buck Lake, as it is the smaller and lesser known of the two lakes." GNIS lists no other features in Florida named "West Buck Lake." GEORGIA

proposals.case_summary: The new name Kilmahew Creek is proposed for a 2.5-mile tributary of Sumac Creek, which runs parallel to Highway N225 in Murray County. The proponent writes: 'Kilmahew' is derived from ancient Gaelic. The prefix 'Kil' means Cill or Church of and 'Mahew' means Matthew, the patron saint of the area. The lands of Kilmahew Castle [in Dumbartonshire, Scotland] were occupied by [my ancestors] for nearly 700 years. Many from the area immigrated to the United States prior to Independence. Their descendants play a huge role in Murray County today. The proponent provided a website which details the lineage and history of 18 generations of the Clan of Napier (his family), including their settlement in North America. His ancestors, including Thomas Napier, were recorded in Murray County as early as 1849. GNIS lists no records with "Kilmahew" in the name.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Reyes Beach is proposed for a small beach on Oahu's east shore and within the census designated place of Waimānalo Beach. The unnamed beach is between Kaiona Beach Park and Kaupō Beach Park, adjacent to Kalaniana'ole Highway. Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X The name would honor the proponent's grandfather and former Lieutenant Governor of Guam, Edward Diego Reyes (1930-2018). The proponent notes, "He raised his children, my mother, in Oʻahu and retired in Hawaii Kai. He dedicated his life to public service and took pride in the values that came from being a Pacific Islander. His family would like to honor his legacy by naming a geographic location after him." She concludes, "Edward Diego Reyes was a Chamoru politician and retired U.S. Air Force colonel. He raised his four children in Hawaii Kai and eventually retired before passing away at home." The Wikipedia page for Reyes notes that he was a Vietnam War veteran with several awards and honors. According to the news site guampdn.com, when Reyes passed in Honolulu, the governor of Guam declared a state of mourning for the island of Guam and ordered flags to be at half- staff in his honor. Reyes is buried in Guam Veterans Cemetery. GNIS lists no features in Hawaii with names that may sound like Reyes (i.e., Reys, Raise, Ray, Rae). ILLINOIS

proposals.title: Change Cherry Hill Woods Slough to Shïshko Mbishke
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize Tribal preference
proposals.proponent: Forest Preserve District of Cook County

proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Cherry Hill Woods Sloughs: USGS 2023; Secretary's Order 3404 Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force name changes announcement and media coverage, 2022 o Laughing Sq___ Sloughs: USGS 1963, 1993, 1997, 2012; local hiking books and articles
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Cherry Hill Woods Slough, located in Palos Township in Cook County, to Shïshko Mbishke. The feature is within the Forest Preserves of Cook County (FPCC) Swallow Cliff Woods Preserve. In the Boodewaadamiimowin (Potawatomi) language, Shïshko Mbishke means "muskrat swamp." The FPCC Naming Committee proposed the name after discussions with the Tribal Office of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation to determine a more preferred Boodewaadamiimowin spelling and name than Zheshk Bitobig ("muskrat sloughs") that had been proposed by the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe - Mille Lacs Band (Review List 451). In April 2022, in response to Secretary's Order 3404 (S.O. 3404), the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe - Mille Lacs Band submitted a number of replacements for names that contained "sq___," including replacing Laughing Sq___ Sloughs with Cherry Hill Woods [sic]. The latter name was the fourth-nearest geographic feature listed in the candidate list. The Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force (TF) submitted the name Cherry Hill Woods Sloughs to the BGN, which approved the change on September 8, 2022. The FPCC had previously proposed the name Muskrat Slough in October 2022 as a change to the S.O. 3404 name. They had submitted this name to the TF, but it was not chosen as the replacement. FPCC reported that it had worked with the American Indian Center and the Chicago American Indian Community Collaborative to choose the name, which referenced a local animal species that is important in the creation traditions of the region's indigenous populations. When asked about the Muskrat Slough proposal, the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe - Mille Lacs Band proposed a Boodewaadamiimowin (Potawatomi) translation of the name, Zheshk Bitobig. FPCC had questions about the most preferred version of the Boodewaadamiimowin words and contacted the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation. FPCC reported that they received a different spelling from the Language Keepers from the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi in Indiana but stated: We have decided to honor the local regional dialect and determined that shïshko mbishke (literal - muskrat swamp) is the most localized spelling of Muskrat Slough, reflecting the regional dialect of Boodewaadamiimowin (Potawatomi) from the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation. [The Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation Tribal Office later confirmed that the name should be capitalized as Shïshko Mbishke.] The former "sq___" name had been labeled on USGS maps since 1963; no information regarding its origin could be found. A 1985 Chicago Tribune article reported that "[a] story, perhaps a legend, says the last Indian sq___ residing in the Palos area after the arrival of the white man refused to leave her wigwam on the top of Swallow Cliff where it overlooked the moraines, lakes and sloughs that had been carved out by the last glacier to move across the area ages before. . . . Some of the best-named watercourses in the [Cook County] forest preserve system . . . include the sloughs--Long John, Horse Collar, Groundhog, Belly Deep and Laughing Sq___; the woods--Swallow Cliff and Paw Paw; and the lake--Bullfrog." The legend may be the source of the name. Papoose Lake is located 0.3 miles south of the slough. The 1963 volume Indian Place Names in Illinois, published by the Illinois State Historical Society, reported that there was a Laughing Sq___ Lake in the Forest Preserve District of Cook County. It is unclear if this refers to the slough feature or a different nearby lake. A 1979 U.S. Department of Agriculture Soil Survey Report labeled a lake southwest of the slough as Laughing Sq___ Sloughs. This lake does not have an official name.

proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature

proposals.name_history: Named for Larry Horner (1939-2013) and his son John Horner (1965-2011), who built the lake in 2003.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: Horner Lake (memorial on lake) o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Horner Lake is proposed for an unnamed 16-acre lake located along an unnamed tributary of Sugar Creek in Montrose Township in Lee County. Other Forest Preserves of Cook County [proponent] Support The proposal would honor the proponent's grandfather Larry Horner (1939-2013) and his son John Horner (1965-2011); she states: The land this lake was built on has been in my family since 1904. This piece of Iowa was owned by and made into a homestead by John B. Miller's father. John B. is my grandmother's uncle. . . . They raised their 6 children on this land and in 2003 a portion of the land was dug and flooded using a combination of natural springs and rainwater. This was done to fulfill a lifelong family dream of Larry Horner's to have a lake on his family farm. The lake was built by Larry and his son John Horner in 2003. The lake has served as the place for many of our celebrations [and] family memories . . . The lake was and is one of the most beautiful things that lives on in our family. The proponent adds that there is a monument on the shore of the lake dedicated to the men who built the lake: "The enormous rock that is carved was dug from the depths of the earth when the lake was dug, and it is engraved 'Horner Lake; Est. 2003 by John and Larry Horner.'" The property is maintained by Larry's surviving youngest son Joseph Horner and his wife. The Horner family members are buried in Oakland Cemetery 6.5 miles from the reservoir. GNIS lists no features in Iowa with "Horner" in the name. KENTUCKY *** Note: A proposal to name a lake in Lyon County was subsequently withdrawn by the proponent. proposals.case_summary: The 12.1-mile-long stream that is currently named Coulee Hippolyte flows generally south into Black Bayou. Coulee Hippolyte has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1942, although the 1932 and 1952 editions labeled it Coulee Polete. The origin of the latter name is not known, nor was the BGN involved in the change. The proponent states that he "was unable to find any information on the origin or meaning of the name Hippolyte. It is unknown who the coulee was named after although the name 'Hippolyte' was a common French first name in the 1700s and 1800s." *Partners on the project

proposals.title: Koenck Coteau
proposals.proposal_type: to make official a commemorative name in local use
proposals.feature_description: Located W of Bayou Zourie, S of Entrance Road, NE of Coopers
proposals.name_history: Named for William (1929-2007) and Johnnie Koenck (1933- 2016), long-time residents and contributors to the community
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: Koenck Coteau (proponent's family) o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the commemorative name Koenck Coteau for an area in Vernon Parish that included property owned by the proponent's family. The approximately 100-acre area is generally defined as a small rise between two valleys. The proponent reports that the name is used by his family, "who have homesteaded this Coteau for over half a century." The name would specifically commemorate William (1929- 2007) and Johnnie (1933-2016) Koenck. William served in the U.S. Army for 21 years, including time in Korea and Vietnam, retiring as Sergeant First Class; both he and his wife Bayou Greenbelt team *Support contributed to the community. The proposal states, "This designation would be a fitting tribute to a family that has cultivated and cared for this land over numerous generations." He adds that the term "coteau" in Louisiana refers to a hilly upland, typically signifying the divide between two low areas. Although the local relief is no more than 10-15 feet, the proponent reports that that is significant in Louisiana. GNIS lists 18 features in Louisiana with names that include "Coteau," of which eight are classified as areas. They are all located in the southeast part of the State, i.e., between Baton Rouge and New Orleans. There are also five communities, including the Town of Grand Coteau in Saint Landry Parish, and four streams. When asked to comment on whether the term is appropriate for Vernon Parish, i.e., in the west-central part of the State, the proponent responded: While many are familiar with the remaining few francophone areas in Louisiana such as Acadiana, the oldest part of French Louisiana extends 70 miles north of the proposed area. Natchitoches is the oldest European settlement in present-day Louisiana. The settlement was founded by the French explorer Louis Juchereau de St. Denis in 1714 in order to prevent additional incursion by the Spanish into this area previously claimed by the French. This area known as the 'Neutral Ground' was claimed by both Spain and France and would remain in dispute even after the Louisiana Purchase until the Adams- Onís Treaty of 1819 was signed. Furthermore, prior to the United States acquisition of this territory through the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803, the primary settlers who came to the area were ethnic French and three years before New Orleans was founded. The French influence in this area is memorialized in the names of several major waterways in Vernon Parish. These include Bayou Zourie, Bayou Anacoco, and Bayou Castor. Additionally, the proposed area's distinct shape and hillside are formed by the bottomlands of Bayou Zourie. Consequently, it would be only right to give the geographic feature overlooking the bayou's bottomland a French name. MAINE

proposals.title: Gladys and Rose Hill
proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Between Long Pond and West Pond, 1 mi. E of Bickford Hill, 1 mi. SE of Collomy Hill
proposals.name_history: The name commemorates Gladys Irene Black (1908-2017) and Rosaria "Rose" Vito (1921-2017)
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: o The Hill (property owners and family) o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Gladys and Rose Hill is proposed for a 738-foot hill in the Town of Parsonsfield in York County. The feature is between Long Pond and West Pond, with approximately 11 acres of the property subject to a Woodland Conservation Easement held by the Town of Parsonsfield and the State of Maine. The name would honor the mothers of the current property owners: Gladys Irene Black (1908-1993) and Rosaria "Rose" Josephine Vito (1921-2017). The proponent, the daughter of Rose Vito, writes that she is submitting the proposal on behalf of her late husband, the son of Gladys Black, to memorialize their families' "compound atop the hill" which overlooks the foothills of the White Mountains, as well as Long Pond and West Pond. She confirms that the two women did not have a direct association with the hill, but adds: Both women were devoted mothers after whom the property owners chose to name the subject property in 1997. Each woman instilled very strong family ties within their respective families and motivated the property owners to create a family compound and preserve on the subject property. Both women were dedicated to the effort and provided immeasurable moral support and encouragement. Hence, the name of this location became [Gladys and Rose Hill], affectionately deemed 'The Hill' by members of both families. Family reunions are a tradition inspired by our mothers' deep sense of family. While Gladys Black predeceased the establishment of 'Gladys & Rose Hill,' it was her 40 years of hosting family reunions for her six children and their families that created the momentum well beyond her death. Similarly, Rosaria Vito strongly fostered our efforts to create Gladys [and] Rose Hill because it was instrumental in reinforcing familial bonds. She did that from afar as well as when present at the Hill. Gladys and Rosaria's contributions were beyond measure, and they are worthy of being recognized for the same. The obituary of Gladys Black notes that she lived in Saco, was a secretary and member of the Order of the Eastern Star in Saco, the Women's Educational and Industrial Union, the Tri-U Club, and served on the executive board of the Rainbow Girls in Old Orchard Beach. She was also a past deaconess of the First Parish Congregational Church, United Church of Christ, Saco, and a member of the church's Madisses. Gladys is buried Laurel Hill Cemetery in Saco. Rosaria Vito's obituary alludes to her devotion to family matters.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Loon Call Island is proposed for a 0.5-acre island located at the north end of Togus Pond in the City of Augusta in Kennebec County. The proponents reports that their family owns the island and "We would like it to be named Loon Call Island as there has been an asylum of loons using our pond as a habitat for years . . . [we] believe this is an appropriate name for the island. We are very [conscious] of the preservation of the loon population (we counted 17 [in the] summer of 2023)." The proponent adds that their tax forms show it as "Hayden Rd. Island"; Hayden Road runs along the shoreline of Togus Pond. The proponent provided a screenshot of a Facebook post in which they asked members of the Friends of Togus Pond group for their opinion. Two comments state their affinity for the pond, one wrote "I like it!," and another wrote "Loon Call is very good." The same proponent previously proposed to name the island Loon-atic Island (Review List 440); however, this name was rejected by the BGN in December 2020, citing the objections of the Augusta City Council and the Kennebec County Commissioners, which expressed concerns that the name "is not appropriate to those who suffer from mental illness," and "is an inappropriate reference to stigmatize a mental health condition," respectively. The Maine State Geographic Names Authority concurred with the city and county recommendations. GNIS lists 25 features in Maine with "Loon" in their names, including two in in Kennebec County: Loon Island and Loon Pond. The island is located in Long Pond, 17 miles northwest of the island in question, while the lake is 19 miles to the southwest. proposals.case_summary: The new name Third Parish Hill is proposed for a 73-foot elevation hill in the Town of Hampton Falls in Rockingham County. The proponent is a local resident who reports that the town center was formerly known as Third Parish of Hampton. Although the local relief is less than 30 feet from the surrounding area, the proponent states, "the hill's rise is noticeable when driving along [U.S.] Route 1 toward Hampton Falls; the road rises steeply until it peaks at the stoplight by the town common, after which it descends." He adds, "The name 'Third Parish' comes from the town's former name, when it was established as the Third Parish of Hampton, a township which formerly extended to include all of modern-day Hampton Falls. The peak is currently unnamed, and the name Third Parish Hill is a worthy tribute to the town's history and a name that is rarely seen anymore. I believe the hill is notable enough within the town to deserve an official name, as it is the location town's common and its sole stoplight." An excerpt from Joseph Dow's History of the town of Hampton, New Hampshire From its settlement in 1638, to the autumn of 1892, titled "The Third Parish in Hampton" and published in 1893, describes its history: In 1732, certain men in the west part of Hampton Falls and the east part of Kingston petitioned the General Assembly to be set off as a "town or parrish [sic]," assigning the usual reason, their great distance from church. The west part of Hampton Falls, however, became the town of Kensington, by an act passed, August 19, 1737. Soon after, the bounds were established and the "third parish of Hampton" was in the exercise of all town privileges, except that of sending a representative to the General Assembly. In 1740, this was also granted, on petition of the inhabitants. The Wikipedia page for the town provides a different timeline but adds: It was not until 1709 that the town was officially established as the Third Parish of Hampton. The Third Parish originally consisted of all land south of the Taylor River and north of the New Hampshire/Massachusetts border, or the modern-day towns of Seabrook, Kensington, and Hampton Falls. proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Negro Point: Office of Coast Survey 1875-present; area maps since at least 1867; Federal documents since at least 1896 o Scylla Point: New York City Department of Parks & Recreation since 2011
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Negro Point in the Borough of Manhattan in New York City to Mulzac Point. The point is within Wards Island Park on the southern end of Wards Island and extends slightly into the Hell Gate of the East River. (Negro Point is sometimes said to be at the southern end of Randalls Island; Wards Island and Randalls Island were formerly separated but are now one island.) The proposal was submitted in response to a previous application to rename the point to Tenkenas Point (Review List 452). The name Negro Point was a 1982 BGN decision. It appeared as early as 1851 on Office of Coast Survey charts and since 1867 on commercial maps of the area. The name did not appear on USGS topographic maps until 2011. The 1982 decision resulted from a request from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to establish the name in local use. The origin of the name Negro Point has not been determined. The 1851 Office of Coast Survey (OCS) chart "Hell Gate and its Approaches" showed the name Negro Point, along with "Negro Point Bluff" 0.2 miles upstream and two rocks labeled as "Negro Head" and "Little Negro Head" 0.7 miles downstream. These rocks were removed from Hell Gate by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in the late 1800s during efforts to improve navigation in Hell Gate; they are not shown on the 1892 chart. Neither the rocks nor the bluff are recorded in GNIS. OCS charts ceased labeling "Negro Point Bluff" after 1916. In 2001, the City of New York Parks and Recreation Department Commissioner submitted a proposal to the BGN to change the name of Negro Point to Scylla Point. This name referred to Scylla and Charybdis, two monsters from Greek mythology said to have been located at the Strait of Messina between Sicily and the Italian mainland (the point lies along a stretch of the East River known as Hell Gate). In 2001, the New York Parks and Recreation Department had already renamed a playground in Astoria, Queens opposite Negro Point as Charybdis Playground. In 2011, the BGN voted not to approve the change, citing "a reluctance to change a name in longstanding use and in the belief that changing it would create a navigation hazard. The committee also cited a lack of evidence that the name is offensive." At the time of the 2011 decision, the BGN had received the following recommendations: Local government Mayor of New York Support Manhattan Borough Council No response State Names Authority New York Geographic Names Committee No objection Federal agencies National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Oppose U.S. Coast Guard Oppose/No objection Other New York Parks and Recreation Department [proponent] Support Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Support Sandy Hook Pilots Association Oppose Manhattan Psychiatric Center No opinion The recommendation from NOAA in 2011 cited input from a spokesperson for the Sandy Hook Pilots Association, who stated "If the name is changed, mariners familiar with the area will still continue to use the present name when giving security calls thus confusing transient vessel operators." The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) supported NOAA's recommendation: "DHS [Department of Homeland Security] [specifically USCG] as a customer of NOAA charts will defer to NOAA. . . . the USCG would have no objection to a name change." The Chair of the Community Board 11 of Manhattan (CB11) submitted the proposed name, which would honor Captain Hugh Mulzac (1886-1971), a Black Captain of a Liberty Ship in World War II and who lived in New York City. CB11 considered three potential replacement names shared by the Manhattan Borough Historian that would honor mariners from New York City's Black community. The Chair wrote: Community Board 11 (CB11) recommends renaming 'Negro Point' on Ward's Island to 'Mulzac Point', in honor of Captain Hugh Mulzac, to discontinue the use of offensive or racist words for American geographic locations - while acknowledging Black / African American history, maritime history, and New York City history. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names (USBGN) has previously shown reluctance to proposed name changes for this location, citing: the longstanding use of 'Negro Point'; navigational hazard concerns brought forward by stakeholders; and, a lack of evidence that the name is offensive. CB11 asks that the USBGN reconsider its position; further discourage the use of inappropriately-named locations for navigation; and seize this opportunity to honor a Black mariner who was a prominent member of the African American community in New York City. The Chair quoted a brief summary of Captain Mulzac's life provided by the Manhattan Borough Historian: [Captain Hugh Mulzac was] an immigrant to the United States from the West Indies and the first Black man to command a ship in the United States Merchant Marine. Although fully qualified to command a ship for more than two decades, his career was limited by racial discrimination until World War II, when he assumed command of the Booker T. Washington, a merchant vessel with -- at his insistence -- an integrated crew. In the 1950s, however, he was attacked for his ties to Communists in the maritime trades, questioned by the House Un-American Activities Committee, and for years was barred from going to sea. A Queens resident, he ran for Borough President on the American Labor Party ticket in 1951 and for New York State Comptroller as an independent socialist in 1958. Mulzac was also a painter and the author of an autobiography, A Star to Steer By, and the father of Una Mulzac, proprietor of the Liberation Bookstore in Harlem. On July 21, 2019, the Netflix show Patriot Act with Hasan Minhaj posted a video on YouTube titled "What's With The Racist Names Of So Many American Places?" In the video, Mr. Minhaj described the BGN and pointed out official place names that contain words that are considered offensive. He stated: In New York City, there's a place called "Negro Point." It's actually on Randalls Island [sic] [it is the southern end of Wards Island; the passage between Randalls Islands and Wards Island has been filled in]. . . . It's no longer Negro Point on Google Maps, but it's still Negro Point on Federal maps. Here's the thing: it doesn't have to be this way. The names of these places can actually be changed. . . . The name changing process is handled by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. Now I had a lot of questions, so I gave them a call. In 2011 there was a hearing to rename Negro Point, but there were several groups opposed to it, including the Sandy Hook Pilots Association, NOAA, and the Coast Guard. These groups claimed that changing the maps would potentially confuse tugboat captains. This is crazy to me. I live by Negro Point. I've been there. You guys, it's beautiful. It doesn't deserve this disgusting name. So I went to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names' website and submitted a form to rename Negro Point once and for all. The video showed a typed BGN proposal form with the "Recommended Name" field "Tenkanas Point - based on the Native American name for the island." The BGN never received this form. Mr. Minhaj went on to encourage viewers to submit proposals to the BGN to change any names that included words considered offensive or racist. The BGN received a few proposals in the following week, but dozens of proposals were submitted during the following two weeks once the Greatest Internet Scavenger Hunt included an item on that year's list for teams to earn points for submitting proposals to the BGN after watching Mr. Minhaj's video. Approximately three dozen proposals were received and determined to be eligible for consideration; many were not processed because they did not satisfy the BGN's criteria. Eight of the original proposals have since been approved, while an additional 14 names were changed to something other than what was originally submitted. Three were not approved, thus retaining the existing name, and three are still pending. Some features had several changes proposed by different teams or individuals. During a May 2023 office move, BGN staff found an unopened letter from Daniel Davis, the then-producer of Patriot Act with Hasan Minhaj. The proposal was handwritten but was for Tenkenas Point, i.e., the same name as in the typed version shown on the video. The Tenkenas Point proposal states that "Wards Island was known as Tenkenas Island at the time of its appropriation from its native inhabitants to the Dutch in 1637. 'Tenkenas' is Native American [sic] for 'Wild Lands' (NYC Gov Parks website) [this site is presumably the one for Wards Island Park]." A 2010 article by Ives Goddard in New York History titled "The Origin and Meaning of the Name 'Manhattan'" includes the following in a footnote: A Dutch deed of 1637 refers to "the two islands, situate in the Hellegadt, of which the larger is called Tenkenas [Wards Island] and the smaller Minnahanonck [Roosevelt Island, formerly Blackwells Island], lying to the west of the larger"; The identification of these islands follows J.H. French, Gazetteer of the State of New York [1860]. . . . Roosevelt Island (called Blackwell's Island until 1973) was about six-tenths the size of Ward's Island and lies southwest of it. Grumet [in Native American Place Names in New York City, 1981] identifies Minnahanonck as Randall's Island, but this was directly north of Ward's Island, to which it is now joined by landfill. NORTH CAROLINA

proposals.title: Change Clingmans Dome to Kuwohi
proposals.submitter: Chris Siewers, Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Associate Attorney General
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize native name
proposals.proponent: Michell Hicks, Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Principal Chief
proposals.feature_description: The highest point in Tennessee and the third-highest summit E of the Mississippi River, 10 mi. N of Bryson City, 21 mi. S of Sevierville
proposals.name_history: Traditional Cherokee name, which translates to "the Mulberry Place"
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Clingman Dome (USGS 1893) o Clingmans Dome (USGS 1912-2019; AMS 1955, 1957, 1960, 1964, 1976, 1983, 2000; NPS documents since at least 1933; numerous printed and online sources) o Clingman's Dome (NPS 1933; "Early Explorers in the Great Smokies", 1933) o Clingman's Mount ("Early Explorers in the Great Smokies", 1933) o Clingmans Peak (BGN work cards) o Ku-wa-hi (The North Carolina Gazetteer, 2010) o Kuwa'hi ("Myths of the Cherokee", 1900) o Kuwahi ("Early Explorers in the Great Smokies", 1933; Place Names of the Smokies, 1999) o Mount Clingman ("Early Explorers in the Great Smokies", 1933) o Smoky Dome ("Early Explorers in the Great Smokies", 1933; The North Carolina Gazetteer, 2010)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal would change the official name of Clingmans Dome, located along the boundary of Swain County, North Carolina, and Sevier County, Tennessee, to Kuwohi, the Cherokee name for the mountain that translates to "mulberry place." In Cherokee, the name is ᎫᏬᎯ. The summit is in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. It is the highest point in Tennessee, and according to the National Park Service, the third-highest point east of the Mississippi River after Mount Mitchell and Mount Craig in North Carolina. The proposal was submitted by the Principal Chief of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI) following an effort started in 2022 by two EBCI members to rename the summit. The proposal, which comprises 156 pages of supporting material, states: 'Kuwohi' is well documented in Cherokee history. It is the mulberry place, and the highest point in traditional Cherokee territory. Today, it is located within the Great Smoky Mountains National Park and can be viewed from the Qualla Boundary, the home of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, a federally recognized Indian Tribe. A version of Kuwohi has been recognized by the US Government as a variant for Clingmans Dome [Ku-wa-hi, Kuwa'hi, and Kuwahi at the time of the proposal; Kuwohi was added after the proposal was submitted]. The summit is identified as Kuwahi in many historical sources. The EBCI Speaker's Council has given the Tribe guidance that Kuwohi is the most culturally appropriate term. The submission of Kuwohi also recognizes the US BGN policy that diacritics are not used in formal namings [sic]. [Note: the Diacritics Policy states "The BGN may approve a geographic name that includes diacritics."] Kuwohi is a place rooted in the stories and teachings of the Cherokee people. It can be seen from our Mother Town, Kituwah, in Swain County, North Carolina, and was a place to gather fruit and for our medicine men. More recently, Kuwohi provided refuge to Cherokee people who the United States Government sought to remove in 1838. The mountain was always known as Kuwohi to the Cherokee people until it was renamed Clingmans Dome right before the Civil War. Clingman did not have any substantial ties to the area. Members of the Clingman family today support restoring the rightful Cherokee name, Kuwohi. We are attaching local letters of support. Every local government in western North Carolina, and governments in eastern Tennessee, have endorsed this submission. Many local groups with an interest in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park have also supported the submission. The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is aware of no formal opposition to restoring the name Kuwohi. . . . The proposed name restoration has been widely broadcast throughout local, regional and national media with no formal or sustained opposition materializing. The Tribal Council of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians formally passed a Resolution in support of studying the restoration of the name Kuwohi in July 2022. In January 2024, a second Tribal Council Resolution formally gave the Principal Chief authority to submit this request. . . . The 2022 ECBI Tribal Council resolution stated the reasons for working to propose restoring the name restore the name, including: • the documented history of the Cherokee name • the importance of the summit to the Cherokee people in general and the ECBI in particular • Thomas Clingman's lack of association with western North Carolina, his argument in Congress that enslavement be preserved, and that he was a Confederate General • Arnold Guyot, an advocate of "scientific racism," applied the name Clingmans Dome • that "recently, the United States Department of the Interior and Secretary Deb Haaland have shown a willingness to engage with tribes to correct the naming of sacred and reverent places back to their historically appropriate names" as well as Secretary's Order 3404 and examples of renaming Mount Doane to First Peoples Mountain; Mount McKinley to Denali; and Ayers Rock in Australia to Uluru • "the history of the re-naming of Kuwahi ᎫᏩᎯ [sic] to 'Clingman's Dome' shows that the name of Clingman was designated by a proponent of scientific racism (Guyot) on behalf of an avowed racist (Clingman), in an action that was disrespectful to Cherokee people, culture, history, and tradition. . . . the name Clingman is not derogatory in and of itself, but the history shows the action of changing the name of Kuwahi ᎫᏩᎯ [sic] to 'Clingman's Dome' was racist and that the racist action should be acknowledged and corrected. . . . There is no valid reason today by which Kuwahi ᎫᏩᎯ [sic] should continue to be known as 'Clingman's Dome,' particularly given Clingman's and Guyot's racist histories and their lack of ties to our lands" The 2024 ECBI Tribal Council resolution also stated that "one of the most important factors in deciding whether to approve a name restoration is local community support" and reported the following: • Community support for the restoration of the Kuwohi name has been overwhelming, including formal support from multiple local governments, including the counties of: Buncombe, Haywood, Jackson, Macon, Swain, Graham, Clay, and Cherokee, and the towns of Asheville, Andrews, Murphy, Hayesville, Fontana Dam, Lake Santeetlah, Robbinsville, Canton, Clyde, Maggie Valley, Waynesville, Dillsboro, Sylva, Webster, the Village of Forrest Hills, Franklin, Highlands, and Bryson City in western North Carolina, and the counties of Knox and Campbell in eastern Tennessee • In November 2022, Lavita Hill and Mary Crowe were given the North Carolina Dogwood Award by Attorney General Josh Stein, who stated, 'Lavita and Mary ate working to make sure that their tribe's history is recognized and honored.' • In April 2023, the Tennessee General Assembly passed H.J.R. 452, which reads, '[W]e honor and commend Mary Crowe and Lavita Hill on their efforts to restore the traditional Cherokee name of Kuwohi to Clingman's Dome in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park and wish them all the best in their future endeavors'; and Governor Bill Lee thereafter signed H.J.R. 452 into Tennessee law. • In May 2023, world famous musician Yo-Yo Ma performed a concert on Kuwohi with Hill, Jarrett Wildcatt, and Bo Taylor, with the help and support of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, where Ma performed a work of music meant to honor the cultural importance of Kuwohi to the Cherokee people [see YouTube video "Restore Kuwohi! Yo-Yo Ma shares stage with Cherokee artists"] • Many non-profit community organizations in both North Carolina and Tennessee have signaled their support for the Kuwohi name restoration efforts. • With the cooperation of many EBCI tribal members, the Great Smoky Mountain National Park instituted Kuwohi Days, during which the Park Service closes down Clingmans Dome Road for a number of afternoons each year so school children can learn about the history of Kuwohi and the Cherokee people. proposals.case_summary: Mount Douglass is proposed as a replacement name for a 3,865-foot summit in Ashe County, one of two in the county currently named The Peak. It is along the boundary of New River State Park and is visible from the Blue Ridge Parkway and from the New River. The other summit named The Peak is 16 miles to the west. Both summits have been named The Peak on USGS topographic maps since the 1890s (in 1893, the other summit was labeled simply "Peak"). The proponent of the name change is one of the former owners who recently conveyed the property to the State of North Carolina to expand the New River State Park and provide public access to the mountain. The proposed name would honor abolitionist and social reformer Frederick Douglass (1818-1895). The proponent states: First, the existing name . . . aside from being a failure of imagination, conflicts with another mountain in western Ashe County also called The Peak. Second and more important the peak overlooks a large part of the New River in Ashe County. The New River uniquely flows North. The New River was historically a part of the Underground Railway, by which an enslaved person could follow the river to Ohio, a free state. After leaving NC, the river flows northwesterly though Virginia and becomes the Kanawha River at the confluence of the Gauley River near Charleston, WV eventually flowing into the Ohio River. The most other prominent mountain in Ashe County is Mount Jefferson, which was noted in earlier times for its caves where slaves shelter on their way to freedom following the New River. However, there is no public land that recognizes the significance of the New River as part of the Underground Railway in Ashe County. By changing the name of The Peak . . . to Mount Douglass the significance would be recognized and honored. Frederick Douglass, of course, was the foremost former enslaved person in the nineteenth century speaking out on behalf of abolition and support for those fleeing slavery on the Underground Railway. Regarding the association between Douglass and the area, the proponent adds: Although he did not have direct connections with North Carolina, in his travels in the United Kingdom when he was speaking and raising money for the abolitionist cause, he was most warmly welcomed by the Scots whose warmth he found endearing. He loved Robbie Burns poetry, and though Burns had died earlier, Douglass spent an enjoyable time with his sister while in Scotland. North Carolina was settled in large part initially by Scots and Scots Irish. North Carolina State Senator Natasha Marcus, in her support for the change, describes the current name as being "unmemorable and overused" and Mount Douglass as "meaningful and emblematic." She adds, "By naming this mountain for Frederick Douglass, the state would be recognizing the historic efforts of enslaved people journeying through North Carolina to find freedom" and "His name is synonymous with the quest for freedom that the Underground Railroad represents." Further, "This is public land and should have a name that honors our state's history and stands as a testament to our commitment to freedom for all. North Carolina has always championed its declaration of freedom that preceded the Declaration of Independence."

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Weddington Creek is proposed for a 2.48-mile-long tributary of Hicks Creek in Iredell County. The proponent, a local resident, wishes to honor Walter Shaw Weddington (1899-1968), who at one time owned and farmed 251 acres of property along the stream. He was employed by Troutman Chair Company, which crafts and sells farm-house shaker-style chairs. Walter donated part of his property to the New Perth Associate Reformed Presbyterian (A.R.P.) Church. Walter is buried in First United Methodist Church Cemetery, Troutman. The Town of Weddington is in Union County, 45 miles north of the unnamed stream. The name is associated with a Weddington family that settled in the area in the 1820s, but it is not known if there is a connection to Walter. Will High Top

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Will High Top, which the proponent reports is in local use. The summit has an elevation of 3,370 feet and is located at the headwaters of Little Owl Creek, Hayes Mill Creek, and Wagon Timber Branch. The land is managed by the U.S. Forest Service as part of the National Forests in North Carolina. The proponent states that their family "has lived on the same property located at the base of this summit since 1857, when [their great-great-great-grandfather] purchased the property. . . The name Will High Top is the name that all my family as well as other locals have used in reference to the summit." He concludes, "I feel this local summit name needs to be documented by the USGS before it is lost to history." The feature was referenced several times in a local newspaper, The Cherokee Scout, in the 1920s as Will Hightop and Will High Top. One article describes its location as "between Owl Creek and Valley River." The proponent was unable to provide any information regarding the origin of the name. GNIS lists 11 "High Top" named summits in North Carolina, and 25 in the Blue Ridge area. The closest is located in Nantahala National Forest, 3.4 miles northeast of the summit in question. OHIO

The proponent, a resident of Connecticut, reports that he "grew up along the creek, playing in it for many years," and that he wishes to commemorate Joseph Conway (1816-1895), a long-time area resident who served as a Morrow County commissioner from 1867 to 1870. An 1857 Morrow County map shows that Joseph Conway owned three parcels of lands at the headwaters of the creek. He is listed in township census records from 1850 to 1880 and is buried in Bloomfield Cemetery. The Conway family owned property along the stream for many years, but according to the proponent, are no longer associated with the area. He notes that another Conway family member is listed among the Prominent Men and Women of South Bloomfield Township in History of Morrow County, Ohio. GNIS lists no features in Ohio named "Conway."

proposals.case_summary: The name Sylvan Run is proposed for a 1.54-mile-long tributary of the Cuyahoga River in Summit County and within Cuyahoga Valley National Park (CUVA). The proponent states, "The geography of 'Sylvan Run' is characterized by its meandering path through dense forestation, with a mix of deciduous and coniferous trees lining its banks. This canopy provides a natural habitat for a variety of local wildlife and supports a rich biodiversity within the stream itself. The stream's serene environment and scenic beauty make it a cherished natural feature among the local community. It is a site for educational field trips, conservation projects, and recreational activities such as bird watching and photography." Further, "The naming of 'Sylvan Run' recognizes its role as a vital water source and natural component within the broader Cuyahoga Valley watershed."

proposals.case_summary: This proposal, to change the name of Chinaman Hat in Wasco County to China Hat, was submitted by the Oregon Geographic Names Board on behalf of a representative of the Black Rock Grazing Cooperative. The co-op is a group of eight ranchers who have acquired grazing rights on the feature from the Bureau of Land Management. The current name has been shown on USGS topographic maps since 1966. In 2019, the BGN received a proposal from a resident of Eugene to change the name to Bath Hat (Review List 437), citing the summit's proximity to Bath Canyon, and adding, "Chinaman is a derogatory slur. Historical usage does not excuse ongoing use of slurs derogatory towards entire populations." Although the Black Rock Grazing Cooperative agrees that the word "Chinaman" should be removed, they report that the name Bath Canyon is rarely used locally (locals call it Long Hollow) and suggest China Hat would be more appropriate. The feature resembles a conical hat worn by Chinese laborers in the Pacific Northwest in the 1800s. In September 2023, the OGNB voted not to endorse the original proposal, and encouraged the cooperative to submit a different name. There are three features elsewhere in Oregon, a stream, a summit, and a spring, with names that include "China Hat," but none named simply China Hat.

proposals.land_ownership: private / Tillamook State Forest / Bureau of Land Management lands
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Jack Creek: Tillamook County Water District records since 1987 o Negro Jack Creek: USGS 1955, 1984; Tillamook County records o N____r Jack Creek: USGS 1942; Tillamook County survey record, 1957
proposals.case_summary: Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other Black Rock Grazing Cooperative (proponent) Support This proposal is to change the name of Negro Jack Creek, a 1.1-mile-long tributary of the Wilson River in Tillamook County, to Jack Creek. The stream heads on Bureau of Land Management land and flows through Tillamook State Forest and private lands. The proponent states that removing the first word of the name "is pretty self explanatory" and that he didn't "find any historical record for why it's named the way it is." Research by the Oregon Geographic Names Board found a reference to the stream and the man named Jack in a 2006 Tillamook County Historical Society tour of the Wilson River: N____R JACK CREEK, Negro Jack or N___r [spelled with one "g" in the account here and in the next instance] as he was called lived in this general area. N___r Jack was a lonely person. Jack took ill. No one knew the cause. He lay in his cabin suffering alone. Those going by could hear the agony of his breathing. There is no record of anyone going to help. He eventually died in his cabin. The neighbors buried him in back of his cabin. No one seemed to know his last name. Some thought he was a runaway slave. He came to the area a stranger and died a stranger. No other information about Jack has been found. The stream was first shown on USGS maps in 1942 with the more pejorative form of the name. The name was changed on USGS maps to its current form in 1955, prior to the 1963 Secretary of the Interior directive to replace all instances of the more pejorative form to "Negro" on all future map revisions. Starting in at least 1987, the Tillamook County referred to the stream as Jack Creek for the purposes of a small water district that no longer operates. The Oregon Department of Forestry's Tillamook District Forester reports that they "fully support the proposed name change" and: Over the years, we have made efforts to solely use Jack Creek on our public maps and databases but there are other mapping services that have not made the change. Our office reviewed historic maps and records and could not find any details or history of the gentleman known as Jack. . . . I hope this name change will honor a man that seems to have traveled great distances to homestead along the Wilson River and maybe it will provide some peace to a tragic story of the end of his life in Oregon.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Stone Butte is proposed for a 556-foot, generally horseshoe-shaped butte in the City of Happy Valley in Clackamas County. The Oregon Geographic Names Board (OGNB) submitted the proposal on behalf of the Director of Economic and Community Development for the City of Happy Valley; the proponent reports that from the late 1890s to the 1920s, the nearby community of Baker Bridge was known as Stone. It is believed that the name referred either to Livingston Stone (1836-1912), the first superintendent of the fish hatchery at Clear Creek on the Clackamas River, or to the many large boulders that are found in the area. Lewis L. McArthur, in his volume Oregon Geographic Names, supports the latter theory. The proposal elaborates: Basalt rock was quarried from the hills in the immediate area and barged down the Clackamas and Willamette Rivers to Portland to be used on building construction at the time. Some were used to build the Tillamook Lighthouse on the Oregon coast and the locks at Willamette Falls. The name of this community was again changed to Carver when a town site at Stone was surveyed and platted by Stephen S. Carver (1866-1933) in 1915. The post office of Carver was established about 1924. During the same period, a post office was established at Stone. GNIS lists a stream in Clackamas County named Stone Creek, 38 miles from the summit. PENNSYLVANIA

proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Heads 0.8 mi. SW of Shady Lake, flows generally S into Muddy Creek
proposals.name_history: Named for Mary Lubich (1923-2018), costume designer and seamstress, who also helped establish Greene County's first kindergartens
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Lubich Run is proposed for a 1.7-mile-long tributary of Muddy Creek. The stream flows adjacent to Kovalchecks Road and along the boundary of Cumberland Township and Jefferson Township in Greene County. The proponent, a member of the Lubich family, initially submitted the name to broadly honor his family, noting that they "have owned [the] homestead for years that [the stream] runs through." When asked to identify an individual who would meet the requirements of the Commemorative Names Policy, he modified the proposal to honor his grandmother Mary Lubich (1923-2018). He writes: Purchasing the property with my grandfather John in 1947, [Mary] enjoyed fishing and catching crayfish in the stream. Mary was instrumental in establishing the first kindergartens in the county at Our Lady of Consolation and St. Marcellus Catholic churches. She served as a costume designer and seamstress for theatrical productions at Waynesburg University and Moschetta's Dance Studio. Mary Lubich's obituary also notes that she began her employment during World War II, constructing Landing Ship Tank troop transport ships in Ambridge and later with the Department of Defense in Washington, D.C. GNIS lists no features in Pennsylvania named "Lubich."

proposals.proposal_type: make official name in local use
proposals.feature_description: Heads on the western slope of Chestnut Ridge, W of Coalpit Run, flows generally NW into McGee Run
proposals.name_history: Named in association with the Town of Millwood
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Millwood Run: (local use; A Brief History of the Derry Water Company)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Millwood Run for a 2.9-mile-long stream in Derry Township in Westmoreland County. The stream heads on the western slope of Chestnut Ridge and enters McGee Run near the intersection of Seger and McBroom Road. The proponent, a local resident, states that he is "submitting the name 'Millwood Run' due to the creek's proximity to the town of Millwood, PA . . . In addition to this, many locals already call it 'The creek above millwood' or some even call it 'Millwood Run.' There are many very old structures along this creek, including several old spring houses, that are evidence that the creek was at one time useful to locals potentially as drinking water. This indicates historical use at sometime in the past." He elaborates: The main reason I am advocating for the naming of this creek is because it is one of the very few streams in Pennsylvania that are labeled as a 'Natural Reproduction Trout Stream.' This means that it is one of the few streams in PA that have enough clean water, adequate shade, deep enough pools, and a pH balance that supports Native Brook Trout. I have fished this creek for the last few weeks and have found that the population of wild trout is substantially high, and I feel that giving this creek a name will help to bring awareness in our area to dwindling populations of native brook trout and the importance of maintaining clean waterways in the Commonwealth. It also allows for locals such as myself to just call it 'Millwood Run.' There are no streams in the Commonwealth named "Millwood." proposals.case_summary: The new name Goodland is proposed for an approximately 5,000-acre unincorporated community/development south of Mansfield, west of Midlothian, and on the west side of Highway 287. The community, which is expected to have a future population of between 40,000 and 50,000, is in Ellis County and Johnson County. The proponent represents a Dallas realty company that has developed and is managing the community. Although the area was initially marketed under the name Prairie Ridge, the company has over the past six years been using the name Goodland, in part to distinguish the location from the City of Grand Prairie, located just to the northeast (a small section of the new development lies within the city's "extraterritorial jurisdiction"). The area proposed to be given the official name Goodland falls within the larger ZIP Code 76084, the official name of which is Venus, although the U.S. Postal Service allows Prairie Ridge as a valid alternate address. The latter name is not recognized as official for Federal use and is not listed in GNIS. When the realty company learned that Prairie Ridge had not been designated by the BGN, they were instructed by the USPS to initiate a proposal to the BGN for Goodland. The proponent has confirmed that if the name is approved, Prairie Ridge will not be retained as a mailing address. A statement co-signed by the City of Grand Prairie City Manager and the Ellis County Judge reports that they "fully support the use of the name Goodland as a strong geographic brand/area." The statement refers to the proposal as a name change from Prairie Ridge. GNIS lists two other small unincorporated communities in Texas named Goodland: one in Bailey County, 350 miles to the west-northwest and the other in Robertson County, 120 miles to the south.
