proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: heads near Bald Knob, flows generally E then SW into an unnamed stream proposed to be named We-hemt-le
proposals.name_history: Named for Thornton L. "Tony" Neathery (1931-2015), a geologist who described the Wetumpka crater which is drained by the stream
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Neathery Creek is proposed for a 1.8-mile-long unnamed stream in Elmore County. The stream flows partly through the City of Wetumpka and is a tributary of an unnamed stream proposed to be named We-hemt-le (Review List 455). The name Neathery Creek was originally proposed for the stream that has since been proposed to be named We-hemt-le. That stream forms the eastern edge of Poarch Band of Creek Indians land near its mouth at the Coosa River. When asked to comment on the original Neathery Creek proposal, the Poarch Band Tribal Historic Preservation Officer responded that the stream was already named We-hemt-le and the name was recorded in Creek Confederacy and a Sketch of the Creek Country in the Years 1798 and 1799 by Benjamin Hawkins, published posthumously in 1848. Hawkins was the General Superintendent of Indian Affairs for areas south of the Ohio River, and principal agent to the Creek Tribe from 1796 until his death in 1816. When advised of the existence of a Native name, a professor of geology at Auburn University (not the original proponent) asked that the name Neathery Creek be applied instead to one of the unnamed tributaries. The name would commemorate Thornton L. "Tony" Neathery (1931-2015), an Alabama geologist who first described the Wetumpka crater in 1976. He worked with other geologists to confirm that it was an impact crater in 2002. The proponent stated that "Tony's groundbreaking research was instrumental in the recognition of the Wetumpka structure as an impact crater. Much of his research was centered near or on the banks of the unnamed stream that we propose be named [for him] in recognition of his pioneering work." He adds that the stream "flows within the famous 'Cliffs' area . . . and is fed in part by spring water coming out of the ground at the head of the large canyon that makes up the 'Cliffs' erosional feature. Tony Neathery specifically referred to the 'Cliffs' site in his 1976 paper and in subsequent guidebooks that he wrote about the area." Mr. Neathery served in the Navy during the Korean War and worked for the Geological Survey of Alabama from 1964 to 1986 as a Staff Geologist and then as Assistant State Geologist. He founded Thornton L. Neathery and Associates, a geology consulting business, and helped found the Alabama State Board of Licensure for Professional Geologists. The proponent of the original application has withdrawn his proposal and now endorses naming the tributary instead.

proposals.title: Change Quisling Cove to Imuqudaagis
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive
proposals.feature_description: on the N side of Kiska Island between Lasso Hill and Russian Ridge
proposals.name_history: Unangam Tunuu word meaning "Pinnacles at a Bay Surrounded by Brinks"
proposals.land_ownership: Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge / Aleutian Islands Wilderness [adjacent]
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Eric Cove: Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, 1967 o Quisling Cove: U.S. Army, ca. 1943; Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, 1967
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Quisling Cove on Kiska Island in the Aleutian Islands to Imuqudaagis. The land on Kiska Island adjacent to the cove is within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge and Aleutian Islands Wilderness. The proponent, who notes that he is an Alaska Native, an original shareholder with the Aleut Corporation, and a Member of the Qawalangin Tribe of Unalaska, states: Quisling Cove is not an appropriate name for anywhere in the United States because it is derogatory to people from Norway and people of Jewish descent. The word 'Quisling' originates from Vidkun Quisling of Norway who collaborated with Adolf Hitler and encouraged Nazis and the Third Reich to invade and occupy Norway, which they did. There are photographs of Vidkun Quisling with Adolf Hitler, Heinrich Himmler, Josef Terboven, Nikolaus von Falkenhorst and officers of the Waffen-SS, war criminals responsible for the homicides of millions of men, women, and children. After World War II ended, Vidkun Quisling was arrested and charged with murder and conspiring with Adolf Hitler to invade and occupy Norway. Quisling was convicted of all charges and executed by firing squad on October 24, 1945. The word "quisling" is in the Scandinavian and English dictionary and vocabulary today for those who collaborate with the enemy and for those who betray their own country. The word "quisling" has been used in books, comic strips, films, and speeches to portray traitors in a manner similar to phrases such as Benedict Arnold or Fifth Column. The name Quisling Cove on Kiska Island in the Aleutian Islands honors Vidkun Quisling and other traitors who betray their own country. The name Quisling Cove is also disrespectful of the Unangax̂ people who paid dearly during World War II and to U.S. Army Private George Fox who was born in Unga, raised in Unalaska, and killed in action in Italy in 1944 while trying to help retake Rome from the Nazis. The proponent has also proposed changing the name of Nazi Creek on Little Kiska Island to Kaxchim Chiganaa (Review List 455) and the name of Nip Hill on Little Kiska Island to Kaxchim Qayaa (q.v.). The proponent provided a notarized affidavit from Moses L. Dirks, an expert in the Unangam Tunuu language and an Unangax̂ elder, stating that he recommended the replacement name, and adding: I grew up in Atka Village in the Aleutian Islands of Alaska. Unangam Tunuu (Aleut language) was my first language. I am an Unangam Tunuu expert in reading, writing, grammar, and transcription of the Aleut language. I have worked for several decades with fellow Unangas and linguists including the late Knut Bergsland (1914-1998), a Norwegian linguist with the University of Oslo and the late Michael Krauss (1934 - 2019), an American linguist with the Alaska Native Language Center in Fairbanks. I have assisted with several major publications in Unangam Tunuu including the Aleut Dictionary, Aleut Tales and Narratives, and Ancient Aleut Personal Names. . . . Since these islands are in the Sasxinan territory, the geographical place names should be based on Unangax names recorded in the Aleut Dictionary. The proposed name means 'Pinnacles at a Bay Surrounded by Brinks.' The proponent added that he has requested letters of support from the U.S. Fish & Wildlife, the Aleut Corporation, the Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association, and from several additional Alaska Native, Jewish organizations, politicians, and leaders, and from Unangax̂ leaders and citizens. He provided a letter from Rabbi Moshe King from Congregation Beth Shalom in Anchorage, which states: On behalf of Congregation Beth Sholom, I am writing to express our support for the applications submitted by Michael Livingston regarding the proposed renaming of geographic features in Alaska, as detailed in the affidavit of Moses Dirks. Quisling's name is synonymous with betrayal and treason, and its use in naming a geographic feature is deeply hurtful to those who remember the suffering caused during World War II. The names recommended by Moses Dirks are appropriate and respectful, drawing from the heritage and culture of the Unangax people who have inhabited the region for centuries. These names honor the indigenous history and are a fitting tribute to the rich cultural heritage of Alaska. We believe that adopting these changes will promote respect and understanding among the diverse communities that make up our society. It is a necessary step towards recognizing the harmful impact of derogatory names and correcting historical injustices. The manager of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife supports the change, adding that Mr. Dirks is a recognized authority on Unangarn Tunuu, the language of the Unangax (Aleut) people. The agency's formal position is pending. Research shows that the Quisling Cove was applied during World War II by the U.S. Army for tactical purposes ahead of Operation Cottage, which took place in August 1943 in an effort to retake Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island from Japanese forces. The name was added to GNIS in 2001, citing Donald Orth's 1967 Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, USGS Professional Paper 567, the introduction of which states: This work is an alphabetical list of the geographic names that are now applied and have been applied to places and features of the Alaska landscape. Principal names, compiled from modern maps and charts and printed in boldface type, generally reflect present- day local usage. [emphasis added] The entry for Quisling Cove is in normal, not boldface, type and reads: cove, 0.5 mi. across, 4 mi. NE of Lief Cove on W coast of Kiska I., Aleutian Is.; 51°58'45"N, 177°23'00"E; (map 14). Var. Eric Cove. This is one of many arbitrary names applied by U.S. military forces to features on Kiska Island during World War II for tactical purposes. Orth lists over 250 names applied to features on Kiska Island and Little Kiska Island as a result of the Army's project. It also lists approximately 60 "arbitrary names applied to features on Kiska I. by USAAF [U.S. Army Air Force] for tactical purposes during World War II." These names do not follow any pattern, but there are groups of plant, animal, and bird names. Although it is unknown why specific names were chosen by the U.S. Army, there appears to be no intentional motive by the U.S. Army in 1943 to "honor" Vidkun Quisling with the name Quisling Cove. The cove was not named on USGS topographic maps until the onset of the USTopo program, which automatically places names from GNIS. It is not known whether the name is used today. GNIS contains an entry for the name Imuqudaagis for an island off the coast of Kiska Island and four miles east-northeast of Quisling Cove; it was added to GNIS in 2010 citing the 1994 Aleut Dictionary: Unangam Tunudgusii by Knut Bergsland. A 2011 undergraduate thesis referred to a village site on Witchcraft Point as Imuqudaagis, seven miles northeast of the cove. The relationship between the existing and proposed names has not yet been determined.

The summit is within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge's Aleutian Islands Wilderness. The proponent, who notes that he is an Alaska Native, an original shareholder with the Aleut Corporation, and a Member of the Qawalangin Tribe of Unalaska, states: Nip Hill is not an appropriate name for anywhere in the United States because it is derogatory a derogatory term for people of Japanese descent, intended to demean and dehumanize people of Japanese ancestry and used to justify poor treatment or violence against Japanese people. As with his proposals to change the name of Nazi Creek on Little Kiska Island to Kaxchim Chiganaa (Review List 455) and the name of Quisling Cove on Kiska Island to Imuqudaagis (q.v.), the replacement name was suggested by an expert in the Unangam Tunuu language and Unangax̂ elder. The proponent is gathering support from stakeholders in the area. In his letter of support, Rabbi Moshe King of Congregation Beth Shalom in Anchorage stated: Nip Hill: The term 'nip' is a racial slur that dehumanizes people of Japanese ancestry. It is a derogatory term that reflects a period of racism and xenophobia, particularly during and after World War II. Using such a term as a place name is inappropriate and offensive. The hill was not named on USGS topographic maps until the onset of the USTopo program, which automatically places names from GNIS. It is not known whether the name is used today. As with Nazi Creek and Quisling Cove, the name Nip Hill was applied during World War II by the U.S. Army for tactical purposes ahead of Operation Cottage. Donald Orth's 1967 Dictionary of Alaska Place Names, which notes that names printed in boldface type, generally reflect present-day local usage. The entry for Nip Hill is in boldface and reads: hill, 200 ft., on S end of Little Kiska I., Aleutian Is.; 51°56'49"N, 177°40'10"E; (map 14). An arbitrary name beginning with 'N' to correspond to 'N' grid used by the U.S. Army for tactical purposes during World War II; published on a 1953 AMS map.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Swan Pond is proposed for a 2.8-acre marshy lake east of Dune Lake and within Yukon-Koyukuk Census Area. The proponent states: This small swampy pond has been referred to as many things over the 35 years I have been associated with the area around Dune Lake. Usually with an outstretched pointing arm with a 'that little muck lake over there' or 'the little pond east of Dune Lake' or 'the muddy pot hole over east.' It's never had its own name just a reference to its location in relation to Dune Lake. The proposed name refers to a pair of trumpeter swans that have used this lake and Dune Lake as their nesting and signet rearing site for many years. The proponent shared a newspaper article that quotes his father, an Alaskan outdoorsman, and his observations of the swans at the lake. It details the yearly routine of the swans at Dune Lake, emphasizing their nesting in the "small swampy pothole" proposed to be named Swan Pond. After hatching, the swan family migrates about a mile and a half to Dune Lake before the pothole dries up. The proponent's father described the journey as extremely challenging for the cygnets due to the rugged terrain. There are ten lakes in Alaska named Swan Lake, one of which is in Yukon-Koyukuk Census Area, approximately 300 miles northeast of the lake in question. ARKANSAS

proposals.case_summary: The new name Paramount Hill is proposed for an unnamed 790-foot summit located along State Highway 52 in the City of San Diego in San Diego County. The highest point is just outside the boundary of Marine Corps Air Station Miramar, while its northern slope appears to extend just inside the base. A city map shows that the area south of the highway is part of Mission Trails Regional Park, but it is not clear if it also includes the summit in question. The proponent describes the feature as "a small, rectangular hill with a flat top," adding, "Paramount means greatest. This name accurately represents the nature of this scenic hill. This name has been circulating between locals for about a year now, and many people are in agreement it is the best choice name for this feature." She included a quote from a local resident: "Paramount hill is a great name for this lovely sight while driving down the highway. It is a fun little easter egg for locals and adds a wholesome element to the freeway environment." There are four features in the GNIS with "Paramount" in their name, the closest being the City of Paramount, 140 miles away in Los Angeles.

proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Big Bird Key: USGS 1941; USACE 1943 o Eleanor Island: USGS 1976, 1995 State Names Authority Colorado Geographic Naming Advisory Board Federal Agency U.S. Forest Service Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Eleanor Island in the City of Treasure Island in Pinellas County to Elnor Island. Although the current name was made official by the BGN on March 11, 1975, the proponent reports that the island was named for Elnor Archibald Clark (1913-1995), who donated the island to Pinellas County in 1979. In 1973, a USGS cartographer asked the BGN to change the name of Big Bird Key, which had been labeled on USGS and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers maps since the 1940s, to Eleanor Key to reflect local use. The form reported: This name derives from a person named Eleanor Archibald, who does and or used to own this key. Persons contacted said Eleanor Island is the name which has been in use locally for at least the past twenty five years, and that this island is not known locally by its variant name [Big Bird Key]. The persons listed below are the best available authorities in this locale [the form listed two dock owners, a charter boat operator, and one other individual, all of whom had lived in the area between 26 and 40 years]. Based on this information, the BGN approved the change from Big Bird Key to Eleanor Island. A 1958 Tampa Bay Times article referred to the island as Elinor Island, noting that it was named for Elinor Archibald. Mrs. Clark's gravestone and the 1979 donation document spelled her name "Elnor." The current proposal was submitted by a representative of the Treasure Island Historical Society and the City of Treasure Island; she states: The previous owner was named Elnor, whose name has graced the island for many years. The name should be legally changed from Eleanor Island back to Elnor Island because it is the appropriate thing to do. . . . It is believed that the island's name, Elnor, was accidentally changed to Eleanor, because Elnor was too unusual or unfamiliar. Now that the city of Treasure Island has an Historical Society, [we] would like to re-recognize the donor's name, and in her memory, continue to use it. Mrs. Clark's first husband, Albert Bertram "Bert" Archibald, was the largest landowner in Treasure Island and an important developer in the area; the family owned many islands in Boca Ciega Bay. The Treasure Island City district commissioner added "I can tell you that Treasure Island residents will be very appreciative of your help in rectifying this misspelling."

The proponent, a resident of Tallahassee, states that the name is intended to "memorialize my family's history and life in Pinellas County" and "our love of this particular island." He adds that his family moved to Florida in 1971, and his father's plan was: . . . to embrace the obvious geography and natural features of Pinellas and guiding us all into boating and camping. We spent days on end navigating and exploring the Gulf, Intercoastal waterways, Tampa Bay, and the numerous creeks and tributaries within and around Pinellas. We, as a family, spent countless weekends camping on the islands in the Pinellas Intercoastal from Fort De Soto to Honeymoon Island and beyond. This particular island was our most favorite. The application further stated: I would like to reiterate that my request to name this island 'Roche Island' is sought not as a means by which to honor myself or our family, but rather a means by which I, my remaining siblings, and our extended family in Pinellas can honor and memorialize our entire family's life, growth, memories, contributions, and commitment to Pinellas County and it's [sic] amazing beauty for years to come. When asked to identify one or more family members who would satisfy the requirements of the Commemorative Names Policy, the proponent listed his great-great-grandfather, First Sergeant David Roche (1838-1914), who served in the 5th U.S. Infantry and who in 1877 received the Congressional Medal of Honor for gallantry in action. He also listed his parents, Norman Paul Roche (1932-2000), an engineer with Dupont and TECO, and Anna Teresa Roche (1932-2009), a nursing supervisor and director, as well as three siblings, Darren Chauncy Roche (1965-2006), James Patrick Roche (1956-2008), and Colleen Ann Roche (1960-2014), all of whom spent many years visiting the island. He added that he and his siblings "[all] contributed to our community in one way or another. From volunteering and working with the VFW (Post 7), the Public School System, missions through Church, working food banks - and of course - cleaning up litter on the many Intercoastal Islands." proposals.title: Vampire Lake
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: 0.96 mi. ESE of Baptist Lake, within Pittman Swamp
proposals.name_history: Named for its sinister atmosphere reminiscent of supernatural swamp monsters; the lake features treacherous muck, a strong odor of decay, a film of pollen and plant matter, and rotting trees. Its outline reportedly resembles a grinning, deformed face.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Vampire Lake is proposed for a 0.48-acre marshy lake east-southeast of Baptist Lake and within Ocala National Forest in Lake County. The proponent states: Federal Agency NOAA Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other The Nature Conservancy *No opinion This small, remote lake is a stagnant, anoxic lake inside a bay swamp, a very rare situation in peninsular Florida. It may be virtually unique in its size, biological configuration and geological history. The only inflows are underground seepage from the surrounding uplands and rainfall. It contains no outfalls. It is underlain by organic muck several feet deep at its margins and likely much deeper in its center, to the point where crossing it on foot could result in a fatal asphyxiating plunge into the muck. It smells heavily of rotting organic matter and is littered with weather and rot sculpted remains of long dead trees. When I visited it, the water was covered with a pale yellow- green film of pollen and plant matter. The proposed name refers to vampires and the proponent believes the name is fitting because "its overall aspect most people would consider creepy, sinister and evocative of tales of supernatural swamp monsters. The aerial outline of this lake also resembles a grinning, deformed face. There is no historical usage of this name, or any name I could find, for this difficult to access lake. . . ." The Florida State Names Authority does not support the proposal, stating "Naming a remote, difficult to get to area on public land, with the word vampire could potentially create some unwanted activity in my opinion." GNIS lists no geographic features in the United States containing the word "Vampire." INDIANA

proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: The northeastern and larger of two lakes currently named Ryden Lakes, 0.75 mi. N of Swede Lake
proposals.name_history: Named to commemorate Louis "Louie" Caprile (1917-1991), an avid fisherman and small-business owner in Chicago
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: Ryden Lakes: USGS 1961, 1969, 1983; Guide to Indiana's Lakes, Indiana Department of Conservation, 1955; Ryden Lake: Indiana Lakes Guide, Department of Natural Resources, Division of Water, 1993
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Lake Louie to one of two lakes in Coolspring Township in La Porte County that are collectively Ryden Lakes. The name would commemorate the proponent's father Louis "Louie" Caprile (1917-1991). The proponent, who has owned property around the lake for 34 years and is building a home at the lake, originally asked that the name Ryden Lakes be changed to Lake Louie, as the existing name "has no significance to the land." The BGN staff advised him that the name has been shown on topographic maps since 1961 and that a search of census, church, and property records showed numerous individuals named Ryden in LaPorte County since the 1870s, including in Coolspring Township. Further, online directories continue to list individuals with that name in the area. The Plat Book of LaPorte County, published between 1925 and 1940, shows that "A. Ryden" owned the parcel containing Ryden Lakes. A 1913 list of farmers in the county also included four named Ryden, and many members of the Ryden family are buried in Carmel Cemetery, 1.6 miles from the lake in question. The proponent responded that he wished to amend his proposal to apply the name Lake Louie to just the "northern" (more easterly) of the two lakes. Louie Caprile was "a small store owner who worked seven days a week [and] raised a family of six in Chicago's inner city." An avid fisherman, he was taken to see the lake by the proponent shortly before he passed away. The proponent confirms that there was no long- term association between his father and the lake, but "I promised myself I would name the lake after my father to honor him. While Louie visited the lake, he drew his family to form a home there, to invest in the local area, and to take root over the last 34 years." Further: I think it is also worth noting as I'm sure you're already aware the lake in question is on private property and is not accessible to the general public. The significance of a geographic name is greatly influenced by its public utility and recognition. In this case, we hope it is unlikely the name change [sic] to Lake Louie would affect overall public opinion, navigation or usage, as the feature is exclusively enjoyed by the surrounding private property owners and their families. The proposed name, Lake Louie, it's not just a whim. It's a deliberate choice that reflects the owner's connection to the land and their vision for investing in its future. It's about legacy, about creating something that will last, something that's meaningful to the family that walks its shores every day. GNIS does not list any hydrographic features in Indiana named "Louie."

proposals.title: Change McPherren Ditch to McPherren Canal
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize local preference
proposals.proponent: Davis Lamm, President; Waterfield Natural Resources
proposals.feature_description: In Jackson Township, extends from NW to SE through the Town of Roanoke and into Cow Creek
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o McPherren Ditch: USGS 1956, 1972; Federal Register 1982; Indiana Department of Natural Resources/Division of Water 1979, 2024
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of McPherren Ditch, a 3.83-mile-long canal in Jackson Township and the Town of Roanoke in Huntington County, to McPherren Canal. The current name has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1956 and recorded in Indiana Department of Natural Resources/Division of Water records since 1979. The proponent of the change is president of Waterfield Natural Resources, a subsidiary of Waterfield Enterprises ("one of the largest private financial service organizations in America"). He states: The proposed McPherren Canal name originated in [an] effort to represent the tributary's features more accurately and to better remember the history of the old canal. Historically the canal was known as the 'N. Branch Cow Creek' before being renamed the McPherren Ditch. At the time, the creek currently called 'Cow Creek' was named 'S. Branch Cow Creek.' McPherren Canal winds through the historic town of Roanoke and was an original lock on the Eire & Wabash Canal. It was built between 1834 and 1837. When the canal was in operation 'the village [Roanoke] became known as one of the best trading and shipping points on the canal.' Today, the town continues to be a destination center for visitors looking for a historic lesson and every visitor cruises by the McPherren Ditch on their way to the heart of downtown Roanoke. The proposal was submitted by an environmental specialist with the City of Marion's Engineering Department and the name was chosen by freshmen students at Linn-Marr High School in collaboration with local citizens. proposals.case_summary: The new name Hertichoak Pond is proposed for a two-acre waterbody in the Town of West Newbury in Essex County. The pond lies adjacent to Lower Artichoke Reservoir on the Artichoke River, and according to the USGS Protected Areas Database of the U.S., it is located partly within a watershed protection area owned by the City of Newburyport (it is outside the city's legal boundary). The proponent, a Newburyport resident, states, "This pond likely came into existence during the flooding and expansion of the Artichoke River to create a public water supply for Newburyport and West Newbury." USGS maps first show the feature as a wetland in 1944 next to the recently impounded Artichoke River, and then as a waterbody starting in 1985. The proponent reported: The proposed name of this currently unnamed feature (Hertichoak Pond) has an unknown origin. . . . This area has a rich historical significance and was likely inhabited for centuries by the Pennacook Indians before the early 17th century. The Artichoke River has thought to be named after the Jerusalem Artichoke, which had been harvested nearby by Native Americans and early settlers. However, a historic map from 1720 [sic] illustrates a different name for the river (Hertichoak). Although the etymology of this name is uncertain, it likely comes from the Pennacook tribe, in which other nearby rivers like the Contoocook River in New Hampshire get their name. In an effort to prevent this name (Hertichoak) from being lost in history, it is reasonable to name a small pond adjacent to the Lower Artichoke Reservoir with this name. The map showing the name "Hertichoak" is "A Plan of The West Parish of Newbury new Town Taken Sept 15 1729 by John Brown Surv[eyo]r." A 1957 article in the Atlantic by John P. Marquand reported: "I am so ignorant as not even to know the origin of the name of the Artichoke River. . . . Certainly no artichokes have ever grown upon its shores in either a wild or a cultivated state, and I doubt if any of our forefathers ever attempted to derive nourishment from this peculiar vegetable. In one of the old maps the river is called "Hertichoke," [sic] and this leads me to believe that we can safely thank the Indians for naming it and that we are now by its peculiar name trying to simulate some tongue-twisting word of the ancient Penacook language. Countless sources report that the Artichoke River is named after the Jerusalem artichoke, which is a sunflower native to New England. Indigenous people and European settlers harvested or cultivated the sunflowers for their roots. It is not related to the artichoke, which is a cultivated crops related to thistles. Older spellings of artichoke include "hartichoak" and "heartichoak."

proposals.title: Change Lake Lansing to Pine Lake
proposals.proposal_type: name change to restore historic name
proposals.feature_description: 1 mi. N of Wildlife Lake; 2.5 mi. SE of Park Lake
proposals.name_history: descriptive name
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Pine Lake (USGS 1928; USACE 1944) o Lake Lansing (USGS 1958, 1972; USACE 1961) o Lansing Lake (USGS 1950)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Lake Lansing, located in Meridian Township in Ingham County, to Pine Lake. The lake lies between Lake Lansing Park South and Lake Lansing Park North. Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Pine Lake was labeled on a USGS topographic map in 1928. However, in 1929, the BGN received and approved (May 7, 1930) a proposal from the Michigan Historical Commission to change the name to Lake Lansing. The request was initiated by the Ingham County Board of Supervisors "to avoid duplication . . . with several Pine Lakes in this vicinity." A petition filed at the time was signed by "a great many property owners in the immediate vicinity of Pine Lake, and truly expressing the sentiment of the people of said locality, asking that this [County] Board recommend to the Department of Conservation of the State of Michigan that the name of Pine Lake be changed to Lake Lansing, which would be a specific name and at the same time indicate [the] location of the lake." The City of Lansing Common Council and the Civic Bureau of the City Chamber of Commerce also supported the change to Lake Lansing. The proponent of the current proposal, in their change.org petition, states ". . . [the name change] was dubious at best, lacking both popular and local legislative votes to enact the change. The name change was driven solely by Frank 'Pine Lake' Johnson. The proposal and petition state: It was Johnson, a rich printer from out of town who bought up the land, destroyed the local environment, and decided to change the name of the lake on a whim because 'there are dozens of Pine Lakes.' This is utterly ridiculous. The new name [Lake Lansing] does not even make sense, considering that the lake is not actually located in Lansing. Changing it back to Pine Lake would help Haslett and Meridian Township in general stand out as more than just another suburb of Lansing but as genuine communities in their own right, culturally and legally independent from the capital. It will bring renewed interest to the lake, helping the local economy from people wanting to check out the lake that recently got a new name. [I]t will bring the garbage pollution surrounding the lake to more people's attention, attracting more people to clean up the lake. . . . The proponent noted that the Ingham County Parks website states that Lake Lansing served as a hunting and fishing ground for Indian Tribes for centuries, with burial mounds pre- dating the Chippewa Indians. In the late 19th century, the area became a popular recreational site accessible by various means of transport. Prominent families from Lansing built summer homes around the lake, and the Pine Lake House resort, built in the 1870s, was a notable landmark until it burned down in 1929. The Izzer Club was established on the lake in the 1890s by a group of Lansing businessmen, and extensive logging took place on the east side. In the 1920s, Frank Johnson developed the east side. The website also states that he successfully pushed to rename the lake to Lake Lansing in 1927. There is no mention in the USGS records of Frank "Pine Lake" Johnson. The book Historic Structures In The Haslett Lake Lansing Area (1974) states: Evelyn H. Raphael in her history maintained that the developer known as Pine Lake Johnson effected the name change in 1927 'because there are dozens of Pine Lakes.' However, Theodore C. Foster in the article 'Place Names of Ingham County' (Michigan History Magazine (1942) stated that the lake was renamed at the suggestion of J.R. Ferguson 'because of the fact that the name Pine Lake carried no idea of location and because there are so many other Pine Lakes in Michigan.' GNIS lists 26 lakes in Michigan named Pine Lake and another dozen or so with "Pine" in their names. None are in Ingham County. The stream that flows from the west side of the lake to join the Cedar River continues to be named Pine Lake Outlet. *provided by the proponent MINNESOTA

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Hindman Creek in Scott County to Heeb Creek. The four-mile-long stream originates at Lake Tywappity, flows generally southwest, then south of the City of Chaffee, and continues west to enter an unnamed channel. The proponent, a local resident whose surname is Heeb, submitted the proposal to give official recognition to the name that he reports to be in well-established local usage. He states: John Martin Heeb [1829-1914], my Great Great Great Grandfather and a Civil War (Union) veteran, owned 1000 acres on both sides of the creek. In 1905 he sold this land to allow for the creation of the town of Chaffee. The stream was thereafter named for the Heeb family to honor their contribution to the town's founding. Since then, the name has been in common local use and appears in many city documents, including a 1978 ordinance that established the boundaries of a newly established ward. John Heeb was listed in the Federal Census of Scott County from 1880 to 1910. The stream has been labeled Hindman Creek on USGS topographic maps since 1934. proposals.proposal_type: make official a name in reported local use
proposals.feature_description: Near the N end of Monkey Mountain
proposals.name_history: Associated with nearby Sni-A-Bar Creek and the former Sni- A-Bar Farm
proposals.land_ownership: Monkey Mountain County Park / Jackson County
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Sni-A-Bar Point for a 940-foot summit in Jackson County. The summit is located at the north end of Monkey Mountain, in Monkey Mountain County Park in Sni-A-Bar Township. The proponent, a resident of Illinois who has submitted a number of other proposals for features in various States, reports that the name refers to Sni-A-Bar Creek that runs along the western edge of the feature, as well as the Sni-A-Bar Farm, on which it was once located. He is not sure how long the name has been in local use but notes that it is listed on peakbagging forums (an individual with the same surname as the proponent appears to have added it). According to Wikipedia, "Sni-A-Bar is possibly a corruption of chenail Hubert (French pronunciation . . . meaning 'Hubert channel/slough.' Alternatively, the name may have come from a French frontiersman named Abar who was charting a course on the Missouri River in the early 1800s. Alexander Majors, one of the founders of the Pony Express, called the creek Big Snye Bear River in his book Seventy Years on the Frontier." Wallace's Farmer, published 1926, stated that Sni-A-Bar Farm had recently won a cattle championship. A portion of the former farmland, located north of the summit, has been designated by the Missouri Department of Conservation as the Sni-A-Bar Conservation Area. In addition to Sni-A-Bar Creek and the Township of Sni-A-Bar, GNIS lists East Fork Sni-A-Bar Creek, Little Sni-A-Bar Creek, and West Fork Sni-A-Bar Creek. NEBRASKA

proposals.stakeholders: Local government Village of Sumner Dawson County Board of Commissioners State Names Authority Nebraska Geographic Names Authority Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X The new commemorative name Lake Fairchild is proposed for an eleven-acre reservoir (formerly a quarry) in the Town of Pittsford, adjacent to Monroe County's Mendon Ponds Park. This name, proposed by the docent of Fairchild Walking Tours (sponsored by the Town of Pittsford) and co-author of a recent history of Mendon Ponds Park, is intended to honor Professor Herman LeRoy Fairchild (1850-1943). Dr. Fairchild led the Department of Geology and Natural History at the University of Rochester from 1888 to 1920 and was a founding member of the Geological Society of America. According to the proponent, Fairchild petitioned the county in 1926 to preserve the area, leading to the establishment of Mendon Ponds Park in 1928, where Fairchild was a primary speaker. The proponent describes Fairchild as "an energetic, outgoing individual much beloved by his students, faculty, and the academic community locally and nationally." In addition, he was an active lecturer, field scientist, and author of 236 publications. Despite the park being named a National Natural History Landmark in 1969, nothing within it has been named for Fairchild. The proponent concludes, "This unnamed, former quarry lake is an opportunity to commemorate the man responsible for this 2500-acre park being here today." According to his obituary published in Selection of Rochester Trust News, Fairchild was renowned as a geologist and professor and was known as "the grand old man of science." He served as the curator of the geological museum from 1896 and became an Emeritus Professor of Geology in 1920. He maintained a long-standing relationship with Rochester Trust, being the owner of its oldest individual account, opened in 1888. His contributions were celebrated during Rochester Trust's 50th Anniversary in 1938, highlighting his influential role in both academia and the local community. GNIS lists no geographic features in New York with the name "Fairchild." *provided by the proponent NORTH DAKOTA Change Halfbreed Creek to Camp Cherith Creek Stakeholder Input Local government Town of Pittsford Board of Supervisors *support Monroe County Legislature State Names Authority New York State Committee on Geographic Names Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X

proposals.case_summary: This proposal, to change the name of Halfbreed Creek in Williams County to Camp Cherith Creek, was submitted by a resident of Bismarck, who believes the existing name is offensive. In an inquiry to the USGS National Map helpdesk, she stated: I thought more places would have had their names changed by now. I was looking at a location on Google Maps that I need to visit and there is a Creek in Williams County with the name of Halfbreed. I find it embarrassing that this hasn't been rectified yet. Please look into changing the name of the Creek to something that isn't offensive. She was advised that the BGN is reactive and that she would need to propose a replacement name to the BGN. Halfbreed Creek has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1979; its origin has not been determined. The stream flows east through land managed by the North Dakota State Land Board and into Lake Sakakawea. The lake is managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers as the Sakakawea Recreation Area. USACE has an agreement with the North Dakota National Guard allowing it to utilize the area for training purposes. Regarding the replacement name, the proponent states: Camp Cherith (also known as Dakota Hills Christian Camp) is [sic] located adjacent to the creek and is [sic] an example of a post 1960-church camp. The architectural site is recorded with the ND State Historical Society. While Camp Cherith is no longer active as a camp, the origins of the name are Biblical. The camp was one of several that were originally (1939) established as Pioneer Girls camps, later renamed as Camp Cherith, and in 1981 as Pioneer Ministries camps. There are six locations in operation today in the U.S. and Canada. When advised by the BGN staff that the BGN has developed cultural sensitivity guidance to address names of interest to Tribes, she responded: As a private citizen, I think it would be more appropriate for the federal agency or agencies to seek THPO comment on the name change. USACE has a PA with many Tribes along the Missouri River that would likely need to be consulted in this process, which to me seems like a rather cumbersome undertaking for a private citizen. In a follow-up email to a number of Tribal representatives, the proponent stated that in preparing to visit the area: I noted that the name of the Creek running through the property had a name that made me cringe. I decided to take it upon myself to look into changing the name, as I knew Secretary Deb Haaland had organized a committee for this purpose. Since USGS doesn't have the ability to consult on name changes, I am contacting you all about the name change proposal. In my previous emails you can see I suggested two possible names based on the former names of the Camps that were located on this property, but I have no particular attachment to either of them. . . . It really is a beautiful location, and but the creek needs a better name. Please take a look through the email chain and decide amongst yourselves. Note: The list of place names compiled by the Advisory Committee on Reconciliation in Place Names, established in response to Secretary's Order 3405, does not include Halfbreed Creek but does list Half Breed Coulee, located 10 miles to the northeast.

proposals.name_history: Named for Wyandot Chief Shateyaronyah (1747-1810), known as "Leatherlips" by white settlers for his unwavering commitment to keeping his promises.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: Local government Williams County Board of Commissioners State Names Authority Nebraska Geographic Names Authority Federal Agency U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X o Gables Drainage: Franklin Soil and Water Conservation District o Turkey Run North: olentangywatershed.org, 2024; Frankly Speaking, Franklin Soil and Water Conservation District
proposals.case_summary: The new name Leatherlips Run is proposed for a 1.9-mile-long stream in Franklin County. The stream heads in the City of Columbus at the community of Gables, flows generally west through Linworth Village and Sharon Township, to enter the Olentangy River near Olentangy Park. The proposal was submitted by a representative of Friends of the Lower Olentangy Watershed, who reports that the stream is known locally as Turkey Run North; this name is mentioned at the websites of the watershed and also in a news article published Franklin Soil and Water Conservation District, which has also used the name Gables Drainage. The name Leatherlips Run would commemorate Wyandot Chief Shateyayonyah (1747- 1810), also known as "Chief Leatherlips" because of his reputation for being a man of his word. An article posted online by the Wyandotte Nation states that Chief Leatherlips refused to join Shawnee chief Tecumseh's effort against the Americans, adhering to a peace treaty signed in 1795. This refusal led to his execution by four Michigan Wyandots, who were influenced by Tecumseh's campaign to unite Tribes against the U.S. Government. Despite the tragic circumstances of his death, Leatherlips is remembered and honored for his integrity and commitment to peace. The Dublin Historical Society further describes the events leading to Chief Leatherlips' execution. After refusing to join Tecumseh's alliance against the Americans, Chief Leatherlips was accused of witchcraft by six Wyandot warriors, leading to a death sentence. Despite efforts by Benjamin Sells and other white settlers to save him through negotiation and offers of money, Chief Leatherlips declined. On the day of his execution, after a council affirmed the sentence, Chief Leatherlips prayed and sang before being executed by a tomahawk. The Wyandotte Nation's article adds: Leatherlips had three Wyandot names. The one most often used was SHA‑TE‑YAH‑RON‑YA but he was sometimes referred to as THA‑TEY‑YAN‑A‑YOH. In later years he was called SOU‑CHA‑ET‑ESS, which means 'Long Gray Hair'. He was of the Porcupine Clan as was his great friend, Chief Tarhe, and he was related to Roundhead, Splitlog and Battise, noted Wyandot warriors of that period. The proposal states: The unnamed tributary is close to the neighborhood street called Leatherlips Trail in Dublin. Also the tributary is close to another tributary known as Bill Moose Run, which was named after the Wyandotte Bill Moose, who visited Chief Leatherlips' burial site to pay his respects before moving along the Olentangy River, so it might be nice to name this tributary after Chief Leatherlips and have it be so close to Bill Moose Run. [There] is a historical marker for Chief Leatherlips located in Dublin, Ohio, and Leatherlips Cemetery is located in Powell, Ohio. . . . GNIS lists no features in the U.S. named "Leatherlips." (*provided by proponent) OREGON

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Coot Creek is proposed for a 0.75-mile-long tributary of the Elk River in Curry County. The stream heads east-northeast of Silver Butte and flows generally northeast into Elk River. The name would commemorate the proponent's grandfather Glen Lee "Coot" Wagner (1938-2016). The proponent writes: Coot was a descendent of the Wagner pioneer family that moved to Coos County from North Carolina in 1870. He worked on the family ranch on the Elk River in Port Orford, Oregon, during his childhood and had many additional jobs as he went on to run the ranch, including logging, driving cattle truck, and hauling hay from eastern Oregon to Curry County. He enjoyed hunting, fishing, playing cards, reading Oregon history books, and visiting with his many friends and family. In 1986 Coot built Elk River Campground on the family ranch. The Campground provided Coot with a great forum to make new friends from all over the country. He and his friends shared a love of fishing on the Elk River. He put his blood and sweat into the property this creek is on and he would be honored to have it named after him. The creek is almost entirely located on the family property which we plan to keep in the family for years to come. According to the GNIS, there are no geographic features in Oregon with "Coot" in their names. PENNSYLVANIA

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the local name Bickel Run for a 0.6-mile-long tributary of Pigeon Creek in Chester County. The stream heads in North Coventry Township and flows into East Coventry Township. The North Coventry Environmental Advisory Council (NCEAC) reports that the stream has been known locally as Bickel Run "for several decades" and that it was first identified in township open space reports in 2002. The adjacent uplands are also referred to as Bickel Hill (this name is not in GNIS, nor has it been proposed). The township acquired property along the headwaters of the stream and named the area Bickel Run Park. The NCEAC presumes the name refers to the Bickel Family, who settled along the stream in the mid-to- late 1800s. George Bickel was the first property owner from that family and his name was noted in the 1883 Breou's Farm Atlas of Chester County. Online genealogy records list many individuals with the surname Bickel in North Coventry Township.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Shenkel Hollow Run for a 2.7-mile-long tributary of the Schuylkill River. The stream heads in North Coventry Township in Chester County, where it flows along Shenkel Road before turning north and flowing into Union Township in Berks County. The North Coventry Environmental Advisory Council reports that Shenkel Hollow Run derives its name from Henry (Heinrich) Shenkel (1718-1785), who in 1767 was granted 147 acres along the headwaters of the stream. The Shenkel family donated a ten-acre tract of land for use as a community cemetery; today this is the site of Shenkel United Church of Christ and Shenkel Cemetery. Shenkels School House is shown at the headwaters of the stream on an 1847 county map. In 2020, the Green Valleys Watershed Association issued the Shenkel Hollow Run Watershed Report (there is no "Shenkel Hollow" in GNIS, nor did the NCEAC ask to make that name official). PennDOT bridge data identifies the stream as "Norris Creek" and "Trib Schuylkill River"; the origin of "Norris" is unknown, although genealogy records list a few individuals with that surname in Union Township.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Kerrville Ponding Lake in the City of Kerrville in Kerr County to Nimitz Lake. The 105-acre reservoir, located along the Guadalupe River, was constructed in 1980 by the Upper Guadalupe River Authority. The associated dam is named Kerrville Ponding Dam. The current name has been shown on USGS topographic maps since 2010; the GNIS entry was collected from the 1981 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Dams and Reservoirs inventory. In 1998, ownership of the dam, water treatment plant, and associated flood easements and deeds was transferred from the Upper Guadalupe River Authority to the City of Kerrville. In 2011, the Kerrville City Council discussed renaming the reservoir. The original suggestion was "Sunset Lake," but a local resident offered the name Nimitz Lake "after a distinguished military officer." After debating the importance of historical significance in naming, the Council voted unanimously to approve the change to "Nimitz Lake." The name is intended to honor Admiral Chester William Nimitz (1885-1966), who served as Commander in Chief of the U.S. Pacific Fleet and Pacific Ocean Areas during World War II. Born in Fredericksburg in neighboring Gillespie County, Admiral Nimitz attended Tivy High School in Kerrville. A 2015 Texas Water Development Board report referred to Nimitz Lake and Nimitz Lake Dam. The name Nimitz Lake is also used by the Kerrville Convention & Visitors Bureau and the Upper Guadalupe River Center Foundation. It is referenced in a City of Kerrville Nimitz Lake Boating Center Study (2019), on the Texas Fishing Forum website, in real estate listings, and in a number of news articles.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of the unincorporated populated place of Kopernik Shores in Cameron County to Starbase. The community is located east of Brownsville along Texas Highway 4 and is associated with the Space Exploration Technologies Corporation (SpaceX) spaceport named Starbase. The area indicated in the proposal is mostly on private land, but according to Cameron County parcel records, also overlaps the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge and Boca Chica State Park. Material submitted in support of the proposal indicates that the intent is not only to recognize the local name for the community but also for it to be recognized by the U.S. Postal Service as a valid mailing address. The community is classified in GNIS as a Populated Place, defined as "Place or area with clustered or scattered buildings and a permanent human population. . . . A populated place is usually not incorporated and by definition has no legal boundaries." GNIS also records names of incorporated populated places that do have legal boundaries. There is no incorporated place with legal boundaries that is associated with the community proposed as Starbase. The community of Kopernik Shores was established in 1967 with the name Kennedy Shores; since then, it has had several unofficial local names. The Handbook of Texas notes: Kopernik Shores is on State Highway 4 a mile inland from the Laguna Madre [sic] and twenty-two miles east of Brownsville in southeast Cameron County. It was developed in 1967 by John Caputa, a radio personality cum land developer from Chicago, Illinois, who became involved in the real estate business in 1963 with Harold Caldwell. Caldwell owned a 3,250-acre tract of land on the Gulf Coast. Caputa aimed his sales pitch at working-class Polish immigrants seeking a better standard of living. He was able to reach a wide range of people through his radio work. He showed movies of retirees on the beach and later took prospective buyers on train tours of the development. He named the community Kennedy Shores for John F. Kennedy. Unstaked lots sold for $1,200 and houses for $12,500. Most of the sales were in cash, often the life savings of the buyers. Caputa built thirty homes, a restaurant, and a hotel. A sand filter water treatment plant was constructed. Sewer and electricity service were also provided. Hurricane Beulah flooded the area in 1967, washed away some of the land, and destroyed the restaurant, as well as the utility system. Only electrical service was restored. Soon thereafter Caldwell's corporate empire started facing financial problems. In 1968 Caputa acquired 1,000 acres of land and tried to break away from his partners. He partitioned the land into 5,000 lots priced at $5,000 each, invested money in a church and shopping center, and had electricity installed. Residents of Kennedy Shores carried their water from Brownsville. In 1975 Stanley Piotrowicz, an eighty-year-old resident, proposed that the community be incorporated. He became mayor and renamed the place Kopernik Shores in honor of the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus. In 1977 Judge Darrell Hester of Brownsville abolished the incorporation. In 1978 the town's population was estimated at twenty- six. . . . After [Caputa's] death [in 1979] it was discovered that many of the Kopernik Shores residents did not hold clear title to their land. In 1982 many of the homes still did not have potable water. In 1990 the population of Kopernik Shores was twenty-six. The population remained the same in 2000. The names "Boca Chica" and "Boca Chica Village" have also been used to refer to the area and the community; the Texas Almanac provides the same text as the Handbook of Texas under an entry for "Boca Chica Village." The proposal to change the name to Starbase was submitted by the Cameron County Commissioners Court, which states: Cameron County (the "County") submits this proposal to the BGN to change an existing name of an unincorporated region of the County located 20 miles east of the City of Brownsville to 'Starbase.' The area is located near Boca Chica Beach, and is currently known by the BGN as 'Kopernik Shores,' which is located at coordinates 25°59'29"N 97°11'1"W. Kopernik Shores was a small, unincorporated community that was formed in the 1960s and originally was comprised of approximately 30 small homes. It was formerly named 'Kennedy Shores' by locals and for the last ten years, locals have referred to the area as Starbase. The area that used to be known as Kopernik Shores is now the center of the area known as Starbase, which has recently grown and now consists of 60 homes with 178 inhabitants in and around the Starbase community. Since 2014, locals have called this area Starbase as it represents the leading edge of space exploration not just in the United States, but around the world. From Starbase, rockets will be launched to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. The State of Texas has already recognized the significance of the name Starbase and that the area is identified by locals and visitors as Starbase. One key indicator is the placing of Texas Department of Transportation-approved signs along State Highway 4 that indicate the direction to Starbase. . . . The Starbase area is served by Texas State Highway 4 and is the site of the world's first commercial space launch complex, which is operated by Space Exploration Technologies Corp. ("SpaceX"). Changing the name of the area to Starbase would align with the local usage and is important because it would better reflect the area's significant space-related activities which have helped transform life in Cameron County. Starbase attracts thousands of visitors a year to watch rocket launches, and changing the name from Kopernik Shores to Starbase will help visitors to more easily identify the area and reduce confusion. In addition to extensive space launch and manufacturing facilities, the area currently includes over one hundred residential housing units, a school, and a restaurant, with plans in place for significant expansion in the near future, including a hotel and hundreds of additional units of residential housing - all of which is known locally as Starbase. At present, more than 1,950 employees and hundreds of local contractors work in the Starbase area in support of the infrastructure development and spaceflight operations for the commercial spaceport. With strong support from locals, the Starbase area is now home to a community that is driving the future of human spaceflight. Changing the name of this area to Starbase will reinforce the community's unique position in the history of spaceflight and would be consistent with the goals of the US National Space Policy, which include facilitating and encouraging the continued growth of a domestic commercial space sector, while also aligning the name of the area with local usage. The proposal included a photo of the Texas Department of Transportation "Starbase" highway sign, and screen captures from Google Maps showing a placemark labeled as "Starbase" and an outline of the extent of the proposed Starbase. The proposal provided the following online resources as supporting evidence: City of Brownsville, Texas official site identifying name and location of Starbase: https://visitbtx.com/members/spacex-launch-facility-starbase/ Cameron County website announcement of testing at a location identified by the County as Starbase: https://www.cameroncountytx.gov/spacex-set-to-launch-the-starship-flight-test-noise- advisory/ Local online news source, ValleyCentral.com: https://www.valleycentral.com/spacex/destination-texas-best-views-of-spacex- starbase/ Local business map: https://starbasebrewery.com/pages/starbase-texas-map#starbase- spacex-updated-maps University of Texas Rio Grande Valley describes its R&D program in the Starbase area: https://www.utrgv.edu/cara/programs/stargate/ Local Facebook page showing activities at Starbase: https://www.facebook.com/starbasetx/ An online store sells "Starbase, Texas" merchandise. Letters of support for the name change state that local use of Starbase "reflects the enthusiasm for this area as the frontier of space exploration, where rockets will be launched to the Moon and Mars, and "Starbase is used much like the way the area surrounding Kennedy Space Center in Florida is known as the 'Space Coast.'" Representative Gonzales' wrote: I write in support of SpaceX's recent proposal to redesignate the area in the 34th Congressional District of Texas known as Boca Chica, Texas [sic], to "Starbase, Texas". Since 2012, SpaceX has called Boca Chica home, where it has invested substantially in the local economy and gained notoriety with its achievements into modern space exploration. . . . Implementing the proposed redesignation will align local and national recognition of the 'Starbase' zone and clarify the location for United States Postal Service mail operations. Redesignating Boca Chica [sic] as Starbase will make this location more easily identifiable and cement the historic nature of SpaceX's investment in South Texas. . . . The resolution from the Brownsville City Commission referred to "an area of Boca Chica within Cameron County" and concluded: WHEREAS, the United States Postal Service has a process for name designations for the processing and delivery of correspondence. NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED AND FOUND by the City Commission of the City of Brownsville, Texas that: • The City of Brownsville, in conjunction with Cameron County, requests that the United States Postal Service ("USPS") designate a mailing name for 'Starbase, Texas' based on the following factors as detailed in the USPS's July 2015 Address Management's Evaluation of Requests: • There is not another "Starbase, Texas" in existence, and "Starbase" is not associated with another zip code belonging under another administrative post office; • The name does not resemble an airport code or that of another country; • "Starbase'" would provide community identification; • The area is recognized by the City of Brownsville, in conjunction with Cameron County, as having distinct boundaries, as the area is located in a secluded section of the southernmost part of Texas on State Highway 4; • "Starbase" is not the name of a company, homeowner's association, or other similar entity; • The name meets acceptable standards of decency; and • Adding the name "Starbase, Texas" would help the USPS more easily and efficiently deliver mail, as the location is more easily identifiable if the name is "Starbase" opposed to Brownsville, which is located approximately 20 miles from the area. . . ." The community lies within U.S. Postal Service ZIP Code 78521, which has a Last Line ("city") name of Brownsville. * Provided by proponent UTAH

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of one of two streams in Salt Lake County that are currently named Elbow Fork. The name Moss Fork was submitted by the Salt Lake County Canyons Management director on behalf of the County Search & Rescue team and in response to a previous proposal to rename the other Elbow Fork to North Elbow Fork (Review List 454); the latter proposal was subsequently withdrawn. The two streams named Elbow Fork are 3.75 miles apart, both within the Uinta-Wasatch- Cache National Forest. The 1.55-mile-long stream in question, proposed to be renamed to Moss Fork, is also within the Mount Olympus Wilderness and has been labeled Elbow Fork on USGS topographic maps since 1928. It flows into Big Cottonwood Creek, while the more northerly one flows into Mill Creek. When asked to comment on the original proposal, the county responded that the more northerly Elbow Fork is "more well-known and integrated into trail regulations and public knowledge than the Elbow Fork in the Big Cottonwood area." They added, "Over the years we have done several rescues at the Big Cottonwood Elbow Fork stream area, and we have never referred to it as Elbow Fork, always 'Moss Ledge stream first and right.' This renaming aims to prevent misidentification of the location and ensure prompt and accurate responses during search and rescue operations." The county added that the reference to Moss Ledge derives from the now-closed Moss Ledge Picnic Area, a name that is still familiar to locals. GNIS lists four geographic features in Utah containing the word "Moss," specifically a community in Davis County, two summits, and a valley. The closest is the community of Moss, located approximately 18 miles to the north-northwest.

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Elizabeth Creek is proposed for a 2.5-mile-long unnamed stream that heads north of Gabriel Peak in the North Cascades Mountains and Whatcom County, then flows into Skagit County where it enters Granite Creek. The stream is on the Mount Baker National Forest. The proposal would commemorate Elizabeth ("Barta") Widel (1917-2017), a pioneering journalist and columnist for The Okanogan County Chronicle. According to her obituary, Elizabeth's career in journalism began in 1954, and she was well-known for her column 'Exploring the Okanogan,' which she wrote for over 60 years, comprising over 3,000 weekly columns. Her work was characterized by her deep connection to the Okanogan community and her passion for local stories. She was celebrated for her ability to capture the essence of the region through her writing, and her contributions were widely recognized, including receiving multiple awards such as the Washington Newspaper Publishers Association's 'Best Feature Columnist.' In 2015, Elizabeth wrote a column highlighting a waterfall she had visited many times on this "unnamed creek." Widel's dedication to journalism was matched by her active involvement in her community. She was a Girl Scout leader, a member of various local organizations, and a strong advocate for the arts. She also had a love for teaching and music, working as a music teacher before transitioning into her journalism career. Elizabeth's ability to blend her personal interests with her professional work made her a beloved figure in the Okanogan area. She was known for her empathetic and engaging storytelling, which endeared her to readers and colleagues alike. In addition to her professional accomplishments, Widel had a rich personal life. She was married to George Widel and had three children. Elizabeth continued to be an active member of her community well into her later years, participating in local events and maintaining her involvement in the church and other civic activities. Her memorial indicates that her legacy is one of dedication, passion, and an unwavering commitment to both her craft and her community. She is survived by her family and numerous friends who remember her as a talented journalist and a cherished member of the Okanogan community. GNIS lists two streams in Washington named Elizabeth Creek, one in Grays Harbor County and the other in Pierce County, located 120 and 170-miles away, respectively. *Contacted by Washington Committee on Geographic Names WISCONSIN *** The following proposal was withdrawn by the proponent. The local name Onsrud Pond was added directly to GNIS based on county use ***

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new commemorative name Boyles Creek to a 2.66-mile-long tributary of the Russellville Reservoir in Franklin County. The name seeks to honor the Boyles family, specifically Arvin Gresham Boyles (1915-1997), the proponent's great- grandfather, who lived on property along the stream his entire life. Mr. Boyles served in World War II, and his ancestors, who settled the land in the 1840s, have resided in the area for nearly 200 years. The proponent describes the importance of the creek to his family, stating: "I believe this feature needs a name to honor those that came before, who used this creek to aid their survival decades ago. They needed this creek to bathe, to wash clothing and dishes, for water to drink, water for their livestock, their crops. It was part of their means of survival. This land means so much to our family, and we would love to do this to honor our ancestors." GNIS lists four features in Alabama with "Boyles" in their names, all in Jefferson County and approximately 75 miles southeast of Franklin County. These include Boyles Gap, Boyles Gap Lake, Boyles Highlands, and East Boyles. ALASKA Herringbone Hill, Moonshadow Peak, and New Years Mountain These three proposals are to make official names for three summits in the Tokosha Mountains in Matanuska-Susitna Borough and Denali National Park. The area is proposed for wilderness designation. The proponent reports that the names were given by him and three of his fellow mountaineers, during their first ascent of the summits in late December 1974 and early January 1975. He believes the summits "require names because [they are all] prominent Tokosha Mountain summits as viewed by explorers and travelers in the area. I believe [they] are appropriate because [they were] the earliest recorded names given to the summits." The proponent also notes that at one time the names were shown on the Denali Viewpoint display sponsored by the Denali State Park, adding: "The display was located on the George Parks Highway near Milepost 135 for a period of time, estimated to be from the 1980s to 1990s." The names were also mentioned in the December 2016 edition of Scree, the newsletter of the Mountaineering Club of Alaska (MCA). proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive
proposals.feature_description: In Golden Gate Park, 0.3 mi. E of Elk Glen Lake, 0.7 mi. W of Lily Pond
proposals.name_history: The name refers to the Great Blue Herons that nest on Strawberry Hill, an island in the center of the lake, during the months of April and May
proposals.land_ownership: San Francisco Recreation and Park Department

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Stow Lake in San Francisco County's Golden Gate Park to Blue Heron Lake. The proposal was submitted by an individual who reports that she is not affiliated with the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department. Stow Lake was created in 1893 and has long been a destination for leisure activities such as boating and walking. It has been named on USGS topographic maps since 1947. The lake was named for William W. Stow (1824-1895), a former State Assembly Member and member of the San Francisco Park Commission. Stow was also noted for antisemitic actions, including efforts to impose taxes on Jewish business owners. On January 18, 2024, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Commission approved the name change to Blue Heron Lake. The new name reflects the presence in April and May of Great Blue Herons that nest on Strawberry Hill, located at the center of the lake. The decision to rename the lake followed public polling, with residents favoring a name inspired by local wildlife. The Recreation & Park Commission voted 4 to 3 in favor of the change, which also included renaming Stow Lake Drive and Stow Lake Boathouse to Blue Heron Lake Drive and Blue Heron Lake Boathouse, respectively. The proponent included three articles in support of their proposal: o San Francisco Recreation and Park Department article detailing the name change, approved by the Recreation and Park Commission on January 18, 2024 (source). o San Francisco Examiner article discussing the support from the San Francisco Board of Supervisors for the name change and the community's involvement in the name change process (source). o San Francisco Chronicle article covering the history of Stow Lake, the community's push for renaming and the broader efforts to reflect more inclusive values in naming practices (source).

proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature

proposals.feature_description: Located on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, 4 mi. SW of Hayfork
proposals.name_history: Named for George K. Sebring (1924-2005), Forest Service surveyor, flight officer and navigation instructor, business owner in Hayfork, and long-time owner of property north of the summit

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Mount George is proposed for an unnamed 4,066-foot summit in Trinity County, four miles southwest of Hayfork and on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest. The new name, submitted by the niece and daughter of the intended honoree, would commemorate George K. Sebring (1924-2005), who in 1941 began working with the Forest Service, surveying government land in the Hayfork area, including at the location of this summit. From 1942 to 1945, he was a Flight Officer, Bombardier and Navigation instructor with the U.S. Army Air Force. In 1952, George purchased 50 acres on West Tule Creek and directly north of the summit in question, where he raised his large family. He also owned Sebring's Hardware Store in Hayfork. Over the years, family and friends and George himself began referring to the summit as Mount George. The proponents add that George was an active member of the community, participating and contributing to a wide variety of community endeavors, and an active Rotarian and Mason. They describe the summit as "an important landmark for our family." CONNECTICUT

proposals.name_history: Named for Dr. Howard A. "Doc" Pearson (1929-2016), a pediatrician and medical director who specialized in hematology/oncology. He served as president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (1992-93) and co-founded the Hole in the Wall Gang Camp at the lake, where children with serious illnesses could experience joy and freedom

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Poole Pond, a 40-acre lake in the Town of Ashford in Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region, to Pearson Pond. The lake is located on property owned by the Hole in the Wall Gang Camp. Poole Pond has been labeled on USGS maps since 1945, and although the origin of the name has not been determined, online genealogy records show that families named Poole have lived in the Ashford area since the 1800s. The proponent reports that the proposed replacement name Pearson Pond is already used locally, and the change would formalize it. The name would honor Dr. Howard A. "Doc" Pearson (1929-2016), a pediatrician and former president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. Along with actor Paul Newman, Dr. Pearson was one of the founders of the Hole in the Wall Gang Camp, which serves children with serious illnesses. The camp's website and a wooden sign at the lake refer to it as Pearson Pond. For more details, see: Remembering Howard Doc Pearson and Dr. Howard Allen Pearson, 1929-2016 | The American Board of Pediatrics (abp.org). GNIS lists Pearson Brook and Pearson Pond in the Southeastern Connecticut Planning Region and the Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Region, respectively. Pearson Pond is located 33 miles southwest of the pond currently named Poole Pond. FLORIDA

proposals.title: Change Cutler Channel to Deering Bay Channel
proposals.proposal_type: change name to reflect local use
proposals.feature_description: in Biscayne Bay, trends SE from Paradise Point past Chicken Key
proposals.name_history: presumably associated with the community of Deering Bay near the start of the channel
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: Deering Bay Channel (local marina dockmaster) o Published names: o Cutler Channel (USGS 2012-2024; NOAA charts since 1968) o Deering Bay Channel (USCG Light List, 2024; USCG Notice to Mariners since at least 2006; SAIL Magazine online article, 2020)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Cutler Channel in Biscayne Bay in Miami-Dade County to Deering Bay Channel. The feature is a private channel, approximately 1.3 miles in length. NOAA is proposing the change to reflect the name used by the adjacent Deering Bay Marina, the Royal Harbor Yacht Club, and the U.S. Coast Guard. Part of the channel passes through the City of Coral Gables, and it also lies entirely within Florida's Biscayne Bay Aquatic Preserve, managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Cutler Channel has been labeled on NOAA charts since 1968 and was added to GNIS in 2003. The name was not shown on USGS topographic maps prior to the first USTopo map in 2012. The name presumably refers to the nearby unincorporated community of Cutler. The Town of Cutler Bay, incorporated in 2005, is southwest of the channel. In 1993, at the request of the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), the BGN approved the name Deering Bay for the newly developed 220-acre unincorporated community northwest of the channel. NOAA has charted a water feature in this location as "Deering Bay" since 1995. The name Deering Bay Channel has been used by the USCG since at least 2006 in its Notice to Mariners and is currently included in the USCG Light List. NOAA charts the lights along the channel as "Deering Bay Channel Daybeacon[s]"; these are maintained by the marina. NOAA currently charts two water features as "Deering Bay": a river and a sea area. The latter is a harbor that serves the Deering Bay Marina and the Royal Harbor Yacht Club. NOAA has submitted these names to be added to GNIS. NOAA reports that the Deering Bay Marina was established after 1993. A channel 9 miles to the north-northeast in the City of Miami has been labeled as Deering Channel on USGS maps since 1947 and on NOAA charts since 1938.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Indian Creek for a 0.43-mile-long tributary of East Branch DuPage River in Milton Township and the Village of Glen Ellyn in DuPage County. The area is managed by the Forest Preserve District of DuPage County as the Churchill Woods Preserve. The proponent states: The name 'Indian Creek' comes from a slideshow posted online which I found while researching a newspaper article for my high school's newspaper. I believe this name was given due to a Native American village being located northeast of the creek's mouth along the East Branch of the DuPage River. I personally believe this feature requires a name simply because it does not have one right now, unlike other tributaries of the East Branch of the DuPage River (such as Glen Crest Creek, St. Joseph Creek, etc.) The website of the Forest Preserve District of DuPage County refers to "500 Potawatomie Indians [who] lived in present-day Churchill Woods." The location of the village, close to the mouth of the stream, is depicted on a 1900 archaeological map entitled "Indian Trails and Villages of Chicago and of Cook, DuPage and Will Counties, Ill. (1804)." A representative of the Glen Ellyn Historical Society was unable to find any reference to "Indian Creek" in their available sources and noted that there might be some concerns regarding the use of the word "Indian." GNIS lists 74 features in Illinois with "Indian" in their names, although none are within DuPage County. 22 of those features are streams named "Indian Creek." MINNESOTA Sunny Lake
