proposals.title: New name Takola Fala Upi Creek
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Heads N of Ivy Lake, flows generally NE to enter Otoucalofa Creek
proposals.name_history: Named for the native pawpaw trees along its banks and to honor the area's Chickasaw heritage
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other Minnesota Department of Natural Resources Support Petition with 17 signatures *Support The new name Takola Fala Upi Creek is proposed for a 1.67-mile-long tributary of Otoucalofa Creek in Lafayette County. The proponent, a local resident, seeks to honor the Chickasaw heritage, while reflecting the natural vegetation along the stream's banks. He states: Takola Fala Upi is Chickasaw for paw paw. Many native paw paw trees are found along its banks. I'd love to get a Chickasaw expert to make sure the spelling and enunciation are correct and that it does mean paw paw. The whole point is to honor that legacy and get it right. It might come to light that the translation that I have proposed in not correct and at the end of the day, getting it right is the most important thing for me. A blog series on indigenous agriculture published by an architect and city planner reports that "Takola Fala Upi" is Chickasaw for pawpaw, and notes the historical importance of pawpaw trees among Southeastern Native American tribes, including the Chickasaw: Ancestors of the Uchee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creeks, and Catawba selectively cultivated pawpaw orchards (aka patches) near their towns. Many other tribes protected wild patches in the woods by clearing away encroaching vegetation. The pawpaw (Asimina triloba) was one of the favorite fruits of indigenous peoples in Eastern North America. Its natural range extended from southern Ontario to northern Florida. The blog does not explicitly cite any sources for the claim that "Takola Fala Upi" is Chickasaw for "pawpaw" and no other references to the term have been found. GNIS does not lists any features in the U.S. with "Takola Fala Upi" in the name. MISSOURI

proposals.case_summary: Local government Jackson Township Monroe County Commissioners State Names Authority Missouri Board on Geographic Names Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X The new commemorative name Eiseley Creek is proposed for a 2.1-mile-long stream in the City of Lincoln in Lancaster County. The new name, submitted by a representative of the Loren Eiseley Society, would commemorate the nature writer Loren Eiseley (1907-1977), who "grew up nearby and played along its banks as a young boy, developing his love of nature there; he wrote about this creek and the surrounding area in a number of his books." Further: As a boy, Eiseley grew fond of the nearby prairie, ponds, and creeks. As he describes in his writing, he gathered specimens for his homemade aquariums in this stream, and from the pond near its source. Inspired by these adventures, while in grade school he professed that he wanted to be a nature writer. Loren attended the University of Nebraska, where he majored in both English and Anthropology. During this time he wrote for and helped edit the then new literary journal 'Prairie Schooner.' He moved on to the University of Pennsylvania, where he got his Ph.D. in Anthropology in 1937. He became a professor of Anthropology, spending most of his career at Penn. In addition to his professional writing, Eiseley also published 20 books of history of science, creative nonfiction, and poetry. He is widely acknowledged and globally recognized as an important contributor to the nature writing genre. Though he spent his adult life in Philadelphia, this stream from his childhood appears often in his writing, especially in 'All The Strange Hours,' 'The Night Country,' and 'The Lost Notebooks of Loren Eiseley.' It inspired his most famous line 'If there is magic in this world, it is contained in water.' The unnamed stream runs through lrvingdale Park. [It is] a prominent landmark and in conjunction with a recent park renovation project, a commemorative bench and plaque in recognition of Loren Eiseley were recently added to a pedestrian plaza space connecting to a channel crossing of the stream. Soon, there will also be a historical marker along the creek, placed by the Nebraska Historical Society.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Aysees Peak to Milky Way Peak. The 6,275-foot peak is located in the southwest corner of Lincoln County, in an area co-managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Desert National Wildlife Refuge) and the Department of Defense (Nevada Test and Training Range). A description of the area published by the Nevada Department of Wildlife states "The entire unit . . . has no public access." The summit has been named Aysees Peak on USGS topographic maps since 1952 and is mentioned by name at a number of scientific and hiking websites; however, the origin of the name is unknown. The proponent, a resident of the United Kingdom, believes the name should be changed because: This specific area is near Area 51, I wanted to name this piece of land Milky Way Peak because I liked the way it looked. I have seen several YouTube videos of creators coming to this area and seeing 'Alien sightings' and even seeing planets in the sky. It is believed historically that aliens may have come to this area to cultivate resources etc. I chose this place specifically as it's closest to Area 51. I truly believe it's important to cherish the natural beauty of our planet and its landmarks and I think this name is quite suitable. I wanted to go for an Astro themed name as I believe through historical means, it's appropriate. A 2012 report published by the USDA National Cooperative Soil Survey referred to "The Aysees series consist[ing] of very deep, somewhat excessively drained soils formed in alluvium derived from mixed rocks." GNIS lists one other feature in the U.S. named "Milky Way": Milky Way Tank is located in Maricopa County, Arizona.

proposals.title: Change Eastman Cove to Abenaki Cove
proposals.proposal_type: change name to a native name
proposals.proponent: Richard Knox, Will Speers; Center Sandwich, NH
proposals.feature_description: on Squam Lake, 1 mi. NNE of The Rattlesnakes
proposals.name_history: the name refers to the Abenaki people who have inhabited the area
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Eastman Cove (USGS 2023) o Sq___ Cove (USGS 1928, 1931, 1980, 1986, 1995; Laws of the State of New Hampshire 1901; New Hampshire Department of Safety 2010; Town of Sandwich Master Plan 2011; Oliverian Canal Route map, 1830; The Granite Monthly, 1887; History of Carroll County, New Hampshire, 1889; Indians of New Hampshire, 1965; Squam Lakes Association 2000, 2019; Sandwich Historical Society 2019; numerous online real estate listings)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Eastman Cove, a 130-acre bay on Squam Lake in the Town of Sandwich in Carroll County, to Abenaki Cove. The proposal was submitted by two families who live and own land along the cove, and is a counterproposal to one included on Review List 454 to change the name to Senskwa Cove, submitted by a different individual who also owns land along the cove. The cove was formerly named Sq___ Cove until it was changed in September 2022 as a result of Secretary's Order 3404. The name Eastman Cove was presumably chosen by the Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force based on the first name on the list of candidate replacement names; Eastman Brook flows into the cove. The Task Force received two public suggestions for potential replacement names. One was for "Suneta Cove," based on the name of a woman in one legend about the boulder. The other, containing two options, was submitted by the New Hampshire Board on Geographic Names. Following conversations with members of the Cowasuck Band of the Pennacook - Abenaki, those names were Olebatak Cove, meaning "It is Good Smooth Water," or Nokemesek Cove, meaning "My Grandmother's Cove"; the first a description of the cove and the second a reference to the ancestors of the original inhabitants of the area. The name Sq___ Cove was mentioned as early as 1830 on a map of a proposed canal in the area; it was also noted in the 1901 Laws of the State of New Hampshire and appears in present-day town, county, and State documents. Another early reference to the name was in an 1887 article in The Granite Monthly, titled "Asquam Lake and its Environs," which reported that "Sq___ Cove derives its name from the fact that formerly there stood upon one of the ledges of the cove a block of granite that bore a strong resemblance to the draped figure of a woman." One local legend tells the story of a young woman named Amata who was married against her wishes to an old man named Mamon. Amata loved a young man named Moowis who came to rescue her. Mamon killed Moowis and Amita knelt to pray that her suffering be made an example for all to see, and she was turned to stone. A version of the legend included in the 1889 History of Carroll County, New Hampshire has the same story but different names: the young woman is "Princess Suneta," the old man is Waunega, and the young man is Anonis. It is unknown if this legend comes from American Indian tradition or if it was developed by European settlers, but supporters of the Abenaki Cove proposal have stated that it is not an authentic Abenaki legend. Sq___ Cove was first labeled on USGS maps in 1928, although the name ceased to appear on USTopo maps published after 2012. The 2023 edition of the USTopo shows the newly approved name Eastman Cove. The proponents of Abenaki Cove report that they learned in 2022 that the name of the cove had been changed to Eastman Cove, which they said: . . . . carries no historic resonance or distinction; it's derived from a 19th-century family of European descent whose land was traversed by a brook that flows into the Cove." The proponents also stated that "[a]t the time it was thought the change from Sq___ Cove to Eastman Cove was a permanent fait accompli. . . . There was widespread sentiment among local residents that they had had insufficient notice or knowledge of the [Department of the Interior] process to express preference for a locally meaningful name. The Abenaki Cove proponents reported that they selected the name "[a]fter consultation with Abenaki community leaders, historians, archeologists, and conservationists" and: a clear consensus has emerged that whatever new name might be chosen, it should memorialize the area's ancient inhabitants, consistent with current-day appreciation for this deep and much-neglected history. We believe "Abenaki Cove" fulfills this objective with a name that carries widely recognized meaning, requires no explanation, and is readily pronounceable. They also provided statements of support from many individuals: • Don Stevens, Chief of the Nulhegan Band of the Coosuk Abenaki Nation (Nulhegan Abenaki Tribe, a Vermont-recognized group but not federally recognized): We are thankful to the families who are wanting to preserve our tribal ties to this place. . . . Squam Lake is a special place that keeps connecting us with the residents who live there today. We appreciate the work these partners are doing to preserve our history and honor our people past and present. We hope you [the BGN] will approve their proposal to rename Eastman Cove to Abenaki Cove for these reasons. • New Hampshire State Representative Sherry L. Gould and Nulhegan Band of the Coosuk Abenaki Nation member: It is with great pleasure I write in support of the proposal to change the name of Eastman's [sic] Cove to Abenaki Cove. . . . The residents on the cove reached out to me and together we engaged other [non federally recognized] tribes in the conversation about what the name of the cove should be. . . . • Jesse Bowman Bruchac, Director of the Middlebury College Abenaki Language School and leader of the Vermont Abenaki Place Names Project: I am writing in support of the name change of Eastman Cove on Squam Lake to Abenaki Cove. I am aware that a group of residents who currently live on the cove have been in consultation with the recognized tribes to develop a proposal for this change. This name is specific enough for the general public to know what it is, and general enough to encompass all the bands of Abenaki who live in the area today. • Robert G. Goodby, Professor of Anthropology, Franklin Pierce University: Since the 1960s, the Abenaki have become increasingly visible through political activism, community organization, and through a revitalization of their traditional language and art forms. As such, the proposed name change would honor the original population with a term that is widely recognized and accepted by indigenous and non-indigenous communities and in the academic field of history and anthropology. It also has the advantage of being broad, inclusive and all encompassing, avoiding possible disagreements that might arise if the name were one tied to a particular Abenaki community past or present. • John H. Coolidge, Trustee, Hoag Island Preservation Trust & Coolidge Farm Preservation Trust; Director, The Upper Asquam Roads Association: There is. . . consensus that any new name should honor the people who inhabited this area for untold generations before the arrival of European settlers. After consultation with Squam neighbors who propose 'Abenaki Cove,' we agree that this choice would best meet these objectives and receive wide acceptance among current-day Abenaki people and non- indigenous residents and visitors. Its meaning and significance would be well-understood. • James Mykland, Director of the Sandwich Historical Society: Eastman Brook. . . is named after the Eastman family who have no great historical importance to the Town (of Sandwich) or the area. . . . I would support renaming the cove 'Abenaki Cove' to celebrate and recognize the native peoples. . . . It would be a respectful and honorable way to remember these original people. The full letter from Don Stevens also included the following: We were informed that the group of families living on the cove wanted to consult with us to ensure the name they chose would complete their intent of honoring our ancestors. I am aware that a proposal was put forth by others that would glorify a colonial myth of our people. I have enclosed the letter of our Tribal Historian that opposed that proposal [BGN staff received this letter from Brian Chenevert in June 2024]. After having time to review this matter and the proposal of Abenaki Cove put forth by the families who live there, we support Abenaki Cove as being a name that honors our people. We prefer to see our ancestors honored in a straight forward way and not to engage in controversy that comes up with stories written by colonials that we have no memory of. The proponents of Abenaki Cove oppose the choice of Senskwa Cove "based on strong concerns raised by the Native American leaders and historians with whom we have consulted over the past two years." They state that "'senskwa' is a newly devised word based on the Abenaki roots for 'rock' and 'woman'" that: . . . alludes to a romantic legend that surfaced in the 19th century involving an Indian maiden whose lover was killed by an old chief to whom she was promised in marriage, whereupon she was turned into a rock by the Great Spirit in answer to her prayer that her plight be made an example to other women. . . . The authorities we have interviewed do not believe this legend is authentic. Mr. Chenevert, the tribal historian of the Nulhegan Band of Abenaki people, calls it "a fantastical colonial myth" similar to "many other . . . love stories found throughout New England (which) likely began in the 1800s and was created by colonial viewpoints." Abenaki linguist Jesse Bruchac casts doubt on the accuracy of the proposed word in the context of Algonquian languages. "For this reason alone and many other colonialized ideas the name perpetuates," Bruchac writes, "I firmly recommend not using the recently created name." Even one of the proponents of "senskwa" last year testified before the Sandwich Conservation Commission that the legend is "a silly story, but harmless." That seems to us a dubious origin for a name that everyone hopes will be a perpetual memorial to the Abenaki people. The Abenaki Cove proponents reported that "[w]e have consulted with the 'senskwa' proponents. By autumn 2023 it became apparent that the two groups had an irreconcilable difference of opinion about a proposed new name for Eastman Cove." In correspondence with DNC staff, one of the Abenaki Cove proponents pointed out that some of the letters of support submitted with the Senskwa Cove proposal did not explicitly endorse that name, but rather endorsed the efforts to change the name of Eastman Cove to a name that honors the Abenaki people, the Abenaki language, and "to the extent possible retains a connection to the long-lived legend of Sq___ Cove." These include the Squam Lakes Association, the Squam Lakes Conservation Society, and the Webster Land Corporation. In June 2024, the historian of the Nulhegan Band of the Coosuk Abenaki Nation reaffirmed the request that "legally recognized Abenaki Tribes that represent the original indigenous people of New Hampshire [be consulted]." New Hampshire State Representative Sherry L. Gould also stated: I have reviewed the colonial myth that Senskwa Cove alludes to. That proposed name is simply an Abenaki word that is a translation of the name Squaw Rock. There is not a known word for this in our language, though sen is certainly our word for rock, and as you I likely know, skwa is a suffix in our language representing a feminine form of any word. However 'stone woman' is not a concept our culture is familiar enough with as to have a specific word to mark it. . . . I don't find the story credible. To my knowledge there has been no consultation with the four state recognized Abenaki Tribes in this matter. I am aware that one group of Abenaki [the Cowasuck Band of the Pennacook-Abenaki People] initiated this change request and the Chair of the NH Commission on Native American Affair has written a letter in support of the petition for change. However they did not consult any of the four state recognized tribes or the NH Intertribal Council to inquire how members of recognized tribes from around the country who are living in New Hampshire might feel about the cove name reverting to the Abenaki translation of "Sq___ Rock" Cove. . . . [T]he Select Board in Sandwich, NH, chose to not take a position in support of the name change after hearing presentations from proponents and opponents-including the group I have worked with on changing the name of the road and the cove. I believe the town's decision to not step into this matter, which is causing division within the community was a wise choice. I am asking that the US Board on Geographic Names not approve the "senskwa" petition at this time to allow for proper consultation with the state-recognized Abenaki Tribes and also with the NH Intertribal group that represents Native Americans from other recognized tribes who are resident in New Hampshire. I also believe it is prudent to give the town people in Sandwich an opportunity to see if they can come to some agreement on what name would work for them all, rather than deepen any conflict this proposal has created. For details regarding the Senskwa Cove proposal, please refer to BGN Review List 454. The Sandwich Town Selectmen discussed the Senskwa Cove proposal in November 2023 and April 2024, but did not take a position and prefers to let the BGN review process go forward. The Carroll County Board of Commissioners did not respond to requests for a recommendation.

proposals.title: Change Negro Hill to Murry Hill
proposals.submitter: Richard Brandt; Vermontville, NY
proposals.proposal_type: Change name considered to be derogatory
proposals.proponent: Town of Franklin Council; Vermontville, NY
proposals.feature_description: 1.5 mi. SSE of Blue Hill, 3.8 mi. WSW of Vermontville
proposals.name_history: Named for the Murry family, Black pioneers and successful farmers in the Town of Franklin. Wesley Murry (ca.1820- 1867) and Phebe Murry (1817-ca.1885) were granted 40 acres of forested land in the northern Adirondacks in 1847.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: Negro Hill (USGS 1955, 1978, 1999, 2010)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal, submitted by the Franklin Town Council, seeks to change the name of Negro Hill, a 1,906-foot summit, to Murry Hill as the current name is considered derogatory. Lands adjacent to the summit are part of the New York State Forest Preserve, managed by the Adirondack Park Agency and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation. The proposed name would honor the Murry family, Black pioneers who owned land on the hill and were successful farmers in the area. The BGN's approval of the change from Negro Brook to John Thomas Brook (April 2023) for the stream located east of the summit sparked community support for renaming Negro Hill. In July 2024, the proponent of the previous change presented on the Murry family history at an event in Bloomingdale. A petition supporting the change to Murry Hill garnered 71 signatures at the event, later growing to 122 names. Local media coverage highlighted broad community support for the proposal. On July 17, 2024, the Town of Franklin passed a resolution endorsing the renaming of Negro Hill to Murry Hill. It noted that the hill was likely named after Wesley and Phebe Murry, who farmed the land. The proposal "aims to honor the Murry family's resilience in the face of racism," adding: The Murry family's strength, courage, and perseverance to successfully homestead and farm in the Town of Franklin, and their ability to further invest in more land and agricultural equipment is a testament to their character and deserves respect. Allowing geographical features to carry racist names meant to humiliate these hard working families, and for these slurs to be printed on maps, is a stain on our history which we can correct by honoring the people who were pioneers on a challenging landscape. Wesley Murry (ca.1820-1876) was born in Maryland and in 1847 was granted 40 acres of land in the northern Adirondacks by abolitionist Gerrit Smith. This grant was part of a broader initiative aimed at helping Black pioneers acquire the necessary property to qualify for voting in New York. Murry's land was located on the northern slope of what is now referred to as Negro Hill. Along with his wife, Phebe (1817-ca.1885), Wesley moved through various towns before establishing a successful 100-acre farm in Franklin by the mid- 1850s. They were part of a small community of Black farmers in the area, which included the Bradys and Thomases. Regional historian Amy Godine advocates for renaming Negro Hill to Murry Hill to honor the contributions of the Murry family and recognize their humanity: [The current name] denigrates the lived experience of the Black pioneers in this neighborhood by reducing their humanity to skin color, and it implies that their skin color was more important, more memorable, than their names, their achievements, their singularity. In this way it diminishes the memory of their humanity. Worse, its long-time appearance on official maps from public agencies has glossed it with respectability. With this suggested name change, we propose not to erase the history, but to restore it - to invoke the presence of a Black farmer of relative long standing on a tough, unforgiving frontier. According to GNIS, there are no geographic features in North Carolina with "Murry" in their names.

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Lake Caroline is proposed for a newly created 12-acre reservoir located east of the Tar River on private property in Pitt County. The reservoir was excavated after the proponent, who owns the property, sold sand from the central part of his land, which he purchased in 2017. The proposed name would honor Caroline Daniels (1995-2011), the proponent's niece, who passed away from a rare form of cancer at the age of 16. The proponent describes Caroline as "a beacon of joy, kindness, and resilience." In her memory, he previously named paths on the property "Caroline Way" and "Caroline Avenue." He adds, "It seems fitting that this natural wonder [the reservoir] should bear Caroline's name - a tribute to her enduring impact on my life and the land she inspired me to cherish. I believe it would be a meaningful way to perpetuate her legacy and celebrate her love for nature." According to her obituary, "Caroline was a loving friend to anyone whom she had the opportunity to come in contact with. She was a young lady who had a passion for dance and was a talented artist. She loved spending time with her family, friends, and church youth group. She had the gift of giving her time and talent to people of all ages." The proponent acknowledges that his niece did not have a direct association with the reservoir. According to GNIS, there are no geographic features in North Carolina with "Caroline" in their names.

proposals.case_summary: The new name North Gambill Lake is proposed for a 3.3-acre unnamed reservoir in Forsyth County, north of Middle Gambill Lake and 0.3 miles northeast of the community of Pfafftown. Middle Gambill Lake is listed in GNIS, having been collected from a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) 1981 inventory of dams and reservoirs. The proponent, a local resident, emphasizes the lake's significance to the community as a site for recreation, birdwatching, and social events, and notes the diverse wildlife in the area. He presumes Gambill is a family name but could not provide any details regarding the origin. Online genealogy records indicate the presence of several individuals with the surname Gambill in Forsyth County since at least the 1930s, including Zeb Gambill, who owned Grand View Guernsey Farm in Pfafftown before his death in 1949. The National Map basemap currently assigns the name Middle Gambill Lake to both bodies of water. The USACE National Inventory of Dams (NID) lists the dam at Middle Gambill Lake as "Gambill Lake Dam Middle," with the more southerly one recorded as "Gambill Pond Dam Lower," owned by the Mickle Dam Homeowners Association, Inc. proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Borges Butte has been proposed for a 790-foot summit east of the City of Happy Valley and just west of Sunshine Valley. The proposed name would honor Carl Christian Frederick Borges (1847-1928), who immigrated to the United States in the 1870s. His son, Frederick Henry William Borges (1893-1965), acquired 160 acres in the southwest quarter of Section 28 in 1885. The proposal also states that Carl Borges is buried in Lincoln Memorial Park on Mount Scott, which borders Happy Valley. The road between their properties is now known as Borges Road. GNIS lists no geographic features with "Borge" or "Borges" in the name. Deardorff (1824-1902) and his wife Rachel (1836-1901), co-founders of the settlement that would become the City of Happy Valley. PLSS Sec. 6, T2S, R3E, Willamette Meridian Case Summary The new commemorative name Deardorff Butte is proposed for a 770-foot butte east of the City of Happy Valley. The name would honor the Deardorff family, who were among the region's earliest settlers. According to the proposal, they arrived in 1851 and benefited from the 1850 Donation Land Claim Act. Christian and Matilda Deardorff (1805-1884 and 1802-1891, respectively) acquired 640 acres in Clackamas County, where they established a farming community near what is now Scouters Mountain. The family played a key role in the early development of the area, with the surrounding valley eventually becoming known locally as Deardorff Valley (not in GNIS). Their son John M. Deardorff and his wife, Rachel (1824-1902 and 1836-1901, respectively), co-founded the settlement that would later become the City of Happy Valley. The proposal also states that the Deardorffs contributed significantly to the local community. John M. donated land for the Christilla Pioneer Cemetery. In 1858, the family built the iconic Deardorff Barn, which stood until 1997. As farmers, John and his son William Albert made regular deliveries of produce to Portland, furthering the family's economic role in the region. John M. also played an important civic role, donating land for a schoolhouse and helping establish infrastructure such as Deardorff Road, which remains a key route in the area today. GNIS lists no features with "Deardorff" in the name. proposals.case_summary: The new name Morden Creek is proposed for a 0.9-mile-long stream that flows through Fairfield Glade Resort and into the north end of Saint George Lake in Cumberland County. The proponent, who owns property along the stream, states: 'Morden' is a combination of the words mór and dūn (derivative of Old English). Mōr meaning 'moor' which is a boggy area and dūn meaning hills. The name is meant to describe the area that the feature lies in. 'Creek' is to describe the actual feature as a natural stream of water normally smaller than a river. It is a year-round water source that can perhaps be more specific and accurately telling of the area. When asked to clarify the spelling (den vs. dun), the proponent explained that she felt "'dun' was less appropriate due to potential negative connotations in slang," adding "'Morden' presents a synonymous and more phonetically accurate spelling based on the language from which the word is derived." She also confirmed that the name is not intended to be commemorative or commercial in nature.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Castle Mountain, a 1,001-foot summit located on Fort Cavazos in Bell County, to Renegade Hill. The proponent represents the 4th Battalion (known as the "Renegade Battalion") of the 5th Air Defense Artillery Regiment; he reports that the proposed name is used locally and that it honors the battalion and specifically commemorates its seven soldiers who have lost their lives in combat. He adds: The designation 'Renegade' was bestowed upon the 4-5 Air Defense Artillery Battalion upon its creation in 1988. The unit served with distinction under First Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, TX (now Fort Cavazos, TX) in Operation Desert Storm and Operation Iraqi Freedom. 'Castle Mountain' has been used by the Soldiers of the 'Renegade Battalion' for training and events dating back to 1988. The unit of 600 Soldiers has referred to the area as 'Renegade Hill' since the late 1980s when conducting training there. We believe it is appropriate to rename 'Castle Mountain' to 'Renegade Hill' as it is referred to by the unit. Although not a commemorative name, this would also allow for the memorialization of the Soldiers from the 'Renegade Battalion' that died in service to this country under the name 'Renegade' [Staff Sergeant Haws, Sergeant Rosenbaum, and Specialists Davis, Ebert, Price, Regnier, and Yoemans]. The proponent provided an article which details the battalion's training. They conduct exercises to validate their combat skills to prepare for real combat situations. The name Castle Mountain has appeared on USGS topographic maps since 1947 and was recorded in a USGS Bulletin in 1902. A 1894 smaller-scale USGS map applied the name Castle Hill to a summit in general vicinity, but it is not clear if this refers to the same feature as present-day Castle Mountain. GNIS lists no features in Texas with "Renegade" in the name.

proposals.land_ownership: Denali National Park and Preserve (National Park Service)
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Mount Carola is proposed for a 4,254 peak between Ruth Gacier and Tokasitna Glacier in Denali National Park and Preserve. The proposed name commemorates Carola "Carol" J. Young (1936-2018), described in the proposal as a miner and pioneer in Alaska. Carola Young served as President of the Yentna Mining District for 23 years and was an active member of the Alaska Miners Association for over 40 years. The proposal states that she was instrumental in advocating against the construction of a visitor center in the Petersville area as part of her role on the South Denali Development Steering Committee. The proposal notes that Carola Young and her mother restored the Fairview Inn in Talkeetna after a fire and operated it from 1971 to 1978. During this time, the inn became a community hub for miners, mountain climbers, and locals. Portraits of Talkeetna pioneers commissioned by Young remain displayed in the inn. Additionally, the proponent states that Young helped establish the VFW Post 3836 in Talkeetna and supported the implementation of SNOWtrac, a program providing groomed winter trails in Alaska. The proposal also describes Young's work at a mining camp near Cache Creek, where she lived without electricity or running water, highlighting her efforts to improve living conditions at the camp, including installing gravity-fed plumbing and constructing a shower house. The Talkeetna Historical Society and Museum emphasized Young's contributions to Talkeetna and her role in preserving the cultural and natural heritage of the area. The Alaska Miners Association highlighted her service to the mining community, including her advocacy for miners and her public service on state committees. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough Historical Preservation Commission and a private citizen also expressed support, citing Young's legacy as a pioneer and community leader. The Mountaineering Club of Alaska stated its opposition, citing the club's longstanding policy against endorsing commemorative names for geographic features. In their statement, they noted: "The Mountaineering Club of Alaska has a longstanding policy that prohibits the endorsement of commemorative names intended to honor people, whether living or dead, for geographic features." The National Park Service (NPS) has expressed opposition to the proposal to name the peak "Mount Carola." The NPS notes that the feature is located within eligible wilderness, and their policy, as outlined in Staff Directive 80-4, states that naming such features is not supported "absent an overriding need identified for purposes of safety, education, area administration, or other management purposes." The NPS further references Policy IV, sections 1 and 2, of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names' Principles, Policies, and Procedures (2016), which align with their position. They conclude that no overriding need has been identified in this case. ARIZONA
proposals.stakeholders: Local government City of Albertville Mayor-Council DeKalb County Commission State Names Authority Alabama Geographic Names Authority Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X o Published names: None found Case Summary The new name Mount Carola is proposed for a 4,254 peak between Ruth Gacier and Tokasitna Glacier in Denali National Park and Preserve. The proposed name commemorates Carola "Carol" J. Young (1936-2018), described in the proposal as a miner and pioneer in Alaska. Carola Young served as President of the Yentna Mining District for 23 years and was an active member of the Alaska Miners Association for over 40 years. The proposal states that she was instrumental in advocating against the construction of a visitor center in the Petersville area as part of her role on the South Denali Development Steering Committee. The proposal notes that Carola Young and her mother restored the Fairview Inn in Talkeetna after a fire and operated it from 1971 to 1978. During this time, the inn became a community hub for miners, mountain climbers, and locals. Portraits of Talkeetna pioneers commissioned by Young remain displayed in the inn. Additionally, the proponent states that Young helped establish the VFW Post 3836 in Talkeetna and supported the implementation of SNOWtrac, a program providing groomed winter trails in Alaska. The proposal also describes Young's work at a mining camp near Cache Creek, where she lived without electricity or running water, highlighting her efforts to improve living conditions at the camp, including installing gravity-fed plumbing and constructing a shower house. The Talkeetna Historical Society and Museum emphasized Young's contributions to Talkeetna and her role in preserving the cultural and natural heritage of the area. The Alaska Miners Association highlighted her service to the mining community, including her advocacy for miners and her public service on state committees. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough Historical Preservation Commission and a private citizen also expressed support, citing Young's legacy as a pioneer and community leader. The Mountaineering Club of Alaska stated its opposition, citing the club's longstanding policy against endorsing commemorative names for geographic features. In their statement, they noted: "The Mountaineering Club of Alaska has a longstanding policy that prohibits the endorsement of commemorative names intended to honor people, whether living or dead, for geographic features." The National Park Service (NPS) has expressed opposition to the proposal to name the peak "Mount Carola." The NPS notes that the feature is located within eligible wilderness, and their policy, as outlined in Staff Directive 80-4, states that naming such features is not supported "absent an overriding need identified for purposes of safety, education, area administration, or other management purposes." The NPS further references Policy IV, sections 1 and 2, of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names' Principles, Policies, and Procedures (2016), which align with their position. They conclude that no overriding need has been identified in this case. ARIZONA

proposals.case_summary: The new name Elisabeth Creek is proposed for a 2.8-mile-long intermittent stream within the protected Watson Lake/Granite Dells city-owned park preserve in Yavapai County. The stream heads in the Town of Prescott Valley on the northwest slope of Glassford Hill, then flows northwest through a State Resource Management Area and the City of Prescott and Granite Dells (a valley) into Granite Creek. The proponent, who serves as Vice President of the Granite Dells Preservation Foundation, states that the name would honor Elisabeth Ruffner (1919-2019), who "was instrumental in obtaining and preserving the Granite Dells with its creeks." Further: Elisabeth Ruffner saved and assured the preservation of numerous historical and natural landmarks throughout Arizona. In her 99 years, she was unrelenting in efforts in leading causes that improved the lives of the people of Prescott and the State. The creation of a park in the Granite Dells is one of her successes. It has become the jewel in Prescott all cherish and enjoy. Naming this previously unnamed creek to commemorate Elisabeth Ruffner would honor her memory and permanently secure her place in the annuls of Arizona history. Those who cross the creek along the rails-to-trails Peavine Trail and Iron King Trail will learn of Elisabeth Ruffner in the signage and maps. She was also inducted into the Arizona Women's Hall of Fame. GNIS does not list any streams in Arizona named "Elizabeth" or "Elisabeth."

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the official name of Cabeza Prieta Peak, a 2,523 foot-summit in the Cabeza Prieta Mountains in Yuma County to S-Chuk Mo'o. The summit is not the highest point of the Cabeza Prieta Mountains and is located in Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge. The proponent states that they are "an O'odham historian, enrolled in the Gila River Indian Community. . . [and a] professor of American Indian and Transborder Studies at Arizona State University." The proponent stated: S-Chuk Mo'o, Black Head, is the original Hia-Ced O'odham name for the peak. Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge encompasses a significant portion of the Hia- Ced O'odham jeved, or homeland. I documented the name S-Chuk Mo'o in a paper I published in the Journal of Arizona History. The paper, titled "Sand People and Yellow Fever: O'odham Himdag, Arizona Territory, Calendar Sticks, and Resistance, 1851-1860" (Summer, 2023) refers to S-Chuk Mo'o on page 167. Please note, the 2023 paper is a sequel to a previously published paper on Hia-Ced O'odham ethnohistory, titled "Hiding in the Shadows of History: Revitalizing Hia-Ced O'odham Peoplehood," which appeared in a 2013 issue of the Journal of the Southwest. The proponent also noted the proposed name in a Cabeza Prieta Natural History Association guide, "A Visitor's Guide to El Camino del Diablo, Leg 2b: El Camino del Diablo from Tule Well to Tinajas Altas" and Harry J Winters Jr.'s 2013 O'odham Place Names: Meanings, Origins, and Histories Arizona and Sonora. Cabeza prieta means dark head in Spanish. The name is associated with three other official names: Cabeza Prieta Mountains, Cabeza Prieta Tanks, and Cabeza Prieta Pass. This proposal would not affect any of these names.

proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o General Creek: USGS 1891, 1893, 1895, 1940, 1955, 1977, 1992 o Phipps Creek: The Lake of the Sky, George Wharton James, 1915 o Sugar Pine Creek: Wheeler survey, 1877; CA State Engineer map, 1882
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of General Creek (BGN 1895), a 9.5-mile-long stream in El Dorado County, to dukMéʔem wáťa. The stream flows into Lake Tahoe and is in Ed Z'berg Sugar Pine Point State Park and the U.S. Forest Service's Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit. The proposal states: California State Parks is submitting this request after receiving it from The Washoe Tribe of Nevada & California, a federally recognized Indian Tribe. The creek is located within Ed Z'Berg Sugar Pine Point State Park, in traditional Washoe territory. The stream is currently named for William Phipps, nicknamed "General," who received a land grant in 1869 including the mouth and much of the course of the stream. Little is known of Phipps' life prior to his arrival in California during the Gold Rush. It appears he was not a general and there is no record of his military service; the nickname appears to have derived from a drinking contest he won and a pun on the word "gin." Phipps is remembered by the Tribe and in the historical record for his antagonism toward Native people, and may have committed serious crimes in the process of appropriating their ancestral lands. A history of the Tahoe area published in 1957 describes Phipps murdering a man called "One-Eyed John" (likely a Washoe ancestor), stealing his beaded footwear and leaving his body to be eaten by wolves. Tribal oral history confirms that Washoe people stayed away from Phipps' land during his lifetime, even though they visited and worked for his immediate neighbors to the north and south. He was quoted as saying "I saved this hyar [here] great country of ours from the clutches of the [derogratory term for Native people]." The stream is known in the Washoe language as dukMéʔem wáťa, meaning "Wave Creek." Archaeological evidence and traditional ecological knowledge held by the Tribe suggest that the traditional name commemorates a historical Seiche (lake tsunami) event. "General" is a spurious title attributed to a man whose behavior was likely abhorrent. California State Parks has enacted the change in our facilities names because it better reflects the natural and cultural history of the area and will provide visitors with better access to the park's natural and cultural resources. Chairman Serrell Smokey, Washoe Tribe of Nevada & California, submitted a letter with the proposal in which he wrote: Washoe elders discussed this area has experienced large waves during the windy weather. One story is "a Wa·siw Man with wegeléyu had a vision of a Tidal wave generating from the North shore Tahoe going across the lake to the South. In his Vision, there is a large Boulder on a ledge under of the water a few hundred feet and there will be an earthquake that will make it fall and cause this to happen." Again, thank you for your consideration to rename this creek to geographically name known to the Washoe Tribe. In 1895, the U.S. Geological Survey asked the BGN to decide on the official name of the stream because there were two names found in published use: General Creek on USGSS topographic maps and Sugar Pine Creek on Wheeler Survey map. The BGN decided that General Creek would be the official name; there is no evidence that they considered the origin of the name in their decision. Four nearby features have names that include "Phipps" and are reportedly named for William Phipps: Phipps Creek (labeled on USGS maps since 1955), Phipps Lake, Phipps Pass, and Phipps Peak. The peak was first labeled on USGS maps in 1889 and the others since 1955. Several sources published information about the name General Creek and William Phipps. These are noted in chronological order. The Lake of the Sky by George Wharton James (1915) reported that the stream was called Phipps Creek, "named on the map General Creek, from General [George] Phipps. At the mouth of the creek this pioneer located on 160 acres. . . ." The July 23, 1944 Oakland Tribune's "Knave" editorial column noted the stream as "General's Creek" which was: Named for Gen. William Phipps and in nearby country are Phipp's Lake and Phipp's Peak, 9300 elevation. General Phipps as he was known to everyone . . . came to Georgetown in 1854, a native of Kentucky, and a veteran of the Indian wars where he won his title of General. He was well known and highly esteemed. Noted for his marksmanship with a rifle he knew every nook and corner of the Sierras from Amador County to the Southern Pacific Railroad. He was 74 years of age when he died March 15, 1887 and was buried in the cemetery at Georgetown. . . ." Tahoe Place Names by Barbara Lekisch (1988) reported that "the Washoes fished at the mouth of the creek, which they called dukhmE'EmwO'tha, but never camped there for long. [citing Freed, Stanley A. "Washo Habitation Sites In the Lake Tahoe Area," Reports of the University of California Archaeological Survey. Notes on Western Nevada Archaeology and Ethnology 66, February 1966: 73-83.]" Lekisch reported that Phipps Peak and Phipps Pass were also named for William Phipps. California Place Names (Erwin G. Gudde and William Bright, 1988) reported the basic information from the 1944 "Knave" column; the same information was provided in earlier editions of the book. COLORADO

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to rename Longs Peak, a 14,256-foot elevation peak in Rocky Mountain National Park, Boulder County, to Beaver Mountain. Longs Peak was officially named in 1911 by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN). The name has been labeled on USGS Topographic Maps since 1906. Additionally, it is the highest summit in Rocky Mountain National Park (ROMO) and the 15th highest in Colorado, standing at an elevation of 14,256 feet. The proponent wrote Longs Peak, the 14,000' peak in Rocky Mountain National Park, is named after the explorer Stephen Long who helped to explore and settle-or conquer and oppress, depending upon one's perspective-the West. Although Stephen Long did not commit the atrocities associated with Governor Evans [a reference to the 2023 renaming of Mount Evans to Mount Blue Sky], Stephen Long does represent an aspect of American history that some may find controversial. The name of the peak should reflect this astonishing rock formation [described above] as opposed to a historical figure that will have less significance with each passing generation and is associated with a controversial aspect of history. The proponent provided a blog link that includes an image of the beaver-like formation. Case Summary This proposal is to rename Mount Meeker , a 13,911-foot elevation summit in Rocky Mountain National Park, Boulder County, to Paddle Tail Mountain. Mount Meeker has been labeled on USGS topographic maps since 1915. Mount Meeker was officially named in 1911 by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN). The recorded decision referenced local usage and other authorities. The proponent wrote Mount Meeker is named for Nathan Meeker who in 1878 became a U.S. Indian agent in Colorado. In 1879, Meeker lost his life during the Meeker Massacre, an attack by a band of Ute Indians that resulted in the death of an additional 13 U.S. troops and the kidnapping of Meeker's wife and daughter. While the renaming of Mount Evans brought to light the Sand Creek Massacre, the Meeker Massacre represents the other side of side of man's inhumanity to man. Mount Meeker should be renamed because better avenues exist to memorialize the difficult aspects of human history. Renaming Mount Meeker to Paddle Tail Mountain is consistent with the renaming of Longs Peak to Beaver Mountain. proposals.case_summary: The new name Lincoln Gate Creek is proposed for a 3.1-mile-long tributary of the English River in Iowa Township in Washington County. The proposal was submitted by the Commissioner of the Washington County Soil and Water Conservation District on behalf of the local 4-H Enterprisers Club, who wrote: In collaboration with the Washington County Soil and Water Conservation District the 4- H Enterprisers club journeyed in naming an unnamed creek on the east side of Riverside that drains into the English River. As part of this year-long legacy project, the club researched the watershed characteristics and even hosted a public event (March 2024) featuring local historian Michael Zahs, with over 100 attendees. This event was recorded and is available on YouTube. After exploring over 20 potential names, the club presented their top three choices to the Riverside City Council in May 2024. At their October 2024 meeting, the Enterprisers cast their final votes and selected Lincoln Gate Creek - a nod to Riverside's rich history in timber harvest, especially making rails for fencing, a job once held by President Lincoln himself as a railmaker. There are approximately 45 townships in Iowa named Lincoln Township. Further, there is the City of Lincoln, two Townships of East Lincoln, and a populated place named Lincoln. Many of Iowa's counties and townships were established during the mid-to-late 19th century, closely coinciding with Lincoln's presidency and assassination.

The name would honor Emory Deaton (1911-2003). The proponent reported: Emory Deaton was a well respected [sic] citizen in Franklin county from the time his father bought their farm in 1926 when Emory was 15 years old, until he died in 2003. Emory was a man who knew no strangers and always took the time to help his neighbors whether they needed help or not. Without him, a total of 6 households would not be able to live and work on or near the property he called home. It's a real shame more people don't know his name. proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the local name Adai Burial Bayou for a 1.3-mile-long tributary of Tapalcat Bayou in Natchitoches Parish. The proposal was submitted by a member and employee of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana, which is not a federally recognized Tribe. When asked about his affiliation with the group, he responded that he is "a volunteer helping with social media, communications, and administrative tasks." The group is a state-recognized tribe in Louisiana. The stream is located within the Census Bureau's Adai Caddo State Designated Tribal Statistical Area. The proponent submitted a second proposal for the name Chief Quemsy Branch (q.v.), for another stream 2.4 miles to the southeast. The proposal for Adai Burial Bayou states: [t]he proposed name has been in current use for as long as anyone can remember as evidenced by the letters of support. . . . The name's origin is for the Adai people (Native Americans inhabiting the local area since time immemorial). The Adai people have been buried and laid to rest along this bayou for generations. The Catholic cemetery (St. Anne Cemetery) at the headwaters of this bayou is where many of the Adai people have been buried for over 120 years. Over 90% of the gravesites are those of Native American Adai ancestry. Former Chief Rufus Davis Jr. and many of his extended family are laid to rest there. The tribe holds an annual ceremony on Mother's Day at the burial site honoring their ancestors interred there. This Native American tradition has been maintained for over 100 years at this location. The proposal included letters of support from John Mark Davis, the Chief of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana; Dr. Mark Hyoung Choi, Secretary, Board of Directors of the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society (LGHS); Gordon O'Con, the Mayor of the Village of Robeline located about nine miles south of the stream; and a local resident and member of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana, who lives about 1.6 miles southwest of the stream. (The stream is not within the incorporated Village of Robeline.) Chief Davis wrote: The Tribal Council of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana unanimously support the proposal to name the subject stream Adai Burial Bayou. The stream is located approximately 2.5 miles north of our museum and cultural center in Robeline, Louisiana. The stream is located within the boundaries of our historic native range and the current U.S. Census Bureau's Adai Caddo State Designated Tribal Statistical Area. The stream has been locally known as Adai Burial Bayou as it runs through our ancestral lands and ancient burial grounds. The stream runs near St. Anne Cemetery, where generations of our people are interred. Today, this rural area consists mostly of farm, ranch and timberland. A large portion of the local population, property owners, members of St. Anne Catholic Church and those interred at St. Anne Cemetery are Adai. St. Anne is the official patron saint of our tribe per the registry at the Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria. The proposal complies with the U.S. Geological Survey's [sic] guidance entitled "Cultural Sensitivity for Native American Names." LGHS Secretary Choi added: After reviewing records of the Roman Catholic Church (Natchitoches Parish and Diocese of Alexandria) and public records including parish and state records, newspapers, genealogical records, military service records, and other archives, the LGHS supports the proposal to name the subject stream after the state-recognized Native American tribe (Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana) and their nearby burial area (Saint Anne's Cemetery). . . . Based on the information reviewed including documents from local residents, property owners and the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana, the stream has been locally known as Adai Burial Bayou for many years. . . . Robeline Mayor O'Con wrote: The Adai people have a long, rich history in the Robeline area. They are the indigenous people of this area, and their contributions have shaped the history of Louisiana. Today, the Adai continue to be outstanding citizens of the local community. Their tribal headquarters and ceremonial grounds are located in Robeline. Many attend Saint Anne's Catholic Church and their ancestors are buried at the Saint Anne Cemetery along the banks of the Adai Burial Bayou. The local resident wrote: I am a local property owner, and I support the BGN proposal to name the bayou by the cemetery to Adai Burial Bayou. Since the early 1980's, I have owned approximately 10 acres . . . in Robeline near the St. Anne Cemetery. I am Adai Indian. My Adai Indian family members are buried in that cemetery. For my entire life, I have participated in our tribe's ceremony honoring our ancestors at the cemetery along the bayou. I will be laid to rest in that same cemetery. * included with proposal

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to apply the new name Chief Quemsy Branch to an officially unnamed 3.72- mile-long tributary of Tapalcat Bayou in Natchitoches Parish. The stream flows through a small parcel of the Red River National Wildlife Refuge. As with the previous proposal for Adai Burial Bayou, this proposal was submitted by a member and employee of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana, which is not a federally recognized Tribe. The group is a state-recognized tribe in Louisiana. The stream is located within the Census Bureau's Adai Caddo State Designated Tribal Statistical Area. The proposal states: [t]he origin of the name is the 18th century chief of the Adai Indians (Native Americans): Chief Quemsy. [He] was an official 'medal chief' of the Louisiana colonial government, meaning he was recognized as the main chief of the Adai Nation (allies of the French and then Spanish colonial governments). Spain bestowed upon Chief Quemsy a medal giving him the authority to negotiate on behalf of the Adai with Spain. During his reign, the Adai were great allies of the Louisiana colony aiding its citizens and the commandant of Fort St. Jean Baptiste des Natchitoches. He provided warriors (up to 15 at a time) to the colonial government to support their activities and missions. During this time, the Adai had villages in present-day Louisiana primarily in Natchitoches and Sabine Parishes. The main village was located on historic El Camino Real (LA HWY 6) between the Sabine River and the town/fort of Natchitoches. . . . Chief Quemsy is documented in many colonial records of that period. . . . Chief Quemsy's exact birth year is unknown as he was born on the Louisiana colony frontier, presumably in an Adai village. Native Americans born during this period outside of colonial towns were rarely documented. . . . As was common in the French then Spanish then Anglicized spelling of names, Quemsy has also been spelled as Quensy. However, the more common and recognized spelling of the name that is consistent with the Adai language is Quemsy. The proposal included letters of support from John Mark Davis, the Chief of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana; Dr. Mark Hyoung Choi, Secretary, Board of Directors of the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society; Gordon O'Con, the Mayor of the Village of Robeline located about nine miles south of the stream; and a local resident and member of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana who lives about 2.5 miles south of the stream. (The stream is not within the incorporated Village of Robeline.) Chief Davis wrote: The Tribal Council of the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana unanimously support the proposal to name the subject stream Chief Quemsy Branch. Chief Quemsy Branch is located approximately 1.5 miles northeast of our tribal museum and cultural center in Robeline, Louisiana. The stream is located within the boundaries of our historic native range and the current U.S. Census Bureau's Adai Caddo State Designated Tribal Statistical Area. The proposal complies with the U.S. Geological Survey's [sic] guidance entitled "Cultural Sensitivity for Native American Names". LGHS Secretary Choi added: After reviewing historical texts and public records including parish and state records, newspapers, genealogical records, military service records, and other archives, the LGHS supports the proposal to name the subject stream after Chief Quemsy. Robeline Mayor O'Con wrote: While I have been long familiar with the Adai people and the Adai Caddo Indian Nation of Louisiana, I only recently learned the history of Chief Quemsy. As a great medal Chief of the Adai and staunch ally of the Louisiana Colony, he helped ensure the security of the colonists and colony that later became the state of Louisiana. His contributions to the formation and history of Natchitoches Parish have more than earned him this honor. The local resident wrote: I am a local property owner. I own approximately 10 acres . . . in Robeline . . . near this stream. I support the BGN proposal to name the stream to Chief Quemsy Branch. Chief Quemsy was one of the most famous chiefs who ruled over this land. He was a medal chief and recognized as an important ally by the French and Spanish governments of Louisiana during that time. Many of us in Robeline and the greater Natchitoches Parish area are familiar with his story. We are proud of his contributions to our local area and to the state of Louisiana. * included with proposal MAINE

proposals.feature_description: Heads between Mount Agamenticus and Second Hill, flows NW, then curves SW, joining Hoopers Brook approximately 0.4 miles downstream of Hoopers Swamp.
proposals.name_history: Name honors Marion Fuller Brown (1917-2011), a dedicated town board member and leader in conserving the Greater Mount Agamenticus Region.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Marions Brook is proposed for a 1.56-mile-long unnamed stream in the vicinity of Mount Agamenticus in the Town of York, York County. The stream originates between Mount Agamenticus and Second Hill, flows northwest, then curves southwest, passing through the Mount Agamenticus Wildlife Management Area before joining Hoopers Brook, a tributary of the York River. This proposal was submitted by Friends of Mount Agamenticus. The proposed name honors Marion Fuller Brown (1917-2011), a lifelong conservationist, civic leader, and former Maine state representative. According to the proposal and the included letters of support, Brown was instrumental in spearheading the movement to protect the Greater Mount Agamenticus Conservation Region. Her legacy includes significant contributions to environmental legislation, including Maine's landmark billboard ban and returnable bottle law. She also served on numerous local and state boards, advocating for land preservation and scenic conservation. The proposal has received strong support from various stakeholders, including the Town of York Selectboard, York County Board of Commissioners, Maine Geographic Names Authority, Maine House of Representatives and multiple organizations and individuals committed to conservation.

proposals.submitter: Kevin Carpenter-Driscoll; City of Greenbelt - Department of Public Works Date submitted same
proposals.proposal_type: New name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Flows E into an unnamed tributary of Beaverdam Creek
proposals.name_history: Means "Waters with Ferns" in the Unami language, a major dialect of the Algonquin.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found o Northway Stream: George Mason University Tree Report, 2019; Greenbelt News Review: "North Woods Stream Needs Name: Maybe Sarah's Creek?"
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to name a 0.37-mile-long stream in the Greenbelt Forest Preserve's North Woods Tract in Prince George's County as Sipi Ahsikemensh. The stream flows into an unnamed tributary of Beaverdam Creek. The proposal was initiated by the City of Greenbelt's Department of Public Works with input from the Forest Preserve Advisory Board (FPAB). The name is derived from the Unami dialect of the Algonquin language and translates to "Waters with Ferns." The proponent writes that the name is pronounced "see pee ah seek ah mansh." This naming effort involved consultation with Rico Newman, a member of the Choptico Band of the Piscataway Chiefdom, who provided linguistic expertise. Newman explained that Algonquin names for waterways "often reflect environmental or riparian features rather than specific waterbodies, as water is viewed as a continuous, dynamic element." The stream has been referred to as Northway Stream in previous documents, including a 2019 George Mason University Tree Report, and was referenced in an August 2019 Greenbelt News Review article titled "North Woods Stream Needs Name: Maybe Sarah's Creek?." The FPAB voted in favor of the name Sipi Ahsikemensh during its June 2021 meeting, after which the recommendation was presented to the Greenbelt City Council, which approved the name in July 2022. MICHGAN

proposals.title: Change Lost Lake to Lake Trillium
proposals.proposal_type: change name in reference to a person
proposals.feature_description: 5.3 mi. WNW of Keweenaw Point, 4.4 mi. SE of Copper Harbor
proposals.name_history: named for the favorite flower of Barbara Fetterman (1954- 2017) a Michigan conservationist
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Lost Lake: USGS 1940, 1948, 1949, 1985
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Lost Lake in Grant Township, Keweenaw County, to Lake Trillium. The lake is on land owned by the proponent. The proposed name is the favorite flower of the proponent's sister, Barbara Fetterman (1954-2017) a Michigan conservationist. The proponent wrote: Asking to change from Lost Lake to Lake Trillium. I purchased all the land around this remote lake. I allow and support everyone to visit and fish the lake. My sister. . . was a conservationist and loved the U[pper] P[eninsula] of Michigan. I would propose to change the name to her favorite flower- trilliums-for the lake. The locals support this change. . . . The locals have not and will not mind the change. . . . Trillium was her favorite flower and sounds much better than Barb Lake. . . . It would mean everything to us for this as her legacy for her commitment to Women's Health and her love of the out of doors. . . . She made a huge difference in Women's health care worldwide. If it wasn't [L]ost [L]ake I wouldn't ask. But changing this will offend no one and honor a great American woman. In an initial email asking about the proposal process, the proponent included the following information about Barbara Fetterman written in 2017 by Dr. Diane Tokugawa, Director of Cytology/Histology/Immunohistochemistry at TPMG Regional Laboratory in Berkeley, California: She is above and beyond an essential member of Regional Lab's Cytology Department and has worked tirelessly and quietly behind the scenes for Women's Health and cervical cancer screening for decades. Her fierce dedication and work with Regional Cytology, Women's Health Leadership, and NIH has improved detection of cervical cancer for our patients and beyond. She's affected so many lives, and people don't know who she is. The proponent also included the following from Dr. John Kunkel, Blood Bank Director and Pathologist, at Kaiser San Rafael: Barbara was committed to delivering exceptional care in the screening of cervical cancer. She was always available to answer any questions I had with regards to CAP stats which she compiled (or any question). Those CAP Pap stats on lablink are truly an unbelievable accomplishment. They attest to her vision of making stats readily available to pathologists so that they could improve their diagnostic acumen when interpreting Pap smears. Many a CAP inspector commented on this valuable resource and stated that this format should be the standard of care. The proponent reported that they had for letters of support from individuals associated with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources and a Fisheries and a Keweenaw Bay Indian Community Wildlife Biologist. The proponent reported that: The Keweenaw Bay Indian Community shared with me they informally support this change. They will not come out against the change. They will supply more if needed later. They have always supported me with fish plants at Camp Josh for the special needs campers. BGN staff informed the proponent that all federally recognized Tribes would be notified of the Review List and asked to comment on any proposal, including this one, and that if the Tribal leadership or Tribal Historic Preservation Officer submitted a recommendation in writing, that would be considered an official recommendation from the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community. BGN staff received three emails or letters of support from four individuals who know the proponent. The opinions stated included that • some of the writers have worked closely with the proponent for many years on local conservation issues • that the name change would be a fitting honor for the proponent's sister who grew up in the area, loved the area, contributed to cancer research • the name change would inspire local young people to know more about the proponent's sister The Executive Director of the Western Upper Peninsula Planning and Development Region (WUPPDR, a regional planning agency that is comprised of 14 local governments including Keweenaw County) wrote: Although geographic names are not something we generally take a position on, I see value to this requested change. Generic names such as Lost Lake do little to showcase our region's rich natural and cultural environment. [The proponent] has made a convincing case for why this renaming would be warranted and appropriate, and it would improve the diversity and distinctness of place and feature names. I think it is unlikely anyone else would seek to make this change; thus, if this request is not granted, the generic name will remain. GNIS contains five features that have "trillium" in their name; none are in Michigan. Over 40 species of trilliums occur in Michigan, but it is unclear how many species occur in Keweenaw County or how rarely they can be found. GNIS contains 369 features with the official name Lost Lake. 47 are in Michigan; the closest is 100 miles to the southwest in Ontonagon County and is associated with a stream named Lost Creek. * obtained by proponent MONTANA New name Moon Creek - see WYOMING NEVADA

proposals.title: New name Fools Fount
proposals.proposal_type: make official name in local use
proposals.feature_description: Located 0.47 mi. S of Tower Mountain, 1.7 mi. WSW of Cherry Spring
proposals.name_history: The name reflects the repeated failed attempts by opportunists to develop the perennial spring, as its challenging location and minimal water flow made such efforts a "fool's errand"
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: This proposal seeks to make official the name Fools Fount, which the proponent reports is used by local ranchers and sheepherders. The feature is a perennial spring, located in the Adobe Mountain Range of Elko County, on the southern face of Tower Mountain. The area is managed by the Bureau of Land Management and shared among local ranchers and shepherds, as well as wildlife such as elk and mule deer that migrate through the range. The proponent states that naming the spring would ensure its "recognition and protection" as an important ecological and historical resource. He states that the name Fools Fount reflects the numerous failed attempts by opportunists to develop the spring, adding, "The rocky slopes of Tower Mountain, the heavy snowload, the high elevation, and the minimal water flow all combined to repel many attempts to develop this water, leading the endeavor to be 'a fool's errand.'" Furthermore, "'Fools Fount' thus serves as a testament to the shared folly of those many who came before. Water resources are valued and respected in Nevada, and thus the naming of this spring would allow for both recognition and protection." GNIS lists no geographic features in Nevada with "Fools" in the name.

proposals.case_summary: The new commemorative name Guinn Peak is proposed for an officially unnamed 6,178- foot summit in the Steamboat Hills in Washoe County. The summit is the highest point of Federal Agency Bureau of Land Management Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X the Steamboat Hills and the location of a National Geodetic Survey mark called "Maguire." (National Geodetic Survey marks are not official geographic feature names.) The Nevada Department of Transportation proposed the name to the Nevada Board on Geographic Names (NBGN) in June, 2024. The NBGN voted to recommend federal approval of the name in November 2024. The name would commemorate Kenneth Carroll Guinn (1936-2010), the 27th Governor of Nevada. Governor Guinn served from 1999-2007. The proposal reported "[t]he Nevada Department of Transportation believes the naming of the summit would be a fitting tribute to one of Nevada's most effective and popular governors." The Nevada Department of Transportation wrote a nine-page biography of Governor Guinn highlighting his popularity and achievements: We have outlined a number of Governor Guinn's accomplishments that in our estimation more than adequately justify the naming of a prominent geographic feature in his honor. An educator himself, Governor Guinn is well known for his lasting impact on Nevada's education system. However, he also left an important legacy in other areas including transportation, health care, governmental reform, and the environment. In a letter to the NBGN, U.S. Representative Mark Amodei wrote: It is my privilege to recommend the naming of a geographic feature in Nevada in honor of a public servant who gave so much to the State and its residents. I remember working with Governor Guinn on many of the key issues facing Nevadans: from prescription medication costs to transportation improvements. Governor Guinn developed a reputation as an executive who moved mountains to get important reforms passed and worked with members of all political parties. He always put the best interest of Nevadans ahead of politics. I recently met with the Nevada State Transportation Board, which Governor Guinn once chaired, to encourage support for designating "Kenny C. Guinn Summit," for the high point on the new 580 between Reno and Washoe Valley. Of course, I quickly found support for this idea within the Nevada Department of Transportation (NDOT), as Governor Guinn's bipartisan legacy is well-known. Thanks to Governor Guinn, thousands of Nevadans achieve a higher education through the Kenny C. Guinn Millenium Scholarship. Governor Guinn also made the tough decisions to keep Nevada fiscally solvent and cut taxes, returning the money to the people when the economy prospered. Additionally, his work lives on through the Guinn Center - a nonprofit dedicated to bipartisan problem solving. I encourage you to memorialize a man once named one of the nation's best governors by Time, but more importantly, a friend who cared deeply for Nevadans. In a letter to the NBGN, the President of the University of Nevada, Reno wrote: Governor Guinn was a mentor and a dear friend of mine who embodied the best qualities of our state and positively impacted thousands of Nevadans. Governor Guinn's lifelong career of public service has been felt for generations throughout our great state, notably within the education system and throughout our transportation infrastructure. Kenny saw the importance of these areas and knew that, for Nevada to reach it's potential, substantial investments needed to be made. He was always one to have honest and open conversations about these decisions and included stakeholders from across the state. I have often said that Governor Guinn belongs "on the Mt. Rushmore of Nevada." This is the next best thing! I fully support this application. * contacted by SNA ** received by SNA NEW YORK New names Blencoe Round Top, Bliss Creek, Bliss Round Top, Clarke Falls, Gaylor Hill, Hade Hill, Hogs Back, Natty Bumpos Cave, Mount Vision, Niskayuna Rock, Prospect Rock, Rathbun Creek, Star Field, The Triangle
