proposals.title: Change Bad Indian Swamp to Queen Catharine Marsh
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive
proposals.proponent: Joann Lindstrom, Director of Planning; Schuyler County, NY
proposals.feature_description: S of Seneca Lake.
proposals.name_history: The name honors Queen Catharine Montour, a prominent Iroquois leader whose life spanned a period of significant upheaval for the Iroquois Confederacy, including the Revolutionary War and the Sullivan Expedition.
proposals.land_ownership: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Bad Indian Swamp: USGS topographic maps 1950, 1961; New York State Museum. Bulletin - New York State Museum. 1976, vol. 482; From Squaw Tit to Whorehouse Meadow, Monmonier, 2006; Roadside Geology of New York, VanDiver, 1985.) o Queen Catherine Marsh: Take a Hike!: Family Walks in the Finger Lakes and Genesee Valley Region, Freeman, 1999
proposals.case_summary: This proposal seeks to rename Bad Indian Swamp, an approximately 1,000-acre swamp located in the Village of Montour Falls and the Town of Dix, south of Watkins Glen, in Schuyler County. The proposed replacement name is Queen Catharine Marsh. The swamp has been labeled on U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps since 1950. The change aims to replace a name with derogatory connotations with one that honors Queen Catharine Montour, a prominent Iroquois leader whose legacy is recognized throughout the region. The area in question is part of the Catharine Creek Wildlife Management Area (CCWMA), a 900+-acre wetland located at the head of Seneca Lake in Watkins Glen, within the Finger Lakes region. The CCWMA was acquired by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) in the mid-1970s. Prior to its acquisition, the wetland had been referred to locally as "Bad Indian Swamp" for over 50 years. Research conducted by the county planning department could not determine the origin of this name. Queen Catharine Montour led Queanettquaga, a Seneca village of Sheaquaga (informally called Catharine's Town), a prominent Seneca village near present-day Montour Falls. In 1779, the village was destroyed during General Sullivan's campaign, a Revolutionary War effort aimed at weakening the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, which had allied with the British. The campaign systematically targeted Indigenous communities by destroying their villages, crops, and resources, forcing the displacement of their populations. The Watkins Glen Area Chamber of Commerce indicates that the wetland marsh feature is known as Queen Catharine Marsh at the State level. Further, the name "Queen Catherine Marsh" appeared in Rich Freeman's Take a Hike!: Family Walks in the Finger Lakes and Genesee Valley Region (1999). Mark Monmonier's analysis in From Squaw Tit to Whorehouse Meadow provides historical context for efforts to address racially insensitive geographic names in New York. He writes, "A classic example is New York's 1988 effort to ferret out racially derogatory names on state maps." This effort, prompted by outrage over the name "Negro Marsh (formerly N____r Marsh)," led the governor to mandate that no state map could "contain any derogatory racial, ethnic or religious name or other epithet" and directed state agencies to "identify and eliminate problem names from all State maps." Monmonier notes that the NYSDEC "took a broad view of 'problem names' and compiled a list of forty-five candidates for renaming," including Bad Indian Swamp. There is no indication that the name was formally changed by the State. Although the term "Bad Indian" does not appear on the Secretary of the Interior's Order 3405 List of Derogatory Geographic Names, the proposal reflects ongoing efforts to replace geographic names with pejorative or offensive connotations. Local community members have expressed interest in submitting a name that better reflects the area's Native American heritage and cultural significance. The proponent adds, "Queen Catharine Marsh is a proposed name that seeks to fulfill this objective while fostering respect for the region's Indigenous history." *** note that the following proposal was withdrawn by the proponent

proposals.title: Change Valentine Pond to Valentine Lake
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize local use
proposals.feature_description: along an unnamed stream SE of Grasshopper Hill
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: o Valentine Lake: reported local use o Published names: o Valentine Lake: local postcard, reportedly 1950; Valentine Lake Cottages, reportedly until 1960s; property maps and deeds, 1960s and 1970s; online real estate listings o Valentine Pond: USGS 1895, 1897, 1958, 1968, 1986, 1989; Map of the County of Warren, 1829; Warren County Atlas, 1876; current Warren County maps; reported local use; online real estate listings
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of the 98-acre Valentine Pond in the Town of Horicon in Warren County to Valentine Lake. USGS maps have used the name Valentine Pond since 1895, as did privately published atlases in at least 1829 and 1876, along with a current Warren County map and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation website. The origin of the name has not been determined; however, online genealogy records list a number of individuals named Valentine in Warren County, including at least one in Horicon and many in the neighboring Town of Chester. The proponent, a resident of Massachusetts, owns property on Valentine Pond; he reports: Valentine Pond . . . has had a dual identity for many decades. The formal name recognized by the USGS [sic] Board on Geographic Names is 'Valentine Pond,' and historical map sources label the feature this way. However, in more recent decades, the majority of homeowners along the lake have come to refer to it as "Valentine Lake," and would like to see the official name of the water body changed. These residents recognize that the name of the road along the eastern shoreline is 'Valentine Pond Road,' and that changing the name of this seven-mile-long roadway and the addresses of the homes along it is impractical. Therefore, they seek only to have the water body itself renamed Valentine Lake. Historically, the name Valentine Pond has been used on maps of the area since at least 1858. However, for the past 75 years, most residents along the lake have referred to it as Valentine Lake. After extensive outreach to residents with property around the lake, and successfully getting replies from 72% of them, a very clear majority of 90% (19 out of 21 responses) preferred the name Valentine Lake. Two families preferred the name Valentine Pond. The proponent provided the following information showing use of the name Valentine Lake: • an undated postcard (reportedly 1950) from the former Valentine Lodge • a 1961 property map • an undated advertisement (reportedly 1967) for Valentine Lake Cottages, a rental operation on the waterbody until the 1960s • a 1973 property deed • a current VRBO listing • T-shirt designs currently being sold online by a local business Online real estate and rental listings use both Valentine Lake and Valentine Pond. When asked to address the Commercial Names Policy (noting that t-shirts are being sold with the "Valentine Lake" name), the proponent responded that these are created by a neighbor's son and there is no commercial intent; that is, the lake is only accessible by property owners around the lake and the design simply reflects "what people call it." On November 14, 2024, the proponent posted a poll on a local Facebook page titled Valentine Pond (Lake) asking members if they were in favor of the name change or not. 82% replied that they were in favor; the sample size is unknown but as of December 18, 2024 the group had 96 members. The proponent acknowledges that although the BGN and USGS do not formally define a difference between a lake and a pond, he notes that it fits the following unofficial definitions of a lake: • greater than half an acre and more than 20 feet deep • a depth that prevents sunlight from reaching parts of the bottom • a defined outlet • a size that allows significant wave action One property owner shared the following comment in an email stating that some local families on the waterbody oppose the change: "This seems such a trivial matter, as I was quite surprised and impressed after reading about this government body, and I feel this would be a waste of time and resources considering your mission to maintain uniform geographic name usage."

proposals.title: Change Conrad Lake to Lake Lindsey
proposals.submitter: Michael Doub; Elkin, NC
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered offensive by proponent
proposals.feature_description: 2 mi. NW of Lewisville, 2.5 mi. SW of Vienna
proposals.name_history: named for a name derived from Lincoln
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Conrad Lake: sources derived from GNIS data
proposals.case_summary: State Names Authority New York Geographic Names Committee Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X This proposal is to change the name of Conrad Lake, a 3-acre reservoir west of Winston- Salem in the Town of Lewisville, Forsyth County, to Lake Lindsey. The proponent, who owns the land wrote: Upon acquiring our new piece of property, we would like the name of the lake changed from Conrad Lake to Lake Lindsey. In the following paragraph, I will detail why this is important. Lindsey is derived from the Old English toponym Lindesege. Lindum Colonia was the Roman name of the settlement which is now the city of Lincoln. Lindum has been reconstructed to Lindon which means pool or lake. Lindsey is the Brittonic form of Lincoln. President Lincoln initiated the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 which freed all enslaved people in states that rebelled against the Union. It has come to our attention that the Hilltop House was a plantation owned by the Conrad family, who owned slaves dating back to River John Conrad. The cook's house, which sits on the northern most end of our property, was where the enslaved cooks stayed. The adjacent property to us also has three former slave homes on it for laborers which are still standing in decent shape today. In keeping up with modern times and culture, we would like to see the name Conrad Lake removed as it identifies itself with antiquated antics that were associated with demoralizing and dehumanizing people. The proponent did not provide any information about River John Conrad or evidence that the reservoir is named for him. After BGN staff informed the proponent that a name that contains "Lindsey" could be construed to be commemorative and asked the proponent to confirm that "Lindsey" does not refer to any individual, living or deceased, the proponent followed up with the following: When looking up a name, we thought of Lincoln as a possibility because it means pool or lake and is tied to the reformation as I had previously stated. But then reading further into the historical side of the name on Wikipedia we saw Lindsey and how it meant, "isle of Lincoln", while not actually an isle it did seem to sound better when saying it. We have groomed and combed historical documents online and have come with another backup name or two. We have thought about Lake Gadsden as there was a successful Revolutionary War battle fought just a few miles from there at Shallowford in favor of the US, but we are willing to ask the Lewisville Historical Society their opinion on it as well. There are no other lakes named that around there as well. So with that said Lindsey would be our first choice and possibly Gadsden for a second. . . . As the new property owners we would like to see the name changed. We are in the process of tearing down the cook's quarters and getting rid of this blemish on the land and are willing to work through the process of making sure this gets done. The name was added to GNIS in 2000 from a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) list of dams and reservoirs and USGS maps did not show any prior name for this reservoir. The USACE National Inventory of Dams record for this dam reports that the dam is named Conrad Lake Dam, was built in 1945, and is owned by Hill Top Farms, LLC. This information may not be current.

proposals.title: New name Milkmere Pond
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: 0.45 NE of the E shore of Lake Catawba, 0.5 mi. N of East Monbo
proposals.name_history: The name reflects the water's pale, serene quality and the nurturing presence of white oaks. "Mere" is an old term for a pond or lake
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Milkmere Pond is proposed for a natural spring-fed one-acre pond located in an area surrounded by white oak trees in Iredell County. According to the proponent, the name "Milkmere" is intended to "evoke the milky, pale quality of the water, as well as the serene, nurturing environment created by the white oaks." The term "mere" is "an old term for a pond or lake," thus tying the name to historical linguistic roots and reflecting the feature's "tranquil nature." The proponent, whose surname is Milch, previously submitted a proposal for "Milch Pond," but it was not accepted because it could be construed to honor himself. According to Iredell County GIS records, the lake is located on four parcels of land, owned by three different people.

proposals.title: New name Respite Branch
proposals.proposal_type: new name for unnamed feature
proposals.feature_description: Heads 0.4 mi. SE of Hoover Mountain, flows generally SE into North Prong Lewis Fork
proposals.name_history: The name refers to the stream's location, which served as a respite for travelers with horses and wagons on their journey from Wilkesboro to Boone.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Respite Branch is proposed for a 2.26-mile-long tributary of North Prong Lewis Fork in Wilkes County. The proponent, a resident of Wilkesboro, reports that the name reflects the stream's historical role as a place of rest and refreshment for weary travelers and their animals. It served as a key resting point for travelers with horses and wagons journeying from Wilkesboro to Boone in the late 1800s. Mrs. Ginney Church, who lived at the site in a lean- to shed made of sawmill slabs, recounted that the branch "was the only stream between Wilkesboro and Deep Gap . . . that the horses and wagons did not have to ford various bodies of water." She described the spring at the headwaters as a crucial source of fresh water for both people and animals. Travelers appreciated this natural resting place, where they could recover before facing the challenging task of crossing the Blue Ridge into Boone. Mrs. Church also recalled the site as "a happy place where children played, people could rest, interact, share experiences, trading items, and looked to a better time of life that the Boone Trail would lead to." proposals.title: Change Tiltons Run to Tildens Run
proposals.proposal_type: change name to recognize family name
proposals.feature_description: Heads in Meigs Township, flows SE into Brookfield Township to enter Dyes Fork.
proposals.name_history: Named for the Tilden family, the last property owners before the Ohio Power Company purchased all the land in the Renrock area.
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: None found o Jewett Run (USGS 1909, 1911, o Jewell Run (Ohio Department of Transportation) o Tiltons Run (USGS 1961, 1980, 1994, 2010)
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Tiltons Run to Tildens Run. The stream is 3.5 miles long and heads in Meigs Township in Noble County, then flows southeast into Brookfield Township in Muskingum County where it enters Dyes Fork. The stream flows through several Ohio Power Company ponds. The name Tiltons Run was officially adopted by the BGN in 1963, replacing the former name Jewett Run. This decision was based on input gathered from local residents by a USGS field engineer, as well as a highway sign that referenced the stream as Tiltons Run. Tiltons Run was labeled on USGS topographic maps between 1961 and 2010. The proponent, a resident of Cody, Wyoming, reports that the current name is a misspelling and seeks to restore the name that would reflect the Tilden family's historical connection to the area. In the early 1830s, Jason Tilden (1805-1883) sold his land in northwest Brookfield Township and purchased property along the stream, which was then known as Jewett Run. The Tilden family remained the last private landowners in the area before the Ohio Power Company acquired the land near Renrock, prompting the relocation of all residents. Research conducted by the proponent, along with a review of land ownership maps and cemetery records, supports the claim that the Tilden family were prominent early settlers in Renrock. Records indicate that no individuals or families named Tilton lived in the area. The Noble County Historical Society has endorsed the proposal, affirming that the original settlers of Renrock were the Tilden family. Their research aligns with the proponent's findings, emphasizing the historical inaccuracy of the current name. They support the Tilden family's request to restore the stream's name to Tildens Run to honor the area's history accurately. GNIS lists a small unincorporated community named Tilton Crossroads, in Licking County and approximately 50 miles northwest of the stream in question. * Provided by proponent

proposals.case_summary: This proposal, submitted by the president of the Trafford Historical Society, seeks to make official the locally used name Blends Run for a 0.75-mile-long tributary of Brush Creek. The stream is located primarily in North Huntingdon Township (Westmoreland County), with a small section in North Versailles Township (Allegheny County). The name honors John Blend, Sr. (1844-1930) and Catherine Blend, who built their home near the stream around 1875. According to the proponent, Mr. Blend worked as a night watchman for the Pennsylvania Railroad and the family played a significant role in the early development of North Huntingdon and Trafford. The proposal states that the stream, "known colloquially as Blend Run, flows in front of the land where the Blends and their descendants have owned and worked on for generations." The proponent provided documents to support the proposal, including historical research, photographs, maps, and community publications detailing the family's connection to the area. Use of the name was confirmed by long-time residents and descendants of the Blend family, including a 93-year- old who currently resides in the Blend homestead. GNIS does not list any no streams in Pennsylvania with "Blend" in the name.

proposals.title: New name Johanna Boston Creek
proposals.proposal_type: new commemorative name for unnamed feature
proposals.proponent: East Stroudsburg Borough Council; East Stroudsburg PA
proposals.feature_description: heads 0.9 mi. SSW of Zacharias Pond, flows SSE then SW into Brodhead Creek
proposals.name_history: named for Johanna Boston (1722-1815), an enslaved woman who Judge Daniel Brodhead sheltered in his nearby home after her escape
proposals.other_names: o Unpublished names: None found o Published names: o Little Sambo Creek: USGS topo map 2019; some local documents since 2011
proposals.case_summary: The new name Johanna Boston Creek is proposed for an officially unnamed stream in the Borough of East Stroudsburg in Monroe County. The 0.5-mile-long stream flows into Brodhead Creek. Between 2011 and 2022, GNIS recorded the official name of this stream as Little Sambo Creek. This name was added based on a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) report, although it was later determined to be incorrect. The name was recorded in connection to other proposals submitted to the BGN to address the names of Sambo Creek (shown on USGS maps since at least 1944) and Sambo Creek Lower Reservoir (added to GNIS in 1990 from a USACE list of dams and reservoirs). The location of Little Sambo Creek was corrected in GNIS in 2022 based on information from the Brodhead Watershed Association. As a result, the stream in question is officially unnamed, although the USGS National Hydrography Dataset and 3D Hydrography Program continue to use the incorrect name Little Sambo Creek. In an effort to eliminate the confusion, the East Stroudsburg Borough Council is proposing the name Johanna Boston Creek. They are also considering possible replacement names for Little Sambo Creek. The proposal for Johanna Boston Creek states: East Stroudsburg Borough Council voted in August 2024 to change the unofficial name from a derogatory slur against African Americans to a name that honors a person of African descent who has ties to Monroe County. Johanna Boston is an excellent example of a person lost to history. According to research by historian Susan Klepp, Johanna was an enslaved woman who lived in the household of Solomon Jennings, one of the notorious 'Walking Purchase' runners. She ran away in the dead of winter and, suffering from hypothermia, was rescued by a Native American named Paemasing. He took her to the home of Judge Daniel Brodhead where her mother lived as an enslaved person. Brodhead and Moravian supporters purchased Johanna's freedom and reunited her with her husband, Joseph. . . . The creek . . . enters Brodhead Creek, named for Judge Daniel Brodhead, at Dansbury Park, also named for Brodhead. The home where he gave shelter to Johanna Boston was located nearby. The proposal also included a 2012 paper presented to the Monroe County Historical Society titled "Johanna, the Slave Who Risked Her Life for Freedom" (currently posted on the Smithfield Township website); it provided the following biography: Johanna, or Hannah, was born a slave in the Hudson River Valley settlement of Esopus on July 11, 1722. She was the daughter and namesake of the elderly Johanna who was owned by Daniel Brodhead in 1749. Her brother John was also the property of Brodhead. Who her father was is unknown. Her first owner was Anthony Slecht who moved her to Kingston, New York. When she was 14, she was sold for L[£?]45 to Isaac Ysslestein, a Moravian, who moved first to Marbletown, Ulster County and then to Bethlehem [Pennsylvania]. In 1743, at age 21, she married Boston, also a slave, who later was known as Joseph Boston. The marriages of slaves had no legal standing and the couple did not live together until many years later. That same year she gave birth to a son, whom she and her husband named Daniel, perhaps after her mother's and brother's owner, Judge Daniel Brodhead. This may have been a strategic move to gain Brodhead's protection and influence --- and as it turned out, Brodhead did provide aid at a crucial moment. Their son Daniel was raised by the Moravians and 'did faithful service in the Nursery' before he died at age ten. At some point she had a daughter who was, by 1749, if not before, owned by Edward Robinson at Walpack. Her name is not given in the few surviving records. Parenthood was no more respected than other family ties. Ysslestein probably sold her to Solomon Jennings shortly before 1749. Strangely, Jennings kept her, not with his wife and family at his Bethlehem farm, but at his Pocono property. The paper details Johanna Boston's escape from Jennings; her rescue by Paemasing, a Mahican trapper who brought her to Judge Daniel Brodhead; and how Judge Brodhead protected her from recapture by Jennings. SOUTH CAROLINA

proposals.case_summary: The new name Fort Sumter Beach is proposed for a beach located within Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park (FOSU), between James Island and Fort Sumter, and southeast of Charleston in Charleston County. The beach formed as sand and other materials naturally collected over time due to a man-made island and a nearby water current. The proponent, who is the Chief Ranger at FOSU, reports that the accretion of sand "has connected Fort Sumter island to James Island from mid tide to low tide and it is believed that it continues to grow." The proposed name refers to its location within FOSU and its proximity to Fort Sumter, named after Revolutionary War Brigadier General Thomas Sumter. The proponent notes that the beach is known locally as "No name beach," adding that "It has grown to be one of the most popular boating beaches in the Charleston Harbor, and park management would like to bring attention to the users that they are within the national park when in the area. A change in name and a park regulations sign with the beach name on it will help accomplish this." proposals.case_summary: The new name Tabaccy Branch is proposed for a 0.5-mile-long unnamed tributary of an unnamed tributary of the Nolichucky River in Greene County. The proponent states she purchased a former tobacco and cattle farm, now named Tabaccy Crick Farm, where the unnamed stream runs entirely on the property. The farm ceased operations in the 1940s after the death of its previous owner. While the aging barns, built with traditional materials for hanging tobacco, still stand, the farm now houses goats, chickens, ducks, guinea hens, and barn cats. The proponent explains that she doesn't sell products, promote the farm, or plan to raise cattle or grow tobacco, producing only bamboo, eggs, and fruit for personal use. The proponent initially confirmed she would like "Crick" instead of "Creek" and explained its importance as a reflection of local dialect and cultural identity, and to preserve the area's traditional speech patterns. The proponent later amended the name to Tabaccy Branch based on feedback from the Tennessee Committee on Geographic Names which did not favor "Crick" and noted that simiilarly-sized tributaries in the region were predominately called "Branch" and not "Creek". The GNIS database contains no official geographic features in the U.S with the word "Tabaccy" or the generic term "Crick" in their official names. Five streams, one in South Carolina and four in West Virginia, include "Crick" as a variant name. TEXAS

proposals.case_summary: The name Moon Creek is proposed to be made official for a 3-mile-long stream that originates at Moon Lake in the Custer-Gallatin National Forest/Absaroka-Beartooth Wilderness in Carbon County, Montana, then flows southeast into Rock Creek in Park County, Wyoming. The proponent, a resident of Cody, Wyoming, reports that the stream is crossed by a timber bridge on the popular Glacier Lake Trail, a heavily used route for recreation in the area. The stream has been identified by hikers as Moon Creek on various mapping platforms, including Gaia GPS and OpenStreetMap, since 2014. The proponent believes the name should be made official, citing its practicality for navigation and emergency response. He adds that the name will help reduce confusion with nearby Rock Creek and improve communication for hikers and first responders, particularly during emergencies, stating: Many hikers take advantage of this bridge to take photos or just look at the considerable amount of water flowing in the stream. A common mistake is to believe this stream is Rock Creek, which is farther south . . . . I became aware that the proposed name does appear on Gaia GPS, a popular hiking app. Later I learned that Gaia GPS takes feature names from OpenStreetMap.org so possibly that is how they got the name. The proponent was asked to address the Wilderness Names Policy. He provided letters from Beartooth Trails and Red Lodge Fire Rescue, both highlighting the importance of naming the stream to enhance public safety and orientation in the area. Both organizations note the stream's location near the wilderness boundary and the heavy use of the trail and bridge as justification for an exception to the policy. * Obtained by proponent

proposals.proposal_type: make official a name in local use

proposals.name_history: This name has been in local use for William Henry Ruffner (1824-1908), a Virginia geologist who surveyed the region in 1882
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: o Ruffner Mountain: Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve website; many books and websites about local history and hiking
proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the local name Ruffner Mountain for a 4-mile-long section of Red Mountain in Jefferson County. The ridge is along the eastern edge of the City of Birmingham and parts of the western edge of the City of Irondale and between Sadler Gap to the northeast and Red Gap to the southwest. Part of the ridge is protected by the Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve, which is a collection of parcels owned by Ruffner Mountain Nature Coalition Inc., Alabama Trust for Public Land, Alabama Forever Wild, and private industrial holdings. The name would not affect the current name or extent of Red Mountain for Federal use. The proponent stated that: This mountain's name has been in use for many decades, beginning in the 19th century when it was a mining site, and there is currently a preservation organization and park with a trail system named for it, but for some reason it does not seem to appear in the USGS names database. According to the "Ruffner Mountain" article on bhamwiki.com ("an ever-growing encyclopedic resource for anyone curious about Birmingham, Alabama and the region around it"): It was named for Virginia geologist William Henry Ruffner [1824-1908] who surveyed the mineral resources of the ridge as part of his work for the Georgia Southern Railroad in 1882. . . . The mountain was intensively mined and quarried by the Sloss-Sheffield Steel & Iron Company until the early 1950s. . . . Developmental pressures spurred area residents to organize and secure the preservation of the ridge as the Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve in 1977. The preserve now encompasses 1,040 acres of forest, which it manages for recreation, environmental education and wildlife conservation. The name Ruffner Mountain is widely used in published sources about Birmingham. According to the "Ruffner Mountain" webpage from the Encyclopedia of Alabama and Mining History of Ruffner Mountain on the Ruffner Mountain Preserve webpage, the area was mined for iron ore starting in the 1880s. Some mines along the ridge were known as the Ruffner Mines; the USGS 1959 1:24,000-scale Irondale quadrangle labeled Ruffner Mines and the feature was recorded in GNIS as a Mine with Feature ID 126012 until 2021 when administrative features were removed from GNIS. The "William Henry Ruffner (1824-1908)" article from the Encyclopedia Virginia reports that he • "was the designer and first superintendent of Virginia's public school system and later served as principal of the State Female Normal School (later Longwood University)" • "spent the years before the American Civil War (1861-1865) as a Presbyterian minister and farmer in Rockingham County" • "owned slaves, and he advocated the gradual emancipation and colonization of the state's African Americans. He raised funds for the American Colonization Society." • "gave Virginia's public school system a lasting foundation and as he defended the system from vigorous opposition and the shortfalls generated by the state's crippling debt" • "spent his later years teaching geology, writing about the history of Washington and Lee University, and advocating the school system he helped create" • "[between the time he was superintendent of Virginia's public school system and principal of the State Female Normal School] accepted a faculty position at Roanoke College, where he taught geology, mineralogy, and the science of teaching. Later in 1882, he and John L. Campbell completed a survey for the Georgia Pacific Railway Company and published A Physical Survey Extending from Atlanta, Ga., … to the Mississippi River … (1883), which played a key role in developing industry in northern Alabama" • "surveyed land in Alabama for the Sloss Iron and Steel Company in 1888" GNIS has a record for Ruffner, an unincorporated populated place, located east of Red Mountain near the southern end of the proposed Ruffner Mountain; it was first shown on the USGS 1959 1:24,000-scale Irondale quadrangle. See below for details about each proposed name. The proposal notes that the Kumeyaay Diegueño Land Conservancy (KDLC) was formed in 2005 to act in a unified, organized, and traditional relevant manner to identify, protect, and preserve sacred sites and ecosystems throughout the traditional Kumeyaay Homelands. The Kumeyaay Homelands stretch over 75 miles north and south of the Southern California International Border. . . . The KDLC Board of Directors is composed of delegates, appointed by resolution through their Tribal Councils, from the following ten (10) federally-recognized tribal governments: Campo Band of the Kumeyaay Nation, Ewiiaapaayp Band of Kumeyaay Indians, Jamul Indian Village, Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation, La Posta Band of Mission Indians, Manzanita Band of the Kumeyaay Nation, Mesa Grande Band of Mission Indians, Iipay Nation of Santa Ysabel (INSY), San Pasqual Band of the Kumeyaay Nation, and the Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians. In July 2021, Elizabeth Schalo, a professional engineer and former Kumeyaay Community College (KCC) student, informed KDLC of four geographic features within Kumeyaay Homelands using names based on the Confederate General Stonewall Jackson and three geographic features with the derogatory term sq___. In response, KDLC formed a Working Group with technical support from Ms. Schalo to identify ethnographic names and determine new names for these places with intention of submitting a name change request through the U.S. Board of Geographic Names (BGN). The KDLC []Working Group meetings occurred in-person at the Kumeyaay Community College Classroom on the Sycuan Reservation with the option of virtual participation. Participants included KDLC delegates whom all are respected Tribal Chairmen and Chairwomen, Tribal Councilmembers, elders, language speakers, historians/researchers, educators, community members, and more. In April 2022, KDLC submitted a comment letter to the Department of Interior Secretary's Order 3404 Derogatory Geographic Names Task Force with proposed names for the three sq___-named features. In September 2022, as a part of Order 3404, the BGN voted on the three names proposed by KDLC final replacement names. Today, KDLC submits this letter to you for proposed names for the four geographic features named for the Confederate General Stonewall Jackson. KDLC interviewed Elders, collaborated with fluent language speakers, reviewed multiple Kumeyaay dictionaries written and published by elders with support of linguists, and researched other historical documents and archives. . . . [The proposed names] would add to Kumeyaay place names within Ancestral Kumeyaay Homelands such as Aapaal'omar (Palomar), Powaii (Poway), Inaja, 'Ekwii 'Aamuc (Cuyamaca), Hamaachaa (Jamacha), Jamul, Otaay, Tijuana, etc. [The] proposed name change[s] within the boundaries of what is now Cuyamaca Rancho State Park would add to Kumeyaay place names throughout our Ancestral Homelands and support representation by uplifting traditional Kumeyaay language. We all know the words we use on a daily basis have power behind them, so let's put our voices together and speak the traditional Kumeyaay language on a daily basis by using the proposed names. . . . In October and November 2021, a San Diego County resident submitted proposals to change the names based on an objection to the names referencing Confederate General Stonewall Jackson: • Stonewall Peak to Cush-Pii ("sharp peak," a name the proponent discussed with the KDLC) • Little Stonewall Peak to Ipuk Spiruk ("broken neck," a name the proponent reported learning from a Kumeyaay tribal member) • Stonewall Creek to Cush-Pii Creek • Little Stonewall Creek to Ipuk Spiruk Creek The names proposed were Iipai Aa (Kumeyaay) names based on research by Elizabeth Schalo (also reference by KDLC; see above). The proponent stated that Once my Black family learned of the name of the peak and its association with Stonewall Jackson, we no longer feel welcome at this State Park or desire to hike the trail. Mountains maintain names like this as a method of intimidating Blacks in an effort to continue to oppress them post-slavery. Mountains whose names are maintained by the federal government should consider ALL people and allow for ALL people to feel welcome visiting and hiking them. This proposed name change is long overdue. After submitting the proposal, the proponent contacted several local groups to get their input about the proposed changes: the KDLC; the California State Parks Tribal Affairs Program; California Department of Parks and Recreation; California State Assembly members; and the San Diego County Supervisors. Beginning in 2022, the California Department of Park and Recreation worked with a researcher and the KDLC to determine the most accurate Iipai Aa (Kumeyaay) names for the features. BGN staff did not receive or learn of any support submitted by these groups. Historians report that the San Diego County gold rush started when a formerly enslaved person from Kentucky discovered placer gold in 1869 a few miles north of Stonewall Peak. Many Confederate sympathizers moved to the San Diego County area during the gold rush. Historians differ on the details of the origins of the Stonewall Mine, crediting the discovery of a gold vein there to either a Tennessee Confederate sympathizer named William Skidmore or to a miner from England named Charles Hensley. The two men staked a claim, naming it the Stonewall Jackson Mine. "Jackson" was likely dropped from the name due to anti-Confederate views of immigrating miners or because the mine was soon owned by pro-Union Republicans Almon Frary Sr., from Illinois, and Joseph Farley, from Ohio. The mine ceased operations in 1895. proposals.case_summary: The new name Engagement Point is proposed for an officially unnamed 5,526-foot summit in Shasta County. The summit is in the Castle Crags Wilderness, Shasta National Forest. The proponent stated: [This is a] Ridge like rocky summit with about 100 ft of prominence and 50 ft higher than Mount Hubris [not an official name for Federal use] in the forest service land north of Castle Crags State Park. Engagement Point holds deep personal significance for me, as it is the place where I proposed to my fiancé. On January 18, 2025, we climbed this peak together. . . . The moment was both intimate and profound, forever connecting us to this remarkable place. I believe naming the peak "Engagement Point" would honor not only the memory of our engagement but also the spirit of love, adventure, and connection that the outdoors inspires. This name would celebrate the peak as a place of unity and significance, inviting others to reflect on their own milestones and meaningful experiences while exploring the beauty of this region. The views from the summit, overlooking iconic landmarks like Castle Crags and Mount Shasta, make this peak a special part of the landscape. By formally naming it Engagement Point, the peak could symbolize not only our personal story but also the enduring power of nature to bring people together and create cherished memories. It would be an honor to see this beautiful location recognized for its personal and symbolic importance. When asked to provide an overriding need to apply a new name in a Federal wilderness, the proponent replied: The point. . . is an increasingly important landmark in a region where climbing and outdoor recreation continue to grow in popularity. As more climbers, hikers, and backcountry explorers venture into this dramatic landscape, the need for clearly named peaks and routes becomes essential. Named landmarks provide vital reference points for navigation, route descriptions, and safety, ensuring that adventurers can communicate effectively and document their experiences with clarity. Despite its striking prominence, this particular point remains unnamed, even as the surrounding area gains recognition for its world-class climbing and rugged beauty. Castle Crags' towering granite spires and sheer faces demand careful route planning, and naming significant features like this one helps establish a shared understanding among those who explore the park. Beyond its functional importance, this point also holds deep personal significance for me, as it was the site of my engagement. . . . However, the true importance of naming this location lies in its role as a destination for countless other climbers and outdoor enthusiasts who seek adventure and inspiration in Castle Crags. Giving it a name cements its place in the evolving history of this remarkable landscape and ensures its recognition for generations to come. GNIS contains only one feature that includes "engagement" in its name: Engagement Hill near Nags Head in North Carolina, a name first shown on USGS maps in 1953.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Sutter Buttes (BGN 1949) in Sutter County to Middle Mountain. The range is mostly on private farming and ranching lands, with parts of the northeastern side in Sutter Buttes State Park (closed to the public) and land owned by the Sutter Buttes Regional Land Trust. The proposal was submitted by the Spokesperson and Tribal Council Secretary for the non- federally recognized Nevada City Rancheria Nisenan Tribe, on behalf of the California Heritage: Indigenous Research Project that "takes direction from the Nevada City Rancheria (NCR) Tribal Council to identify, fund, and implement programs and projects to address and mitigate the ongoing social, environmental and racial injustices brought to the Tribe's Homelands in 1848 that continue today in the form of historical trauma, illness, poverty, substance use disorder, marginalization, and hopelessness." The Nevada City Rancheria Nisenan Tribe was federally recognized until 1964. The proponent noted the Cultural Sensitivity for Native American Names, stating "I am the Tribal Spokesperson of the Nevada City Rancheria (NCR) Nisenan Tribe and the NCR Tribal Council approves of the proposed names and details in this form." The proposal is a counterproposal to the name Sacred Buttes on Review List 455 which was proposed by a former director of the Sutter Buttes Regional Land Trust Board, who submitted the proposal as a private citizen and not on behalf of the Sutter Buttes Regional Land Trust or Sutter Buttes Regional Land Trust Board. The proponent wrote: Middle (estom) Mountain (yanim) is the direct translation of the original Nisenan name for this sacred place. This place is the center of all life for the Nisenan people and where we go when we die. Our spirit travels to the mountain and has its first spirit food before going off to the Milky Way. This place was central to our Ancestors and played a critical role in Nisenan Culture for millennia. Other than Middle Mountain, the Nevada City Rancheria Nisenan Tribe would also be in favor of the following proposed name changes, which would be Culturally supportive: -Spirit Mountain -Sacred Mountain -Sacred Buttes (previously proposed by another person/group) We would also be in favor of the name change back to Marysville Buttes, which the range was called prior to its current name. While this name is not Culturally supportive, it is far less offensive than the current name. We wouldn't be adverse to other proposed names, so long as they are not offensive. proposals.case_summary: The name Bryant Creek is proposed for a 1.8-mile stream within White River National Forest. The stream heads on the southwest slope of Lenawee Mountain and flows generally southwest into Snake River. The proposal states: The [stream] is named for Greg Ernest Bryant. Greg Bryant was a Geographic Information System (GIS) expert who was an early proponent for digitally mapping the hydrography of the United States, particularly in Colorado where he worked for the Denver Water Board. As a pioneer in contemporary mapping techniques, his work contributed to the Hydrography theme of The National Map. The modern hydrography of Colorado, which was used to create The National Hydrography Dataset, is a result of Greg's work. Greg was not only a technical expert in hydrography mapping, but also an inspirational leader for mapping, scientific, engineering, and water management organizations to develop Geographic Information Systems. Many people throughout Colorado and the United States followed the contributions made by Greg E. Bryant. A memorial service was held only one week after his passing in January 2011, yet there were over 300 people in attendance. In addition, tributes flooded in over the GIS Colorado listserve for at least four weeks afterward. This is an area of Colorado heavily used in recreation, and it is appropriate that the perennial streams be named for reference by users. . . . Greg Ernest Bryant was born and raised in Colorado. He attended Colorado State University in Fort Collins, where he earned a BS degree. Greg then worked for the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) during the 1980s via TGS, a Fort Collins-based federal contractor that produced digital maps for the US Geological Survey. Greg supervised the conversion of USGS 1:24,000-scale topographic maps to digital format for Indian Reservation lands throughout the United States. These digital maps were used as base maps in the Geographic Information System (GIS) for management of Reservation lands at the BIA. Later, Greg worked for Stoneman-Landers, producing GIS data to support Indian Water Rights claims. In 1992, Greg began working for the Denver Water Board, the main utility for providing drinking water to the growing Denver metropolitan area. During the following years, he earned his MS Degree from the University of Colorado - Denver. While working at Denver Water, Greg was pivotal in developing a GIS for managing their raw water collection system. Not long afterward, he became involved in the development and refinement of the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) by cooperation among various regional agencies. He was also one of the founding members of GIS Colorado, a professional organization for the exchange of ideas between those involved in what are now called the "Geospatial Sciences." It is fitting that a stream be named for Greg E. Bryant because of his impact on the mapping of streams in the United States. It is also particularly fitting for this specific perennial tributary to be named for Greg because it is one he referenced in his promotion of local agency involvement that later became the Stewardship Program of The National Hydrography Dataset. The proponent provided a photo showing Greg E. Bryant speaking about the stream at a national U.S. Geological Survey stewardship meeting in Denver, CO on April 15, 2009. The submission also included letters in support of the name from various friends, family members and colleagues of Greg E. Bryant. GNIS lists no features in Colorado with "Bryant" in the name.

proposals.land_ownership: private These two names, R.E. Wynn, DVM Pond and Shiner Pond, are proposed for two ponds within Pasco County. The two lakes lie approximately one-third of a mile from Wynn Lake (approved by the BGN in 2022), a 24-acre waterbody submitted by the same proponent, who also owns the surrounding property. The proponent states that the naming proposals are "to bring attention to the Wynn Family History and desire to keep and maintain a legacy for the years owning and maintaining the property since 1953." The proponent stated: I am of the 4[th] generation living on what is remaining of the Wynn Family Property (formerly Fairwinds Ranch). My Grandparents O.E. Wynn (9/2/18-8/5/89) and Evelyn R. Wynn (4/4/17-8/28/08) along with my Great Grand mother Mary Ann "Mollie" Tuten (7/16/1897-9/22/76) are the original purchasers of the land in the 1950's. . . . In addition my Father Dr. Richard E. Wynn (1/2/45-5/4/08). . . acquired additional land in the 1980's that abutted the original ranch. . . . I am compiling a history and property legacy for my daughter. . . . I am continuing to provide her the history of our family and the cherished land we have owned and maintained in our family since 1953. This parcel of land has been recently acquired by MIHOMES and is going to be developed. I reached out to MI HOMES and presented this opportunity to name these two [waterbodies] on this parcel to provide some historical presence to their future community. . . . The one small pond/cypress head that my late father Dr. Richard E. Wynn, DVM[,]a Veterinarian and animal lover and an avid outdoors man who loved working the land[,] actually planted these cypress trees when he was a boy from the local cypress swamp. . . . In the 1980's he provided a more substantial area to hold the water surrounding the trees. This area does not show upon Google maps but does show up on the Pasco County appraisers website. I am not sure how Google maps missed this or could add it. The proponent initially proposed the names "Dr. Richard E. Wynn, DVM Cypress Head Preserve" and "Ole Shiner Pond" for the features. BGN staff informed the proponent that a name that included "Preserve" could not be reviewed for a reservoir and that the BGN discourages full names of proponents and those that include educational titles. BGN staff also asked why the name was being proposed as "Ole Shiner Pond" rather than "Old Shiner Pond" or "Shiner Pond," the name noted in the initial proposal. When the proponent then provided the name "Richard E. Wynn, DVM Pond," BGN staff again asked why the long name, including the degree, should be considered. The proponent replied that they would like the name "R.E. Wynn, DVM Pond" to be considered and that "[t]he animal care giver is important in his legacy." R.E. Wynn, DVM Pond

proposals.case_summary: The name Sharlette Lake is proposed for a 5.2-acre lake in a residential neighborhood in Hernando County. The proponent, who owns the lake, states: Sharlette Lynn Wilkins Peters [(1964-2013)] was my sister. I wanted to name this lake after her for her love of nature, camping and fishing with children. She was a local nurse who always provided a space in her home for needy children. She often would buy bikes, clothing and supplies for needy children in the neighboring areas. She gave homeless children a place of solace in times when their own home lives were filled full of chaos and abuses. She could often be seen fishing with children at my lake and the neighboring rivers. It was not the fish she gained and caught, it was the trust and respect of needy children in the areas. [Her] funeral at 48 years old was conducted by the children who loved her. One twin girl walked about 30 miles to attend, when asked why she did not call for a ride she said she needed a good cry. She donated her entire paycheck to funeral expenses as most of our family depleted our savings trying to save Sharlette's life from cancer. This lake will exist forever in my family for the enjoyment of children, to fish, kayak, camp, and picnic on the island. Recently I watched a young girl fishing while her older brother paddled the canoe. She caught large bass, and other fish, she simply talked to each, gave them a kiss and released the fish. I see no better memorial for Sharlette than this lake representing her. proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to change the name of Heavy Liquor Pond in Floyd County, Georgia to Effluent Equalization Basin and to change the location of the name. The proposal was submitted by the Environmental Manager of International Paper's Rome Mill. The proposal reported: International Paper purchased this property in 2012. Unsure of the naming nomenclature that was previously used prior to International Paper ownership, but it is incorrect based on our wastewater treatment system. The current label "Heavy Liquor Pond" is in on a smaller pond that is part of our wastewater treatment system, southwest of the "Effluent Equalization Basin". The smaller pond should not have a label/name, but the larger pond should be labeled Effluent Equalization Basin. This proposal was the result of an Information Quality - Information Correction Request under the Information Quality Act. That request stated: We are requesting a name change for a pond at our facility which is labeled incorrectly. In the USGS database, a smaller pond in the system is labeled as the Heavy Liquor Pond which is inaccurate. This smaller pond should not have a label, but the larger pond next to it should be labeled Effluent Equalization Basin (EEB). In 1967, USGS maps first showed only the small reservoir to the west with the label "Industrial Waste Pond." The name Heavy Liquor Pond was added to GNIS in 1992 from a 1979 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) list of dams and reservoirs with coordinates that fell within the feature labeled "Industrial Waste Pond" on USGS maps. The USGS National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) applies the name Heavy Liquor Pond to the smaller feature (a reservoir in NHD) and no name to the larger feature (a Lake/Pond in NHD). GNIS contains records for many reservoirs that are used for industrial purposes. None contain "Liquor," but three (all added from versions of the USACE list of dams and reservoirs) contain "Effluent" in their names: • Final Mill Effluent Treatment Pon [sic] in • Round Hill Effluent Reservoir • Effluent Treatment Pond Number Four Until 2021, when administrative features were removed from GNIS, there were four other records that contained "Liquor Pond" that were added from versions of the USACE list of dams and reservoirs: • Heavy Liquor Pond Dam in Floyd County, Georgia • Spent Caustic Liquor Pond Dam, Spent Leaching Liquor Pond Number 3 Dam, and Spent Leaching Liquor Pond Number 4 Dam in Clark County, Nevada (located where "Tailings Ponds" were labeled on USGS maps from 1952 to 1987) Three dams contained "Effluent," two of which were associated with reservoir names noted above: • Simplot Effluent Irrigation Dam • Round Hill Effluent Dam • Effluent Treatment Pond Number Four Dam KENTUCKY

proposals.case_summary: The new name Lake Shelton is proposed for an officially unnamed 1.75-acre reservoir in Jefferson County. The reservoir is on land owned by the proponent's family. The name would commemorate Winston Laverne Shelton (1922-2019), an inventor and engineer who built his home on the property that contains the reservoir. The proponent included links to a Wikipedia article, "Winston L. Shelton," and a West Virginia Public Broadcasting obituary titled "American Inventor Winston Shelton Passes Away." Mr. Shelton was born in West Virginia and worked at General Electric between 1948 and 1968, then founded a company with his brother that was renamed Winston Industries in 1984. He is known for inventions improving home washing machines and food preparation, many of which are still used today. In the proposal, the proponent wrote: We want to name it after Winston Laverne Shelton who owned and cared and loved his property. Winston was an American inventor, and engineer, who held 76 patents. His patents had impacts relating to washing machines and long story short after enlisting he was called in to do research at Princeton. I don't have time to write it all so we attached corresponding evidence [the articles linked above]. Winston. . . was a wonderful husband a great dad and an even better grandfather! Just Google Winston Laverne Shelton, please! Winston bought the property and built his home with his own two hands. The property can never be developed and is being overseen by his eldest daughter. . . my mother. Her birthday is coming in July so I'd like to surprise her and the family. proposals.title: Change Negro Islands to Wewətanagok
proposals.submitter: Dr. Meadow Dibble
proposals.proposal_type: change name considered derogatory
proposals.proponent: James Eric Francis, Sr.; Penobscot Nation
proposals.feature_description: two islands in the Bagaduce River northwest of Lords Cove
proposals.name_history: a Penobscot word meaning "at the place where they come together, converge"
proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found State Names Authority Kentucky Geographic Names Committee Federal Agency n/a Federally Recognized Tribes All federally recognized Tribes contacted under Policy X Other • Published names: o Nego Island (The Dictionary of Maine Place-Names, 1970) o Negro Island (OCS 2000-2016; Blue Hill Heritage Trust, 2018) o Negro Islands (USGS 1902, 1904, 1905, 1941, 1943; OCS 1881-1993; Atlas of Hancock County, Maine, 1881) o N_____ Islands (History of Castine, Penobscot, and Brooksville, Maine, 1875)
proposals.case_summary: The Penobscot Nation's Director of Cultural and Historic Preservation proposed changing the name Negro Islands, a pair of islands in the Town of Castine, Hancock County to Wewətanagok. The pair of islands in the Bagaduce River is made up of Lower Negro Island, managed by the Maine Coast Heritage Trust, and Upper Negro Island, which is privately owned. Proposals to rename these islands were included on Review List 441 and Review List 450 (see below for details). The proponent wrote: The proposed name "Wewətanagok" is derived from the Penobscot language, where "wewət" translates to "together, surface to surface, point to point, end to end, confront, come together, converge." The addition of the locative ending "- anakok" signifies "at the place where they come together, converge." This name beautifully encapsulates the essence of the two islands that merge at low tide, highlighting their physical and symbolic connection. . . . While the islands are known locally, they have not been officially named in a way that reflects their unique characteristics and cultural heritage. The Penobscot language represents the rich history and connection of the Penobscot people to the land, making this name not only appropriate but significant in honoring that heritage. The islands, remnants of the western shore of the Bagaduce River, serve as a geographical marker and a cultural touchstone for the Penobscot community. . . . The feature requires a name to acknowledge its cultural and historical significance, as well as to enhance navigational clarity. Naming the islands "Wewətanagok" will provide a meaningful reference that reflects their unique identity. This name change also promotes awareness and appreciation of the Penobscot language and its relevance to the local environment. By adopting the name "Wewətanagok," we acknowledge the interconnectedness of these islands and the cultural narrative they embody, fostering a deeper appreciation for the region's natural and historical landscape. USGS maps applied the name Negro Islands between 1902 and 1943; the islands were labeled individually beginning in 1973. The collective name first appeared on Office of Coast Survey (OCS) charts in 1881. It was incorrectly entered into GNIS as Negro Island; this name appeared on OCS charts after 2000 and on USGS maps after 2011. The Maine Coastal Island Registry lists both islands. The volume History of Castine, Penobscot, and Brooksville, Maine (Wheeler, 1875) used the more pejorative form of the name without applying names to the individual islands. The author wrote in a footnote: "Is it not possible that the name of these islands is derived from the 'Negew,' over which Edward Naylor had command, in 1662? There is no satisfactory tradition to account for the name of these islands." In 1970, Phillip Rutherford repeated this supposition as fact in The Dictionary of Maine Place-Names by reporting the name as Nego Island, explaining "For the 'Negew,' ship commanded by Edward Naylor, 1662." No connection could be found between the islands and the ship, which operated primarily in the nearby Penobscot River. In July 2020, a Town of Penobscot, Hancock County resident, submitted a proposal to replace the word "negro" in the three related names with "Bagaduce" based on their location in the Bagaduce River: • Lower Negro Island to Lower Bagaduce Island • Upper Negro Island to Upper Bagaduce Island • Negro Islands to Bagaduce Islands In November 2022, the Town of Castine submitted names selected by the Town's Island Name Change Committee and voted on by Town residents: • Lower Negro Island to Emanuel Island • Upper Negro Island to Esther Island • Negro Islands to Meguntic Islands Emanuel and Esther are the names of two of the earliest known individuals of African descent recorded in Castine. Meguntic is reportedly an Abenaki word that reportedly means a smooth area of water within rougher water, or a "smooth area in choppy waters" and reflects the river at this location and the Native history of the area. Between March 2023 and March 2025, a group of interested parties began to discuss and research possible counterproposals to the names proposed by the Town of Castine. This group included, at different times: • the current owner of Upper Negro Island • the Regional Steward for the Maine Coast Heritage Trust (which manages Lower Negro Island) • James Eric Francis, Sr., the Penobscot Nation's Director of Cultural and Historic Preservation, Tribal Historian, and Chair of Penobscot Tribal Rights and Resource Protection Board • Rachel Talbot Ross, the then-Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives (now a Maine State Senator) • two staff members of Atlantic Black Box who had served on the 2022-2023 Place Justice Project of the Maine Permanent Commission on the Status of Racial, Indigenous, and Tribal Populations; they later helped lead the Place Justice Project through their roles at Atlantic Black Box • the Executive Director of the Castine Historical Society In March 2023, the current owner of Upper Negro Island emailed BGN staff: We appreciate the time spent on researching and considering these names, but even the [Island Name Change C]ommittee felt that not enough time was allotted . . . . More time was given, but the committee primarily relied on existing research and did not, as hoped, engage the vote of Black or Indigenous people in the committee's choice of recommended names. It would seem remiss to come this far without seeking the input and the blessing of those whom these island's names have most offended. Currently and seemingly serendipitously, the Permanent Commission on the Status of Racial, Indigenous and Tribal Populations in Maine, has sponsored an initiative called Place Justice which seeks to engage Wabanaki and Maine communities in examining a wide range of commemorative practices to better understand and respond to the ways in which racialized and indigenous populations are represented in or absent from the narratives inscribed on our natural and built environments. . . . The Commission is under the watch of Maine State Legislator, Rachel Talbot Ross, whose father was responsible for creating the initial legislation to address renaming offensively named places in Maine. I know this continued effort is very important to her. . . . This group is an incredibly valuable resource, and they are interested in helping with renaming considerations for Castine's Negro Islands. My family and I feel very fortunate for the opportunity to hear their input. As I would assume you agree, what feels more important than expediency is getting the names right! Spending additional time to ensure the appropriateness of names that will live into perpetuity is abundantly reasonable. Consulting with the people most offended by the current names is a must. Our hope is that you will allow more time to solidify new names for Castine's Negro Islands. We would like to pursue conversations with Place Justice's help, and either confirm support for the Town's recommendation of names, or present another set of names for your consideration by the end of September, 2023. BGN staff acknowledged that the group wished to do more research and that the BGN would not vote on the proposals until the group submitted counterproposals. BGN staff followed up in September 2023. The island owner replied: While we were not fully behind the individual names recommended by the Castine Town Survey, our primary concern is with the collective name, "Meguntic," which does not seem to be a real word, but rather an anglicized abbreviation. To come this far and not get it right seems like a missed opportunity. We very much appreciate your recent extension of time, and hope you can allow a bit more time for us. . . . Regarding Meguntic, it seems this name was introduced very late in the process, and was said to mean choppy seas or swelling seas. I was told the committee very much liked this name and quickly adopted it. As I remember, either days before or after the committee's names were presented to the town, [a] committee member. . . sent an email to the group worried that she could not find evidence of the word Meguntic. She feared it was not an actual Native American word, but a possible abbreviation for Megunticook. I also tried researching Meguntic, and found no information. The Director of Atlantic Black Box also wrote: Speaker Talbot Ross is requesting that the BGN hold off on considering the name change proposal for Upper and Lower Negro Islands in Castine. The Speaker would like more time to consult with members of Maine's multigenerational African American community not only about the islands' names but about their place in Maine's commemorative landscape. In February 2024, BGN staff followed up with the group and met virtually to discuss the status of the proposals and the BGN review process. The group planned to submit a counterproposal for Meguntic Islands with input from James Eric Francis, Sr., the Penobscot Nation's Director of Cultural and Historic Preservation and Tribal Historian. In February 2025, BGN staff contacted the group to let them know that the proposals to change the names of the individual islands would be placed on the April DNC meeting docket for a vote and asked about the status of their counterproposal. The group members were divided on whether or not the individual island name change proposals should be voted on separately from the proposed change for the official collective name. One local resident, who represents a group called Castine Friends, expressed concerns in December 2022 regarding the Town's actions and the name changes. The resident believes the change would "hide local history," adding "There is historical reference to the island being used by British Loyalists to shelter Negro Loyalists during the winter of 1783-84 when they were bound from New York City to Nova Scotia. They were on one of the last vessels to evacuate British forces and civilian Loyalists from NYC in November 1783. They were either British Army civilian workers or members of the British military unit called the Black Pioneers." His own survey showed that "most Castine residents do not want to change the name." He also cited recorded deeds with the name Negro Island dating back to 1785 and suggests a change would lead to confusion. The individual representing Castine Friends also shared a statement from an individual who owned Lower Negro Island for 50 years reporting that he was always told "the island was a dropoff point for escaped Negro slaves, who would be hidden in the cellar of the house and by stealth picked up and transported to Canada. If nothing else, long periods of customary use should be sufficient to preserve the name." Castine Town minutes reported that in August 2022, a local resident noted that the BGN had changed all occurrences of the N___ word to "Negro" in 1967 [sic] and therefore "there is nothing wrong with it." MARYLAND

The proposal states: The Harsh Family Farm is identified on Map 95 as parcels 38, 53 and 55, just South of Redhouse, MD and on both sides of US-219 was founded in 1900. proposals.other_names: • Unpublished names: None found • Published names: None found
proposals.case_summary: The new name Riggs Ridge, submitted by the Nevada State Board on Geographic Names, is proposed for an unnamed ridge located in Carson City. The approximately four-mile ridge lies on land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and trends approximately north-northwest to south-southeast. It is bounded in part by the Carson River to the west and north, and by Brunswick and Sand Canyons to the east. The Southern end of the ridge begins near the Bunker Hill Mine, just northwest of McTarnahan Hill. The proposal was supported by the Nevada State Board on Geographic Names (NSBGN) following its November 2024 meeting. The NSBGN conducted outreach to the Washoe Tribe, though no response was received. The NSBGN also sent the proposal to the Carson City Board of Supervisors, with no comment returned. The name would honor John Arthur Riggs (1946-2016), a decorated Vietnam veteran and prominent public servant in Nevada. He received numerous military awards, including the Bronze Star, two Purple Hearts, and the Combat Infantry Badge. As noted in the proposal, "he worked and helped better conditions for both the male and female inmates" of the Nevada State Prison complexes. He also taught high school level courses to incarcerated individuals and was "appointed Supervisor of Education at the Maximum Security Prison," where he later became Assistant Director. His efforts in prison education earned him widespread respect, especially among Native American inmates. According to the proposal, Riggs also contributed significantly to historical research in Nevada, notably providing much of the research for Nevada Place Names by Helen Carlson. Beyond his work in corrections and history, Riggs was deeply involved in civic life, including serving as president of the Nevada Junior Chamber of Commerce (Jaycees) and holding leadership roles in the Young Democrats of Nevada. He organized a Jaycees chapter within the prison and was named Outstanding Young Educator by the Prison Jaycees in 1974. Artifacts from his life and career have been donated to the Nevada Historical Society, further commemorating his contributions to the state. The proposed name, located near the Nevada State Prison, was chosen specifically "in coordination with its proximity to the prison in Carson City." GNIS lists two existing features in Nevada with "Riggs" in the name, Upper Riggs Spring and Lower Riggs Spring, both located approximately 190 miles southeast of the proposed ridge.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Bear Brook is proposed for an officially unnamed 0.3-mile-long tributary of Kitchen Branch in the Town of Montreat, Buncombe County. The stream was not shown on USGS maps until 2022 after the stream was included in the National Hydrography Dataset. The proponent initially submitted the name as "BearBrooke Branch," writing: The subject property and brook have been in our family for over 60 years. We often see local Black Bears casually walking through our property down to the brook, where they will drink the cool water and sometimes lay down to cool themselves in the warm summer months. My wife and I will be building a small cabin on this lot later this year, and we have named our cabin - BearBrooke Cabin. We would like to name this brook- BearBrooke Branch. BGN staff asked the proponent to address the following issues: • "Bear Brooke" rather than "BearBrooke"; the BGN has not yet approved a name in which two words are combined into one without spaces • if "Brooke" referred to or could be construed to refer to a person • if the cabin was commercial in nature The proponent replied that • "We only used 'Brooke' as it was 'different', and felt like it created a unique aspect to the stream and our cabin. There is no significance or reference to a person, living or deceased. We just thought it was unusual. We are willing to drop the 'e' if it would be easier to approve, again, as there is no significance to its use." • "Our cabin will be for personal use only and is being built as our personal retirement home. (Construction will begin in April of this year). We will not rent the cabin for any purpose." The proponent owns two parcels near the source of the stream. The stream flows through or under some other private parcels in the area, including a College of Montreat parking lot.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Lead Shot Run for a 0.25-mile-long tributary of Waynesborough Run, located in Easttown Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania. The stream flows through the Waynesborough Country Club. The stream is not recorded in the U.S. Geological Survey's National Hydrogaphy Dataset or mapped on USGS topographic maps; 3D Hydrography Program data has not yet been released. The proponent, who represents Protecting Our Streams & Environment, Inc. (POSE), initially stated: The stream is colloquially referred to as Lead Shot Run which signifies the connection to its location at the heart of the [Waynesborough Country] Club and as an homage to the lead shot during a golf tournament. . . . In the game of golf, a "lead shot" can metaphorically symbolize a decisive, well-placed stroke that positions a player or team ahead in the competition. In the context of a golf scramble, where teamwork and strategy are crucial, a "lead shot" might refer to the best shot of the group-the one that sets the pace for the rest of the play. This makes the name fitting for a stream that winds its way through the course, much like a well- placed golf shot cutting a strategic path through the landscape. Much like a well-executed shot in golf, a stream follows a natural and often unpredictable course. This is ultimately the meaning of the term "Lead Shot." When BGN staff asked for more specific evidence that "lead shot" is a golf term and about evidence in POSE documents noting that local use of the name Lead Shot Run refers to local trapshooting at the country club, the proponent confirmed the local meaning of the name. GNIS lists a Lead Run located within Columbia County, Pennsylvania approximately 80 miles from the stream.

The proponent states that the unnamed feature needs name because "[t]he northern tip of Howland Island currently lacks an official name. Naming it 'Earhart Cape' will enhance geographic recognition, historical memory, and navigation reference points for the island.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to make official the name Bennett Creek for a 1.17-mile-long spring-fed tributary of Tea Creek, located in the Monongahela National Forest in Pocahontas County. The proponent notes that the stream has been informally known as Bennett Creek for decades and states, "One of those features was always referred to as 'Bennett Creek.' When giving directions in the area, we often refer to 'Bennett Creek' as an official landmark and have written it on our personal maps and marked it by waypoint on our GPS." The name would honor Dale Bennett (1927-2016) and Don Bennett (1929-1999), brothers who grew up hunting in the area and are remembered by the proponent and others for their long- standing connection to the forest. According to the 1950 U.S. Census, both were listed as coal miners (supply man and lamp man) in Nicholas County, West Virginia. Dale Bennett served in Korea during WWII, taught school in Pocahontas and Nicholas Counties, and preached in several churches. He lived in Marlinton for many years. Don Bennett, born in Nicholas County and later a resident of Greenbrier County, was a minister and missionary who served 38 years in Brazil with Baptist Mid-Missions. The proponent, who has hunted, hiked, camped, and fished in the area for over two decades, writes, "I do not believe anyone else to have such a personal connection to this landmark in the area as us and I would like to petition for an official name to be given." The proposal also notes, "This would not only be in memory of Don and Dale Bennett who have passed on, but also their surviving children and grandchildren who still enjoy this area." Though the proponent did not know the honorees personally, he adds, "I have heard countless stories of their legacy and their love for this area in the National Forest."
