The proponent's stated interest in the name of this feature is because "[t]he State agency has already changed the offensive name internally." In response to the Name Changes Policy, the proponent gave the following reason for why the name should be changed: "Oregon Bill 3532 was passed in June, 2025 to remove all offensive or derogatory names in Oregon." Oregon House Bill 3532 (HB3532) Section 1(2) reads The executive secretary of the Oregon Geographic Names Board shall: (a) Compile a list of geographic features including, but not limited to, mountains, buttes, gulleys, gulches, rivers and creeks in Oregon that bear offensive names; and (b) Begin a process of determining new names for the geographic features. The bill defines "offensive" as "insulting and derogatory to any of Oregon's nine federally recognized Indian tribes or to any race, nationality or ethnicity." The bill states that the OGNB Executive Secretary shall submit proposals to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names recommending names that are not offensive for all geographic features on the list compiled under subsection (2)(a) of this section no later than the date that is three years following the effective date of this 2025 Act. The name was shown on USGS maps published in 1961 and 1990. The origin of the name is unknown and was likely a name found in local use at the time. The proponent reported that "[i]n 2017 the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife internally renamed the feature Raccoon Point and erected signs that identified the feature as Raccoon Point." The proponent provided a letter from Mark Nebeker, the Sauvie Island Wildlife Area Manager, to the OGNB stating that "[t]he Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, Sauvie Island Wildlife Area would like to inform you that the location name 'Coon Point' was renamed 'Raccoon Point' in February 2018." The OGNB is removing this name from their HB3532 list. GNIS does not record any features in Oregon that include "Raccoon" in their names. GNIS records 34 other features in Oregon that include "Coon" in their names as a single word; all of these are on the OGNB's HB3532 list. USGS mapping indicates that the unnamed stream flows into another unnamed tributary that ultimately joins Duck Creek. Historical plat records and a death certificate provided by the proponent indicate land ownership in the area by members of the Pamperin family. The proponent reports: W.J. Regarding the need for an official name, the proponent states: The stream is labeled as "Unnamed Tributary of Lancaster Creek" on BrownDog, the Official GIS Map of Brown County, WI. proposals.case_summary: The new name Gilbert Point is proposed for a 7,600-foot cliff in Coconino County, Arizona. The feature is located on Powell Plateau in Grand Canyon National Park. The proposal was submitted on April 16, 2026, by Stephen Pyne, with a mailing address in Queen Creek, Arizona. Regarding the need for an official name for Federal use, the proponent stated: All other points on the plateau are named - and all for prominent explorers of the region. GK Gilbert was a protégé to John Newberry of the Ives Expedition; primary geologist on the Wheeler Expedition; and member of the Powell Expedition. Gilbert and the presently unnamed point merit each other. Regarding the meaning and significance of the name: Grove Karl Gilbert (1843-1918) is one of the founders of American geology. He explored the Grand Canyon through two major expeditions, the Wheeler Survey (1871-75) and the Powell Survey (1875-79). He then served as first chief geologist of the USGS and was elected to the National Academy of Science. Regarding the appropriateness of the name: Gilbert completes the suite of celebrated explorer-geologists who first studied the Canyon and who have features on Powell Plateau named for them. He belongs with his colleagues, and the unnamed point, presently conspicuous by lacking a name, deserves one. Regarding the proponent's interest in the naming of the feature: I wrote a biography of GK Gilbert for my PhD dissertation (later published as a book) and have been to Powell Plateau numerous times when I was a member of the North Rim fire crew. The proponent provided the following biographical information regarding the honoree: Grove Karl Gilbert, born May 6, 1843, died May 1, 1918. Member of Ohio State Geological Survey (1869-70), Wheeler Survey (1871-74), Powell Survey (1875-79), UGSG (1879-1918), incl. tour as chief geologist. National Academy of Sciences memoir: https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/gilbert-grove.pdf Regarding the honoree's direct or long-term association with the feature: He had no known direct contact with the feature or Powell Plateau. But he contributed to Grand Canyon geology through the Wheeler and Powell Surveys, was a protege of JN Newberry and a close colleague of JW Powell and Clarence Dutton, all of whom have features named for them on the plateau. Regarding the honoree's contributions to the community, the proponent stated: He contributed to the geologic knowledge of the Grand Canyon; influenced Powell and Dutton in their Canyon studies; named the Colorado Plateau; identified and named both the basin-range province and the laccolith; and codified erosional processes in the region. Regarding the honoree's outstanding national or internation recognition: Gilbert became the USGS's first chief geologist (which created a Gilbert Fellowship to honor its centennial). He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences (and has the longest memoir in its series). He is the only man twice elected to the presidency of the Geological Society of America. In follow-up correspondence regarding the Wilderness Policy and the question of overriding need, the proponent wrote: Gilbert completes the suite of explorers to the Canyon. Naming the feature corrects a historical oversight, though, honestly, society has functioned without it since the 1870s. Adding his name is a cultural choice; so is not adding it. Deciding is why we have the BGN. GNIS lists five features within Arizona with "Gilbert" in their names, though none are classified as points or cliffs.

proposals.case_summary: The name Iselin Inlet is proposed for a tidal waterway located in City of Rochelle and Town of Mamaroneck, Westchester County, New York. The passage divides Echo Island from Premium Point, a peninsula projecting into the surrounding waters. The proposal was submitted on May 8, 2026, by Michael Pryor, a resident of New Rochelle, New York. Regarding the need for an official name for Federal use, the proponent stated: This inlet at Premium Point, Echo Bay, NY lacks an official name despite navigational and historical significance on Long Island Sound. An official name is needed for nautical charts, maritime coordination, emergency response, and preservation of local history. Regarding the meaning and significance of the proposed name: Iselin honors C. Oliver Iselin (1854-1932), five-time America's Cup syndicate manager who built All View Estate directly on this inlet's shore c. 1890. Echo Bay served as home anchorage for his Cup defenders Vigilant, Defender, Columbia, and Reliance. Regarding the appropriateness of the name: Iselin lived at All View Estate on this inlet for ~20 years. His Cup yachts anchored in Echo Bay. Endorsed by the New York Yacht Club, Larchmont YC, Echo Bay YC, Westchester County Historical Society, and the City Historian of New Rochelle. Regarding their interest in the naming of the feature: I am the owner of All View Estate, 116 Premium Point Road, the historic home built by C. Oliver Iselin c.1890, located directly on the eastern shore of this inlet. I am also a USCG-licensed captain who navigates these waters. Regarding the bibliographical information of the individual, the proponent stated: Charles Oliver Iselin (b. June 8, 1854 …d. January 1, 1932). Columbia University LL.B. 1874. Partner, A. Iselin & Co., Wall Street banking firm. Built All View Estate, Premium Point, c.1890. Five-time America's Cup syndicate manager, 1893…1903. Inducted America's Cup Hall of Fame, 1994. Iselin built and resided at All View Estate on the eastern shore of this inlet c.1890…1911. His America's Cup defenders „ Vigilant, Defender, Columbia, and Reliance „ anchored in Echo Bay during his tenure. The inlet provided his primary water access to Echo Bay and Long Island Sound. Iselin's stewardship of five consecutive America's Cup defenses (1893... 1903) brought international attention to New Rochelle and Long Island Sound. New Rochelle City Historian Barbara Davis and the Westchester County Historical Society confirm his profound impact on the region's waterfront heritage. Regarding the honoree's outstanding national or international recognition: Inducted into the America's Cup Hall of Fame at the Herreshoff Marine Museum in 1994. Managed the defense of America's most prestigious sporting trophy five consecutive times, working with yacht designer Nathanael Herreshoff. Recognized as one of America's greatest yachtsmen of the Gilded Age. The proponent shared six letters of support. The following quotes summarize each interest party's support. • Mamaroneck Historical Society President / Village and Town of Mamaroneck Historian o "The Iselin name is not memorialized anywhere on these waters today. The designation of this inlet as Iselin Inlet would be a fitting and lasting tribute to one of Mamaroneck's most distinguished historical figures and would ensure that his remarkable legacy is recognized in the very waters he made famous." • New Rochelle City Historian / Executive Director of the Westcherster County Historical Society o "Despite the Iselin family's role in New Rochelle's waterfront heritage, the Iseling name is not memorialized in the city, except for a small street in the far northern part of the town. The naming of this waterway would be a fitting and lasting tribute to the family, and C. Oliver Iselin, in particular. Iselin Inlet will allow for the extraordinary history of the Iselin family to be recounted, appreciated, and remembered." • New York Yacht Club Commodore on behalf of the Club o "The New York Yacht Club has no objection to the renaming of said body of water to Iselin Inlet." • Horseshoe Harbor Yacht Club Commodore on behalf of the Club o "We believe that formalizing the name 'Iselin Inlet' is a meaningful act of local stewardship. It ensures that the legacy of one of our most distinguished neighbors is permanently anchored to the geography he once called home." • Echo Bay Yacht Club Commodore on behalf of the Club's Board of Directors o "The Club holds a State Water Land Grant conveying partial ownership of the submerged lands beneath the Inlet that abuts the Proponent of the Proposal's proprietary ownership. Hence, the Club also holds both a direct proprietary as well as a historical reference to the Inlet. By recognizing the lselin name, the historical contributions of the lselin family and C. Oliver lselin in particular, to Echo Bay and New Rochelle will be forever memorialized." • Larchmont Yacht Club Secretary on behalf of the Club o "The Iselin family has a long-standing association with our club and the surrounding community. . . . [O]fficially designating this feature as 'Iselin Inlet,'. . . will preserve a physical link to a pivotal era of American maritime history and provide a clear, historically grounded reference point for the modern mariners who navigate these waters today." There are no records with "Iselin" within their names in GNIS in the state of New York.

proposals.case_summary: The name Berky Dell Brook is proposed for an unnamed tributary of Valley Run, located in Washington Township, Berks County, Pennsylvania. The proposal was submitted on April 23, 2026 by Kyle Traylor, a resident of Bally, Pennsylvania. County GIS data depicts the stream extending farther upstream than the USGS National Hydrography Dataset (NHD). Regarding the need for an official name, the proponent states: Official recognition would ideally bring greater community awareness and involvement in the stewardship efforts of this and other streams in our township. Among other distinctions, the stream was the source of water power for a rare mill recorded with the National Registry of Historic Places. Regarding the meaning of the proposed name: This geological feature runs through a dell. It was referred to as "Dell Brook" by the individual this proposal is seeking to honor. His surname was Berky, a name not common in the general population but one which has had a presence in Berks County since the early 1700s. Regarding the appropriateness of the proposed name: For Berky's love of nature, for his contributions to our community, for his strong familial and personal ties to this stream and, not least, his affection for it, as we find in his writings, the proposed name is appropriate. Regarding their interest in the naming of the feature: I have land through which this stream runs. My hope is that in naming this stream it will both honor a community naturalist and bring awareness to the importance of our area's natural resources. The proponent identified the following landowners involved in the feature location: Ben and Karah Davies, Marvin and Esther Mae Burkholder, Matthew and Kelly Boyer, Karen Wright, Betty Traylor, and Kyle Traylor. Land preservation organizations include: Berks Nature 501(c)(3) and Berks County Agricultural Land Preservation Board. The proponent provided the following biography of the honoree: Ralph W. Berky (9/21/1890-4/8/1977) poet, musician, lover of nature, follower of his faith, was a lifelong township resident. Son of a schoolteacher, he and his brothers graduated from Perkiomen School. While his brothers pursued fields in medicine and science, Ralph pursued a life close to nature, one that inspired his poetic gifts. The home where he lived most of his life stood near this stream. Generations of his family owned a farm through which this stream runs. His brother owned a farm along its north side. A road next to the stream was one he walked often during his life. Nearby, years ago, he planted the conifer trees that today mark a tract once owned by his father. Support letters accompanied the proposal submission. The Berks County Conservation District stated that naming the tributary would support watershed restoration efforts and "bring much-needed attention to the headwater tributaries" associated with ongoing streambank and habitat enhancement projects. The Berks County Agricultural Land Preservation Board stated that establishing an official name would benefit "local mapping, planning, and emergency management efforts" while supporting "the rural character of the area." Washington Township stated that formally recognizing the brook by name would help "preserve the character and identity of our community" and provide "clarity and consistency for residents, local officials, and visitors alike." Berks Nature stated that it has worked with several landowners along the stream and supports honoring Ralph Berky while continuing conservation efforts in the area. The proponent submitted additional materials outlining biographical information, poems of the honoree, their obituary, and land deeds.

proposals.case_summary: This proposal is to provide the new commemorative name Browning Brook to an unnamed approximately 1-mile-long stream that flows into Trout Creek in Tredyffrin Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania. The proposal was submitted on March 23, 2026, by Thomas Smarr, Executive Director of the Jenkins Arboretum & Gardens, on behalf of the organization. Regarding the need for an official name, the proponent stated: To identify the waterway and inform the public about a site of stormwater and streambank stabilization work underway with municipal government cooperation and assistance. People care more about things they name. Regarding the meaning and significance of the name: The stream begins just above and passes through a public arboretum-Jenkins Arboretum & Gardens. The name would honor one of two families who preserved their property as a green-space sanctuary, for public benefit. Regarding the appropriateness of the name: The stream flows through the properties of both arboretum benefactor families, who lived as next-door neighbors. The public garden is named for those who first left land in trust. The Browning name would honor the second benefactor, who added property to the first preserve. Regarding their interest in the naming of the feature: Our interest is in demonstrating good stormwater management practices and publicizing the erosion control and streambank restoration projects along the waterway. Regarding the biographical information of the individuals, the proponent stated: Edward Browning, (b. 10/21/1886-d. 10/11/1927), was a distinguished WWI veteran, whose lung injuries from gas attacks prevented him from living past 40 yrs. Louisa Browning, (b. 4/2/1897-d. 10/22/1973), raised their 4 children. She donated her valuable Devon, PA, property to be part of a public garden. Living along the stream, Ed. & Louisa Browning had a wildlife pond for their children. Edward was a founding Boy Scout leader and his troop met at his household. Despite having heirs, Louisa wanted her land preserved as green space, adding to a public garden trust. Louisa Browning's donated parcels doubled the area preserved for the arboretum, along with an architecturally significant house. Her land gave the garden a unique naturally-wooded viewshed across the stream and roadway. Edward Browning was an early WWI volunteer. First attached to the French Army and then joining 1st Engineers, 1st American Div. Participated in major engagements of Cantigny, St.-Mihiel, Montdidier-Noyon, Soissons, and Meuse- Argonne. He was gassed twice and received a distinguished conduct citation at St. Mihiel. The proponent identified approximately 25 private landowners, two non-profit religious institutions, a historic Scout camp, and an electric utility right-of-way along the stream. The proponent provided several letters of support. The Tredyffrin Environmental Advisory Council wrote that "Naming the stream will help our efforts to preserve and protect the township's watershed." The Chairperson of the Trout Creek Watershed Residents Association wrote, "We feel this is a fitting tribute to the Browning Family, who donated this property to the Arboretum." The Trustee and President of Devon 50, Inc. wrote that the name would "honor [Mr. Browning's] service in World War I, in founding Troop Devon 50 and to our community." The president of Jenkins Arboretum & Gardens wrote that the name would strengthen "community interest in that waterway" and honor "a family that thought ahead to preserve our green space." The Chester County Water Resources Authority wrote: We agree with the Tredyffrin Township Historical Commission that the name will help to preserve and protect a headwater of Trout Creek, a state designated Warm Water Fishes and Migratory Fishes stream. The health of smaller streams, such as the one selected, is essential to the health of their downstream waterways. Moreover, we believe that named streams, which have been designated as Warm Water Fishes and Migratory Fishes, are more likely to receive recognition, public support, and protection than unnamed streams. We also feel that stream naming is a worthwhile effort to better educate the public and achieve our County-wide water resource goals.

proposals.case_summary: The new name Paemasing Creek is proposed for an officially unnamed stream in the Borough of East Stroudsburg in Monroe County. The 0.5-mile-long stream flows into Brodhead Creek. The proposal was submitted on March 3, 2026 by Kelly Lewis, the East Stroudsburg Borough Manager. The proposal would apply an official name to a stream sometimes locally called "Little Sambo Creek." In 2011, GNIS staff added the name for this stream based on a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) report using the name. In 2022, DNC and GNIS staff determined that this was an error; information from the Brodhead Watershed Association showed that the name was locally used for a tributary of Sambo Creek. GNIS staff corrected the location of Little Sambo Creek. As a result, the stream in question is officially unnamed, although the USGS National Hydrography Dataset and 3D Hydrography Program continue to use the incorrect name Little Sambo Creek. Local sources continue to use the name Little Sambo Creek for this stream. The Borough had previously submitted a proposal to apply the new name Johanna Boston Creek to this officially unnamed stream (Quarterly Review List 458); that proposal is now withdrawn. The Borough submitted a proposal to change the name of the section of Sambo Creek only within the Borough of East Stroudsburg, but this proposal cannot be considered because of the BGN-DNC's Principle 5, "One Name for One Geographic Feature"; proposals must apply to entire features, not sections of features bounded by property lines or municipal boundaries. The name Sambo Creek has been shown on USGS maps since at least 1944. Sambo Creek Lower Reservoir is located on Sambo Creek and was added to GNIS in 1990 from a USACE list of dams and reservoirs). The proponent stated that the name should be changed because: [t]he Borough of East Stroudsburg is submitting this proposal to align Federal geographic naming with community values and to remove terminology widely regarded as derogatory. This was also the Borough's stated interest in the name of the feature. The proponent originally stated that: "Paemasing". . . reflects the Indigenous heritage of the region. The name acknowledges the original stewards of the land within the Brodhead watershed. Staff asked for more information about Paemasing as a commemorative name. The proponent provided the following responses about Paemasing and his association with the feature or region: Paemasing, a Mahican Native American living in the Smithfield area, sheltered and aided Johanna Boston after she collapsed from hypothermia during a severe winter storm. His assistance preserved her life and established a documented local historical connection between Paemasing and the East Stroudsburg area. Paemasing is recognized in local history as one of the last Native American leaders living in the Smithfield Township area that later became the Borough of East Stroudsburg. His name represents the Indigenous people who inhabited and stewarded the region before European settlement. Paemasing lived in the vicinity of the stream and the surrounding Smithfield area. His long-term association with the landscape predates the establishment of East Stroudsburg, making his name directly connected to the area's Indigenous history and cultural heritage. Paemasing's recorded aid to Johanna Boston and his association with the Indigenous community of the Smithfield area provide an opportunity to recognize the Native American history of the region. Renaming the stream honors one of the area's last known Native American leaders. The proponent stared that "[v]arious private landowners and municipal entities have been alerted by multiple surveys, emails, public notices, and public meetings." The proponent addressed the Derogatory and Offensive Names Policy (which does not apply to this proposal because it is a new name for an official unnamed feature, not a name change) by providing the reason the current name is considered derogatory or offensive and how the proposed name relates to the current official name: The term "Sambo" is historically recognized as a racially derogatory term used to demean African Americans. Continued official use is inconsistent with contemporary standards of respect. The proposed name replaces the existing name in its entirety to eliminate derogatory terminology while maintaining recognition of the stream as a geographic feature. A 2012 paper presented to the Monroe County Historical Society titled "Johanna, the Slave Who Risked Her Life for Freedom" (currently posted on the Smithfield Township website) includes some details about Paemasing including how he rescued Johanna Boston while she was suffering hypothermia during her escape from Solomon Jennings, and brought her to Judge Daniel Brodhead who purchased her freedom with help from the local Moravian community. Brodhead Creek is named for Judge Brodhead and the home where he sheltered her is near the stream.

proposals.case_summary: The name Wenner Run is proposed for an unnamed tributary of Buffalo Creek located in Kelly Township, Union County, Pennsylvania. The proposal was submitted on March 17, 2026 by Elizabeth "Betsy" Quant a resident of Lewisburg, Pennsylvania. Regarding the need for an official name for Federal use, the proponent stated: Many small headwater streams to Buffalo Creek, which is within the Chesapeake Bay Watershed, are all labeled as "unnamed tributary" (UNT). Officially naming this stream as Wenner Run allows outreach and implementation of water quality improvement projects to be better specified and focused. Regarding the meaning and significance of the proposed name: This unnamed tributary begins at a spring on a farm formerly owned by the Wenner family (since the 1940's). It then runs for about a third of its length along a township road called Wenner Road. Regarding the appropriateness of the name The name Wenner Run is appropriate because of its origin on the former Wenner Farm and its initial course near Wenner Road Regarding local use of the proposed name My family and close neighbors have called this stream Wenner Run for 5 decades. The name is proposed to commemorate members of the Wenner family, whom the proponent describes as longtime residents of the Kelly Point area near the stream's headwaters. The proponent states that Sheldon Wenner (b. 1900-1970) and Marie Wenner (1903-1997) moved to the area by 1944 and raised their family on a farm near the stream. The proponent describes David Wenner (b. 1932-2021) as "the unofficial mayor of Kelly Point," stating that he "made sure that all the neighbors got together every year or two and kept all the communication lines open." The proponent further states that David Wenner assisted neighboring families in learning "how to make hay, raise livestock, plant trees for windbreaks, etc." and helped foster relationships within the rural community. Regarding Donald Wenner (1926-2009), the proponent states that he was "community- minded" and served as chair of the Kelly Township Planning Commission. The proponent further notes that the "Wenner place" remained associated with the family until 2010 and that members of the community remembered Don and Arlene Wenner as welcoming neighbors and mentors. The proponent identified approximately 11 landowners along the stream, including private citizens, two trust-land easements, and an LLC. Regarding landowner awareness of the proposal: On Feb. 10, 2026, I mailed each of the landowners a letter telling them of my intent to submit this proposal and asking each of them to let me know if they agreed or disagreed with my idea of naming Wenner Run. As of March 17, I have received 9 "agree" and 0 "disagree" answers from the 11 adjoining landowners. The letter is its own separate attachment to this proposal. Regarding the proponent's interest in the name: For this stream to be better discussed and respected, it needs a name. When living here, the Wenners were a positive part of the local community for many decades. The stream's origin on the former Wenner Farm along Wenner Road makes Wenner Run an appropriate name. In a letter of support, the Union County Conservation District stated: There are many small headwater streams within the Buffalo Creek Watershed that are labeled the exact same way ["unnamed tributary" or UNT], and. . .it makes it difficult to point out where exactly [restoration] work is being implemented. [An official name] can specify and focus where outreach and project implementation should occur to improve water quality. Many conservation organizations are targeting small tributary streams to do outreach and project implementation in what is considered to be a "delisting catchment." That typically requires a stream to have a name, so developing more named tributaries will lead to more successful watershed restoration. Also, with the historical information of the Wenner family once owning a farm along this stream channel and with Wenner Road running parallel, this is a very fitting name. The Merrill W. Lynn Land and Waterways Conservancy wrote: Wenner Run is already locally recognized, and can create confusion for newcomers or outside contractors looking for a location that is not officially recognized on available map platforms. Establishing the stream's official name will serve to more precisely identify the locations of our work in that part of the watershed. GNIS lists one record with "Wenner" in its name: Wenner Swamp, approximately 40 miles to the east-northeast.

proposals.case_summary: The name Heron Lake is proposed for an approximately 14.3-acre reservoir in the City of Ellensburg, Kittitas County, Washington. The proposal was submitted on May 27, 2026, by Martina Preston, with a mailing address in Ellensburg, Washington. Regarding the need for an official name, the proponent stated: This waterbody runs parallel to a primary road of commerce and transportation in Ellensburg, WA. A number of businesses border the waterbody, and people both catch-and-release fish as well as sunbathe, skip rocks, and interact with the water on a daily basis. Regarding the meaning and significance of the name: The great blue heron is often used as a symbol of environmental stewardship, and the WDFW classifies it as a priority species. Some also see the heron as a sign of resilience and strength. WA has a revered population of great blue herons, and the bird is a symbol in many local and native legends. Regarding the appropriateness of the name: For years now, a great blue heron has been nesting on the side of the bank opposite to the businesses, creating a tranquil scene for both clients and employees who look out the water-facing windows on a daily basis. The heron fishes along the stretch of the lake, remaining undisturbed and sacred Regarding their interest in the naming of the feature: We work at one of the businesses bordering the waterbody and would love to see it officially recognized. The proposal was originally submitted as Lake Doom, a name the proponent indicated had personal literary meaning. In follow-up correspondence, staff requested clarification regarding the significance of the name to the wider community. The proponent subsequently submitted a revised proposal for Heron Lake "after talking it over with a few of the other businesses who border the waterbody." GNIS lists four records within Washington with "Heron" in its name; "Heron Lake," 62 miles to the east, "Heron Pond", 152 miles to the northwest, "Blue Heron Lake", 32 miles to the northeast, and "Blue Heron Beach" 173 miles to the northwest.
